paragraphs: Optimal Brain Surgeon is a second-order method for pruning neural networks. This paper extends it to general error measures and explores an implementation that reduces computation and storage through a dominant-eigenspace decomposition. The aim is to broaden the method’s applicability while making its second-order calculations more manageable.

Simulations on nonlinear, noisy classification problems show improved generalization and favorable performance compared with Optimal Brain Damage. The authors find that the retraining steps required by Optimal Brain Damage can lead to worse generalization. They interpret this as potentially introducing noise back into the system, linking the pruning outcome to what happens after parameters are removed.

The paper also considers networks whose training was stopped at the minimum validation error. Optimal Brain Surgeon further reduced test error in that setting, while Optimal Brain Damage did not. This indicates that pruning can provide an additional benefit after validation-based stopping. The results also support the approximation used by Optimal Brain Surgeon and the concern that retraining a heavily pruned network may harm performance.
summary.tldr: Extensions to Optimal Brain Surgeon improve its practicality and show generalization benefits beyond validation-based stopping in reported simulations.

title: Optimal Brain Surgeon: Extensions and performance comparisons

The task assigned to the radial basis function networks is the estimation of emission probabilities associated to Markov states. The model is contex(cid:173) tual because the estimation of emission probabilities takes into account the left context of the current image segment as represented by its pred(cid:173) ecessor in the sequence. The new system does not outperform the previ(cid:173) ous system without context but acts differently.

paragraphs: This paper presents an offline handwritten word recognizer that combines radial basis function networks with hidden Markov models. The two components have distinct roles. The neural networks estimate emission probabilities associated with the Markov states, supplying probabilities that connect image evidence to the states used by the sequence model.

The proposed extension makes these estimates contextual. When processing the current image segment, the network also uses left context represented by the preceding segment in the sequence. The probability assigned to the current visual evidence can therefore depend on what came immediately before it. This changes the information used at the emission-estimation stage of recognition.

The reported result is that the contextual system does not outperform the earlier system without context, although it behaves differently. That distinction is central to interpreting the contribution: including neighboring information changes the recognizer, but the comparison does not establish an improvement in overall performance. The paper explores a specific way to incorporate context within a hybrid neural and probabilistic sequence architecture.
summary.tldr: Adding preceding-segment context changes a hybrid handwriting recognizer's behavior but does not improve on its context-free predecessor.

title: Handwritten Word Recognition using Contextual Hybrid Radial Basis Function Network/Hidden Markov Models

It was shown to be equivalent to Lasso (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator), in the sense that both procedures produce the same estimate. Lasso can thus be viewed as a particular quadratic penalizer. From this observation, we derive a fixed point algorithm to compute the Lasso solution. The analogy provides also a new hyper-parameter for tun(cid:173) ing effectively the model complexity. We finally present a series ofpossi(cid:173) ble extensions oflasso performing sparse regression in kernel smoothing, additive modeling and neural net training.

The analogy provides also a new hyper-parameter for tun(cid:173) ing effectively the model complexity. We finally present a series ofpossi(cid:173) ble extensions oflasso performing sparse regression in kernel smoothing, additive modeling and neural net training.

paragraphs: This paper develops consequences of an equivalence between Adaptive Ridge regression and Lasso. Adaptive Ridge balances a separate quadratic penalty on each model parameter. The equivalence is stated at the level of the resulting estimate: the two procedures produce the same estimate, allowing Lasso to be viewed through a particular adaptive quadratic-penalty formulation.

The authors use that connection to derive a fixed-point algorithm for computing the Lasso solution. The alternative formulation therefore has a practical role in designing a solver. The analogy also supplies a new hyperparameter for controlling model complexity, offering another way to tune the balance between fitting the data and restricting the model.

The paper then presents possible extensions of Lasso-style sparse regression to kernel smoothing, additive modeling, and neural-network training. These extensions are proposed possibilities, while the fixed-point algorithm follows from the stated equivalence. The broader significance is that a connection between two penalty formulations can generate both a computational method and new directions for applying sparse estimation.
summary.tldr: The equivalence of Adaptive Ridge and Lasso yields a fixed-point solver, a complexity-control hyperparameter, and possible sparse-modeling extensions.

title: Outcomes of the Equivalence of Adaptive Ridge with Least Absolute Shrinkage

abstract: We study a population decoding paradigm in which the maximum likeli(cid:173) hood inference is based on an unfaithful decoding model (UMLI). This is usually the case for neural population decoding because the encoding process of the brain is not exactly known, or because a simplified de(cid:173) coding model is preferred for saving computational cost. We consider an unfaithful decoding model which neglects the pair-wise correlation between neuronal activities, and prove that UMLI is asymptotically effi(cid:173) cient when the neuronal correlation is uniform or of limited-range. The performance of UMLI is compared with that of the maximum likelihood inference based on a faithful model and that of the center of mass de(cid:173) coding method. It turns out that UMLI has advantages of decreasing the computational complexity remarkablely and maintaining a high-level decoding accuracy at the same time. The effect of correlation on the decoding accuracy is also discussed.

It turns out that UMLI has advantages of decreasing the computational complexity remarkablely and maintaining a high-level decoding accuracy at the same time. The effect of correlation on the decoding accuracy is also discussed.

paragraphs: Decoding a neural population requires inferring information from its joint activity, often without knowing the brain's true encoding process. The paper studies maximum-likelihood decoding with an inaccurate or deliberately simplified model. Its chosen simplification ignores pairwise correlations between neurons, reducing the statistical dependencies that the decoder must represent.

The authors prove asymptotic efficiency when neuronal correlations are uniform or limited in range. This is a conditional result about the specified correlation structures and an asymptotic regime. It shows that ignoring correlations can still preserve a strong statistical property under those conditions, despite the mismatch between the decoding model and the encoding process.

The work compares this decoder with maximum-likelihood inference using a faithful model and with center-of-mass decoding. The reported outcome is markedly reduced computational complexity alongside high decoding accuracy. The authors also discuss how correlation affects accuracy. Together, these results explain why a simplified population model can be useful: some representational inaccuracies can coexist with effective inference under the conditions studied.
summary.tldr: A decoder that ignores pairwise neural correlations can remain asymptotically efficient under specified correlation structures while reducing computational complexity.

title: Population Decoding Based on an Unfaithful Model

abstract: The principle of maximizing mutual information is applied to learning overcomplete and recurrent representations. The underlying model con(cid:173) sists of a network of input units driving a larger number of output units with recurrent interactions. In the limit of zero noise, the network is de(cid:173) terministic and the mutual information can be related to the entropy of the output units. Maximizing this entropy with respect to both the feed(cid:173) forward connections as well as the recurrent interactions results in simple learning rules for both sets of parameters. The conventional independent components (ICA) learning algorithm can be recovered as a special case where there is an equal number of output units and no recurrent con(cid:173) nections. The application of these new learning rules is illustrated on a simple two-dimensional input example.

paragraphs: The paper applies mutual-information maximization to representations with more output units than input units and with recurrent interactions among outputs. Such a network must learn both how inputs drive the representation and how output units influence one another. The authors use one information-based objective to address both sets of connections.

In the zero-noise limit, the network becomes deterministic, allowing mutual information to be related to the entropy of the output units. Maximizing that entropy with respect to feedforward and recurrent connections produces simple learning rules for each. The zero-noise setting is therefore an explicit condition supporting the derivation described in the abstract.

The formulation also recovers the conventional independent component analysis learning algorithm as a special case: equal numbers of input and output units, with recurrent connections absent. This connects the new rules to an established representation-learning approach. A simple two-dimensional input example illustrates their application, demonstrating the construction on a small case while establishing the relationship between information maximization, overcomplete representations, and recurrence.
summary.tldr: Information maximization yields learning rules for overcomplete recurrent networks and recovers conventional ICA as a special case.

title: An Information Maximization Approach to Overcomplete and Recurrent Representations

abstract: We describe a probabilistic approach to the task of placing objects, de- scribed by high-dimensional vectors or by pairwise dissimilarities, in a low-dimensional space in a way that preserves neighbor identities. A Gaussian is centered on each object in the high-dimensional space and the densities under this Gaussian (or the given dissimilarities) are used to deﬁne a probability distribution over all the potential neighbors of the object. The aim of the embedding is to approximate this distribu- tion as well as possible when the same operation is performed on the low-dimensional “images” of the objects. A natural cost function is a sum of Kullback-Leibler divergences, one per object, which leads to a simple gradient for adjusting the positions of the low-dimensional im- ages. Unlike other dimensionality reduction methods, this probabilistic framework makes it easy to represent each object by a mixture of widely separated low-dimensional images. This allows ambiguous objects, like the document count vector for the word “bank”, to have versions close to the images of both “river” and “ﬁnance” without forcing the images of outdoor concepts to be located close to those of corporate concepts.

Unlike other dimensionality reduction methods, this probabilistic framework makes it easy to represent each object by a mixture of widely separated low-dimensional images. This allows ambiguous objects, like the document count vector for the word “bank”, to have versions close to the images of both “river” and “ﬁnance” without forcing the images of outdoor concepts to be located close to those of corporate concepts.

paragraphs: Stochastic Neighbor Embedding places objects in a low-dimensional space while trying to preserve who their neighbors are. It accepts either high-dimensional vectors or pairwise dissimilarities. Each object's neighborhood is expressed as a probability distribution, using Gaussian densities for vector inputs or the supplied dissimilarities.

The method constructs corresponding neighbor probabilities in the lower-dimensional representation and tries to make them match the original distributions. Its objective sums a Kullback-Leibler divergence for each object, yielding a simple gradient for adjusting the embedded positions. The representation is therefore optimized around probabilistic neighborhood agreement.

The same framework allows an object to have several widely separated representations. This is useful for ambiguous objects: a word such as bank can appear near both river-related and finance-related concepts. Those separate representations need not pull the two surrounding groups together. The contribution thus includes both a probabilistic neighborhood-preserving embedding and a way to express ambiguity without requiring one location to serve every meaning.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Neighbor Embedding preserves probabilistic neighborhoods and allows ambiguous objects to occupy multiple low-dimensional locations.

title: Stochastic Neighbor Embedding

abstract: We provide a method for mass meta-analysis in a neuroinformatics database containing stereotaxic Talairach coordinates from neuroimaging experiments. Database labels are used to group the individual experiments, e.g., according to cognitive function, and the consistent pattern of the experiments within the groups are determined. The method voxelizes each group of experiments via a kernel density estimation, forming probability density volumes. The values in the probability density volumes are compared to null-hypothesis distributions generated by resamplings from the entire unlabeled set of experiments, and the distances to the nullhypotheses are used to sort the voxels across groups of experiments. This allows for mass meta-analysis, with the construction of a list with the most prominent associations between brain areas and group labels. Furthermore, the method can be used for functional labeling of voxels.

The method voxelizes each group of experiments via a kernel density estimation, forming probability density volumes. The values in the probability density volumes are compared to null-hypothesis distributions generated by resamplings from the entire unlabeled set of experiments, and the distances to the nullhypotheses are used to sort the voxels across groups of experiments. This allows for mass meta-analysis, with the construction of a list with the most prominent associations between brain areas and group labels. Furthermore, the method can be used for functional labeling of voxels.

paragraphs: The paper presents a method for combining evidence across neuroimaging experiments stored as Talairach coordinates. Database labels divide experiments into groups, such as studies of a particular cognitive function. The objective is to identify consistent spatial patterns within those groups and connect them to the labels used to define them.

For each group, kernel density estimation converts the reported coordinates into a probability-density volume over brain voxels. The method then compares values in these volumes with null distributions created by resampling from all experiments without using their labels. This supplies a reference based on the overall database against which group-specific patterns can be assessed.

Distances from those null distributions are used to rank voxels across experiment groups. The resulting list highlights prominent associations between brain locations and group labels, enabling meta-analysis across many categories at once. The method can also assign functional labels to voxels. Its output expresses associations supported by the grouped coordinate evidence.
summary.tldr: Density estimation and resampled null distributions identify prominent associations between brain locations and neuroimaging experiment labels.

title: Mass Meta-analysis in Talairach Space

abstract: We establish a mistake bound for an ensemble method for classification based on maximizing the entropy of voting weights subject to margin constraints. The bound is the same as a general bound proved for the Weighted Majority Algorithm, and similar to bounds for other variants of Winnow. We prove a more refined bound that leads to a nearly opti- mal algorithm for learning disjunctions, again, based on the maximum entropy principle. We describe a simplification of the on-line maximum entropy method in which, after each iteration, the margin constraints are replaced with a single linear inequality. The simplified algorithm, which takes a similar form to Winnow, achieves the same mistake bounds.
originalAbstract: We establish a mistake bound for an ensemble method for classification based on maximizing the entropy of voting weights subject to margin constraints. The bound is the same as a general bound proved for the Weighted Majority Algorithm, and similar to bounds for other variants of Winnow. We prove a more refined bound that leads to a nearly opti- mal algorithm for learning disjunctions, again, based on the maximum entropy principle. We describe a simplification of the on-line maximum entropy method in which, after each iteration, the margin constraints are replaced with a single linear inequality. The simplified algorithm, which takes a similar form to Winnow, achieves the same mistake bounds.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes an ensemble classifier that chooses voting weights by maximizing their entropy subject to margin constraints. The constraints require the votes to support classification decisions with a specified margin, while the entropy objective governs how weights are distributed. The central question is how many mistakes this learning principle can incur.

The authors establish a mistake bound matching a general bound for Weighted Majority and resembling bounds for variants of Winnow. A more refined analysis leads to a nearly optimal algorithm for learning disjunctions. These results connect the maximum-entropy formulation to established online-learning guarantees and show that the principle can support strong theoretical performance.

The paper also simplifies the online procedure by replacing its margin constraints with one linear inequality after each iteration. The resulting update resembles Winnow and retains the same mistake bounds. This is significant because the simplified constraint representation preserves the stated guarantees, giving a more streamlined algorithm without weakening the particular bounds proved in the paper.
summary.tldr: Maximum-entropy ensemble learning achieves established mistake bounds, and a simplified Winnow-like version preserves those guarantees.

title: Mistake Bounds for Maximum Entropy Discrimination

abstract: Given $n$ noisy samples with $p$ dimensions, where $n \ll p$, we show that the multi-stage thresholding procedures can accurately estimate a sparse vector $\beta \in \R^p$ in a linear model, under the restricted eigenvalue conditions (Bickel-Ritov-Tsybakov 09). Thus our conditions for model selection consistency are considerably weaker than what has been achieved in previous works. More importantly, this method allows very significant values of $s$, which is the number of non-zero elements in the true parameter $\beta$. For example, it works for cases where the ordinary Lasso would have failed. Finally, we show that if $X$ obeys a uniform uncertainty principle and if the true parameter is sufficiently sparse, the Gauss-Dantzig selector (Cand\{e}s-Tao 07) achieves the $\ell_2$ loss within a logarithmic factor of the ideal mean square error one would achieve with an oracle which would supply perfect information about which coordinates are non-zero and which are above the noise level, while selecting a sufficiently sparse model.

Thus our conditions for model selection consistency are considerably weaker than what has been achieved in previous works. More importantly, this method allows very significant values of $s$, which is the number of non-zero elements in the true parameter $\beta$. For example, it works for cases where the ordinary Lasso would have failed. Finally, we show that if $X$ obeys a uniform uncertainty principle and if the true parameter is sufficiently sparse, the Gauss-Dantzig selector (Cand\{e}s-Tao 07) achieves the $\ell_2$ loss within a logarithmic factor of the ideal mean square error one would achieve with an oracle which would supply perfect information about which coordinates are non-zero and which are above the noise level, while selecting a sufficiently sparse model.

paragraphs: The paper studies sparse linear estimation when the number of variables greatly exceeds the number of noisy observations. Its main result shows that multistage thresholding can accurately estimate the sparse parameter vector under restricted eigenvalue conditions. These conditions support model-selection consistency under weaker requirements than previous results.

The analysis also permits comparatively substantial numbers of nonzero parameters. In particular, the authors identify settings where the method works although ordinary Lasso would fail. This makes the contribution about both accurate estimation and the range of sparse problems for which the theory supports successful variable selection.

A further result concerns the Gauss-Dantzig selector. If the design matrix satisfies a uniform uncertainty principle and the true parameter is sufficiently sparse, its squared-error performance is within a logarithmic factor of an ideal oracle benchmark while selecting a sufficiently sparse model. That oracle knows which coordinates are nonzero and which exceed the noise level. The guarantee therefore measures how closely the method approaches an informed reference under explicit assumptions.
summary.tldr: Multistage thresholding achieves sparse estimation under restricted eigenvalue conditions, with a separate conditional near-oracle guarantee for the Gauss-Dantzig selector.

title: Thresholding Procedures for High Dimensional Variable Selection and Statistical Estimation

abstract: Network models are widely used to capture interactions among component of complex systems, such as social and biological. To understand their behavior, it is often necessary to analyze functionally related components of the system, corresponding to subsystems. Therefore, the analysis of subnetworks may provide additional insight into the behavior of the system, not evident from individual components. We propose a novel approach for incorporating available network information into the analysis of arbitrary subnetworks. The proposed method offers an efficient dimension reduction strategy using Laplacian eigenmaps with Neumann boundary conditions, and provides a flexible inference framework for analysis of subnetworks, based on a group-penalized principal component regression model on graphs. Asymptotic properties of the proposed inference method, as well as the choice of the tuning parameter for control of the false positive rate are discussed in high dimensional settings. The performance of the proposed methodology is illustrated using simulated and real data examples from biology.

paragraphs: The paper focuses on analyzing groups of related components within a network. In biological or social systems, a subnetwork may capture behavior that is difficult to understand from individual components alone. The authors propose a method that incorporates available network structure into the analysis of arbitrary subnetworks.

Their approach combines dimension reduction with statistical inference. It uses Laplacian eigenmaps with Neumann boundary conditions to obtain a reduced representation, then applies a group-penalized principal component regression model on graphs. The method brings information about network organization into both the representation of the data and the analysis of component groups.

The authors discuss asymptotic properties of the inference procedure in high-dimensional settings, together with choosing a tuning parameter to control the false positive rate. Simulated and real biological examples illustrate performance. The contribution is a framework for studying subnetworks as meaningful units while using dimension reduction to make their analysis more manageable and regularization to structure the resulting inference.
summary.tldr: The method combines graph-based dimension reduction and group-penalized regression to support statistical analysis of subnetworks.

title: Penalized Principal Component Regression on Graphs for Analysis of Subnetworks

abstract: Topic models have the potential to improve search and browsing by extracting useful semantic themes from web pages and other text documents. When learned topics are coherent and interpretable, they can be valuable for faceted browsing, results set diversity analysis, and document retrieval. However, when dealing with small collections or noisy text (e.g. web search result snippets or blog posts), learned topics can be less coherent, less interpretable, and less useful. To overcome this, we propose two methods to regularize the learning of topic models. Our regularizers work by creating a structured prior over words that reflect broad patterns in the external data. Using thirteen datasets we show that both regularizers improve topic coherence and interpretability while learning a faithful representation of the collection of interest. Overall, this work makes topic models more useful across a broader range of text data.

paragraphs: Topic models seek recurring semantic themes in text, potentially helping people search, browse, and understand document collections. Their usefulness depends on whether the resulting topics make sense to readers. Small collections and noisy text, including search snippets and blog posts, can produce themes that are difficult to interpret and consequently less useful for these applications.

The paper proposes two ways to regularize topic-model learning using external data. Both create a structured prior over words that reflects broader patterns found outside the target collection. This prior guides learning toward more coherent topics while the model still learns from the particular documents it is meant to represent.

Across thirteen datasets, both regularizers improve topic coherence and interpretability while preserving a faithful representation of the collection of interest. That combination matters because readable topics must also describe the actual documents to support useful browsing or retrieval. The findings show that external patterns can guide topic learning without replacing the collection-specific information, broadening the range of text for which topic models can be useful.
summary.tldr: Two regularizers use external word patterns to make learned topics more coherent while preserving their fit to the target collection.

title: Improving Topic Coherence with Regularized Topic Models

abstract: We present explicit classes of probability distributions that can be learned by Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) depending on the number of units that they contain, and which are representative for the expressive power of the model. We use this to show that the maximal Kullback-Leibler divergence to the RBM model with n visible and m hidden units is bounded from above by (n-1)-log(m+1). In this way we can specify the number of hidden units that guarantees a sufficiently rich model containing different classes of distributions and respecting a given error tolerance.
originalAbstract: We present explicit classes of probability distributions that can be learned by Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) depending on the number of units that they contain, and which are representative for the expressive power of the model. We use this to show that the maximal Kullback-Leibler divergence to the RBM model with n visible and m hidden units is bounded from above by (n-1)-log(m+1). In this way we can specify the number of hidden units that guarantees a sufficiently rich model containing different classes of distributions and respecting a given error tolerance.

paragraphs: The paper asks how the number of units in a restricted Boltzmann machine determines the probability distributions it can represent. The authors identify explicit distribution classes available to models of different sizes. These classes make the model's expressive power concrete by connecting its architecture to the kinds of distributions it can accommodate.

Using that characterization, the authors derive an upper bound on the worst-case Kullback-Leibler divergence to an RBM with n visible units and m hidden units. The stated bound is (n−1)−log(m+1). This expresses an approximation guarantee in terms of architecture size, relating the number of hidden units to a measure of distributional mismatch.

The result allows the authors to specify hidden-unit counts sufficient for a model to contain particular distribution classes while meeting a chosen error tolerance. Its significance is a principled link between model capacity and approximation requirements. A sufficient size guarantee establishes that the architecture is rich enough for the stated purpose; it does not establish that every smaller architecture must fail.
summary.tldr: Explicit representable distribution classes and a worst-case KL bound connect RBM hidden-unit counts to sufficient approximation capacity.

title: Expressive Power and Approximation Errors of Restricted Boltzmann Machines

abstract: We develop a new algorithm to cluster sparse unweighted graphs -- i.e. partition the nodes into disjoint clusters so that there is higher density within clusters, and low across clusters. By sparsity we mean the setting where both the in-cluster and across cluster edge densities are very small, possibly vanishing in the size of the graph. Sparsity makes the problem noisier, and hence more difficult to solve. Any clustering involves a tradeoff between minimizing two kinds of errors: missing edges within clusters and present edges across clusters. Our insight is that in the sparse case, these must be {\em penalized differently}. We analyze our algorithm's performance on the natural, classical and widely studied ``planted partition'' model (also called the stochastic block model); we show that our algorithm can cluster sparser graphs, and with smaller clusters, than all previous methods. This is seen empirically as well.
originalAbstract: We develop a new algorithm to cluster sparse unweighted graphs -- i.e. partition the nodes into disjoint clusters so that there is higher density within clusters, and low across clusters. By sparsity we mean the setting where both the in-cluster and across cluster edge densities are very small, possibly vanishing in the size of the graph. Sparsity makes the problem noisier, and hence more difficult to solve. Any clustering involves a tradeoff between minimizing two kinds of errors: missing edges within clusters and present edges across clusters. Our insight is that in the sparse case, these must be {\em penalized differently}. We analyze our algorithm's performance on the natural, classical and widely studied ``planted partition'' model (also called the stochastic block model); we show that our algorithm can cluster sparser graphs, and with smaller clusters, than all previous methods. This is seen empirically as well.

paragraphs: The paper develops an algorithm for dividing a sparse, unweighted graph into groups with relatively dense internal connections and few connections between groups. Here, even connections within a group can be very rare, and their density may shrink as the graph grows. This makes genuine group structure harder to distinguish from noise.

The central insight concerns two kinds of disagreement with a proposed grouping: absent edges inside a group and present edges between groups. A clustering method must balance these errors. The authors argue that sparse graphs require different penalties for the two, making the treatment of missing connections a central design choice.

They analyze the algorithm under the planted partition model, also known as the stochastic block model. In that setting, they show recovery capabilities for sparser graphs and smaller clusters than previous methods. Experiments display the same advantage. The theoretical comparison is tied to this model, while the empirical results support the usefulness of the penalty choice.
summary.tldr: Differently penalizing missing internal edges and existing cross-cluster edges improves clustering of sparse graphs under the planted partition model.

title: Clustering Sparse Graphs

abstract: Imitation Learning has been shown to be successful in solving many challenging real-world problems. Some recent approaches give strong performance guarantees by training the policy iteratively. However, it is important to note that these guarantees depend on how well the policy we found can imitate the oracle on the training data. When there is a substantial difference between the oracle's ability and the learner's policy space, we may fail to find a policy that has low error on the training set. In such cases, we propose to use a coach that demonstrates easy-to-learn actions for the learner and gradually approaches the oracle. By a reduction of learning by demonstration to online learning, we prove that coaching can yield a lower regret bound than using the oracle. We apply our algorithm to a novel cost-sensitive dynamic feature selection problem, a hard decision problem that considers a user-specified accuracy-cost trade-off. Experimental results on UCI datasets show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art imitation learning methods in dynamic features selection and two static feature selection methods.

paragraphs: Imitation learning trains a policy from demonstrations, often using an expert or oracle as its target. The paper identifies a problem when the expert's abilities exceed what the learner's policy class can represent. Even iterative methods with strong guarantees may then struggle, because those guarantees depend on how accurately the learner can imitate the training demonstrations.

The proposed solution introduces a coach that demonstrates actions the learner can more easily reproduce and gradually moves toward the oracle's behavior. This adapts the teaching target to the learner's capabilities. By reducing learning from demonstrations to online learning, the authors prove that coaching can provide a lower regret bound than learning directly from the oracle.

The method is applied to dynamic feature selection, where decisions must respect a user-specified trade-off between accuracy and feature cost. On UCI datasets, it outperforms the compared state-of-the-art imitation learning approaches for dynamic selection and two static feature-selection methods. The findings support adjusting demonstrations to what a learner can currently express when direct expert imitation is difficult.
summary.tldr: A coach supplies learnable demonstrations that gradually approach expert behavior, potentially improving regret bounds and empirically improving feature selection.

title: Imitation Learning by Coaching

abstract: This paper presents a novel non-parametric approximate dynamic programming (ADP) algorithm that enjoys graceful, dimension-independent approximation and sample complexity guarantees. In particular, we establish both theoretically and computationally that our proposal can serve as a viable alternative to state-of-the-art parametric ADP algorithms, freeing the designer from carefully specifying an approximation architecture. We accomplish this by developing a kernel-based mathematical program for ADP. Via a computational study on a controlled queueing network, we show that our non-parametric procedure is competitive with parametric ADP approaches.

We accomplish this by developing a kernel-based mathematical program for ADP. paragraphs: The paper develops a nonparametric approach to approximate dynamic programming. A central design challenge in parametric approaches is specifying an approximation architecture carefully enough to represent the decision problem well. The proposed method aims to reduce that burden by using a kernel-based formulation.

The authors construct a mathematical optimization program for approximate dynamic programming and establish approximation and sample-complexity guarantees that are independent of dimension. These guarantees concern the quality of approximation and the samples required by the proposal. They provide theoretical support for treating the kernel method as a viable alternative to established parametric approaches.

A computational study on a controlled queueing network supplies the empirical comparison. In that study, the nonparametric method is competitive with parametric approximate dynamic programming. The stated result supports the possibility of obtaining useful performance without requiring the designer to carefully prescribe an approximation architecture. The theoretical guarantees and computational evidence address complementary parts of that case: what can be established about the method and how it performs in the studied control problem.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based approximate dynamic programming method offers dimension-independent guarantees and competitive results on a controlled queueing network.

title: Non-parametric Approximate Dynamic Programming via the Kernel Method

abstract: Probabilistic models for binary spike patterns provide a powerful tool for understanding the statistical dependencies in large-scale neural recordings. Maximum entropy (or maxent'') models, which seek to explain dependencies in terms of low-order interactions between neurons, have enjoyed remarkable success in modeling such patterns, particularly for small groups of neurons. However, these models are computationally intractable for large populations, and low-order maxent models have been shown to be inadequate for some datasets. To overcome these limitations, we propose a family of "universal'' models for binary spike patterns, where universality refers to the ability to model arbitrary distributions over all $2^m$ binary patterns. We construct universal models using a Dirichlet process centered on a well-behaved parametric base measure, which naturally combines the flexibility of a histogram and the parsimony of a parametric model. We derive computationally efficient inference methods using Bernoulli and cascade-logistic base measures, which scale tractably to large populations. We also establish a condition for equivalence between the cascade-logistic and the 2nd-order maxent or "Ising'' model, making cascade-logistic a reasonable choice for base measure in a universal model. We illustrate the performance of these models using neural data."

paragraphs: Binary spike patterns reveal dependencies across a neural population, but low-order maximum-entropy models can miss structure and become computationally difficult at large scale. This paper proposes distributions capable of representing arbitrary patterns while retaining a manageable statistical backbone. Flexibility is combined with a parametric starting model.

A Dirichlet process is centered on a well-behaved base measure, joining histogram-like expressiveness with parametric parsimony. Efficient inference is derived for Bernoulli and cascade-logistic bases. The authors also identify a condition under which the cascade-logistic formulation is equivalent to a second-order Ising model.

Neural-data examples illustrate the resulting models. The contribution permits departures from low-order assumptions without discarding their useful structure entirely. Universality refers to representational capacity over all binary patterns; centering and efficient inference make that broad family usable without requiring a separate freely estimated parameter for every possible pattern from the outset.
summary.tldr: Centered Dirichlet-process models flexibly represent neural spike-pattern distributions while retaining efficient inference and useful parametric structure.

title: Universal models for binary spike patterns using centered Dirichlet processes

abstract: The problem of f-divergence estimation is important in the fields of machine learning, information theory, and statistics. While several divergence estimators exist, relatively few have known convergence properties. In particular, even for those estimators whose MSE convergence rates are known, the asymptotic distributions are unknown. We establish the asymptotic normality of a recently proposed ensemble estimator of f-divergence between two distributions from a finite number of samples. This estimator has MSE convergence rate of O(1/T), is simple to implement, and performs well in high dimensions. This theory enables us to perform divergence-based inference tasks such as testing equality of pairs of distributions based on empirical samples. We experimentally validate our theoretical results and, as an illustration, use them to empirically bound the best achievable classification error.

paragraphs: An f-divergence measures a difference between probability distributions, but estimating it from samples also requires understanding estimation uncertainty. A mean squared error rate describes average estimation accuracy without fully specifying the estimator's distribution. This paper addresses that additional question for a previously proposed ensemble estimator of multivariate f-divergence.

The authors establish asymptotic normality: as the sample size grows, an appropriately normalized estimation error approaches a normal distribution. The estimator already has a mean squared error rate of O(1/T), is simple to implement, and is reported to perform well in high dimensions. The new theory adds distributional information that makes the estimator useful for statistical inference.

One resulting application is testing whether two sample sets come from the same distribution. The authors experimentally validate the theoretical findings and illustrate their use by empirically bounding the best achievable classification error. The contribution thus connects divergence estimation with uncertainty-aware decisions, allowing estimated distributional differences to support inference tasks beyond producing a single numerical value.
summary.tldr: An asymptotic normality result turns an ensemble f-divergence estimator into a tool for distribution testing and classification-error analysis.

title: Multivariate f-divergence Estimation With Confidence

abstract: We propose a general framework for regularization based on group majorization. In this framework, a group is defined to act on the parameter space and an orbit is fixed; to control complexity, the model parameters are confined to lie in the convex hull of this orbit (the orbitope). Common regularizers are recovered as particular cases, and a connection is revealed between the recent sorted 1 -norm and the hyperoctahedral group. We derive the properties a group must satisfy for being amenable to optimization with conditional and projected gradient algorithms. Finally, we suggest a continuation strategy for orbit exploration, presenting simulation results for the symmetric and hyperoctahedral groups.

paragraphs: Regularization controls model complexity by restricting or penalizing its parameters. This paper proposes a framework based on transformations of parameter space. A mathematical group acts on the parameters, and a selected orbit collects the points reached through those transformations. The allowed parameter region is the convex hull of that orbit, called an orbitope.

This construction places several familiar regularizers within a shared geometric framework. The authors also connect the sorted 1-norm with the hyperoctahedral group. These relationships matter because they explain apparently separate regularization choices through the group structure used to generate their feasible regions, rather than treating each penalty as an unrelated construction.

The paper then addresses computation by deriving properties that make a group suitable for conditional-gradient and projected-gradient optimization. It also proposes a continuation strategy for exploring orbits and presents simulations involving symmetric and hyperoctahedral groups. The contribution combines a unifying description of regularization with conditions for practical optimization; it does not assert that every group yields an equally tractable learning problem.
summary.tldr: Orbit regularization unifies complexity constraints through group-generated convex regions and identifies conditions for gradient-based optimization.

title: Orbit Regularization

abstract: We describe an embarrassingly parallel, anytime Monte Carlo method for likelihood-free models. The algorithm starts with the view that the stochasticity of the pseudo-samples generated by the simulator can be controlled externally by a vector of random numbers u, in such a way that the outcome, knowing u, is deterministic. For each instantiation of u we run an optimization procedure to minimize the distance between summary statistics of the simulator and the data. After reweighing these samples using the prior and the Jacobian (accounting for the change of volume in transforming from the space of summary statistics to the space of parameters) we show that this weighted ensemble represents a Monte Carlo estimate of the posterior distribution. The procedure can be run embarrassingly parallel (each node handling one sample) and anytime (by allocating resources to the worst performing sample). The procedure is validated on six experiments.

paragraphs: Optimization Monte Carlo performs inference for simulator-based models without requiring a likelihood evaluation. It begins by making the simulator's random inputs explicit. Once a particular random-number vector is fixed, the simulated output becomes deterministic, allowing an optimization procedure to search for parameters whose simulated summaries resemble those of the observed data.

Repeating this process for different random-number vectors produces a collection of fitted parameter samples. The method then weights them using the prior and a Jacobian correction. That correction accounts for the change in volume between summary-statistic space and parameter space. The authors show that the weighted collection gives a Monte Carlo estimate of the posterior distribution.

Each sample's optimization can run independently, making the method readily parallelizable across computing nodes. It also supports an anytime strategy that directs additional resources toward the worst-performing sample. Validation uses six experiments. The contribution connects deterministic optimization under fixed simulator randomness with weighted probabilistic inference, while providing a computation structure that supports both parallel work and incremental refinement.
summary.tldr: Fixing simulator randomness turns likelihood-free inference into independent optimization problems whose weighted solutions estimate the posterior.

title: Optimization Monte Carlo: Efficient and Embarrassingly Parallel Likelihood-Free Inference

abstract: Imagine a random walk that outputs a state only when visiting it for the first time. The observed output is therefore a repeat-censored version of the underlying walk, and consists of a permutation of the states or a prefix of it. We call this model initial-visit emitting random walk (INVITE). Prior work has shown that the random walks with such a repeat-censoring mechanism explain well human behavior in memory search tasks, which is of great interest in both the study of human cognition and various clinical applications. However, parameter estimation in INVITE is challenging, because naive likelihood computation by marginalizing over infinitely many hidden random walk trajectories is intractable. In this paper, we propose the first efficient maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) for INVITE by decomposing the censored output into a series of absorbing random walks. We also prove theoretical properties of the MLE including identifiability and consistency. We show that INVITE outperforms several existing methods on real-world human response data from memory search tasks.

paragraphs: In the INVITE model, a random walk produces an observable output only when it reaches a state for the first time. Repeated visits remain hidden, so the observed sequence contains distinct states even though the underlying process can revisit them. Earlier work found this repeat-censoring mechanism useful for explaining human memory-search behavior.

Learning the model is difficult because many hidden trajectories can produce the same observed sequence. A direct likelihood calculation would sum over infinitely many possibilities. This paper develops an efficient maximum likelihood estimation method by decomposing the censored sequence into a series of absorbing random walks, making the hidden-path problem computationally manageable.

The authors prove identifiability and consistency properties for the estimator, providing theoretical support for recovering model parameters from observations. They also report that INVITE outperforms several existing methods on real human responses from memory-search tasks. The contribution makes a previously challenging cognitive model practical to estimate while connecting its empirical performance with formal properties of the learning procedure.
summary.tldr: An absorbing-random-walk decomposition enables efficient estimation of a repeat-censored model of human memory search.

title: Human Memory Search as Initial-Visit Emitting Random Walk

abstract: We consider the problem of finding the best arm in a stochastic Mutli-armed Bandit (MAB) game and propose a general framework based on verification that applies to multiple well-motivated generalizations of the classic MAB problem. In these generalizations, additional structure is known in advance, causing the task of verifying the optimality of a candidate to be easier than discovering the best arm. Our results are focused on the scenario where the failure probability $\delta$ must be very low; we essentially show that in this high confidence regime, identifying the best arm is as easy as the task of verification. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by applying it, and improving the state-of-the art results in the problems of: Linear bandits, Dueling bandits with the Condorcet assumption, Copeland dueling bandits, Unimodal bandits and Graphical bandits.

In these generalizations, additional structure is known in advance, causing the task of verifying the optimality of a candidate to be easier than discovering the best arm. Our results are focused on the scenario where the failure probability $\delta$ must be very low; we essentially show that in this high confidence regime, identifying the best arm is as easy as the task of verification. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by applying it, and improving the state-of-the art results in the problems of: Linear bandits, Dueling bandits with the Condorcet assumption, Copeland dueling bandits, Unimodal bandits and Graphical bandits.

paragraphs: Finding the best option in a stochastic multi-armed bandit problem requires learning from uncertain observations. When additional structure is known, checking that a proposed option is best can be easier than discovering that option initially. This paper builds a general framework around that difference between discovery and verification.

The analysis focuses on demands for very high confidence, expressed through a very small allowed failure probability δ. In this regime, the authors essentially show that identifying the best arm becomes as easy as verifying a candidate’s optimality. The result connects the cost of a full search with the potentially simpler task enabled by known problem structure.

The framework is applied to linear bandits, dueling bandits under the Condorcet assumption, Copeland dueling bandits, unimodal bandits, and graphical bandits. These applications improve the stated state of the art for the respective problems. The contribution is a reusable route to high-confidence identification guarantees across several structured settings, rather than a separate discovery strategy tailored to each one.
summary.tldr: A verification-based framework shows that high-confidence best-arm identification can essentially match verification difficulty in several structured bandit problems.

title: Verification Based Solution for Structured MAB Problems

abstract: Several learning applications require solving high-dimensional regression problems where the relevant features belong to a small number of (overlapping) groups. For very large datasets and under standard sparsity constraints, hard thresholding methods have proven to be extremely efficient, but such methods require NP hard projections when dealing with overlapping groups. In this paper, we show that such NP-hard projections can not only be avoided by appealing to submodular optimization, but such methods come with strong theoretical guarantees even in the presence of poorly conditioned data (i.e. say when two features have correlation $\geq 0.99$), which existing analyses cannot handle. These methods exhibit an interesting computation-accuracy trade-off and can be extended to significantly harder problems such as sparse overlapping groups. Experiments on both real and synthetic data validate our claims and demonstrate that the proposed methods are orders of magnitude faster than other greedy and convex relaxation techniques for learning with group-structured sparsity.

paragraphs: Some high-dimensional regression problems have relevant features concentrated in a small number of groups, and those groups may overlap. Hard thresholding is efficient for ordinary sparsity, but extending it to overlapping groups creates a computational obstacle: the required projections can be NP-hard. This paper develops methods that avoid those difficult projections.

The approach uses submodular optimization within the structured sparsity setting. The authors establish strong theoretical guarantees even for poorly conditioned data, including situations with extremely highly correlated features that existing analyses cannot handle. The methods also expose a trade-off between computational effort and accuracy, making that balance part of the algorithmic design.

The framework can be extended to harder structures such as sparse overlapping groups. Experiments on real and synthetic data support the theoretical and computational claims, with reported speed advantages of orders of magnitude over other greedy and convex-relaxation techniques for group-structured sparsity. The contribution combines a way around a projection bottleneck with guarantees that accommodate difficult correlations among the features.
summary.tldr: Submodular optimization avoids NP-hard projections in overlapping-group regression, yielding strong guarantees and large empirical speedups.

title: Structured Sparse Regression via Greedy Hard Thresholding

abstract: Bregman divergences play a central role in the design and analysis of a range of machine learning algorithms through a handful of popular theorems. We present a new theorem which shows that ``Bregman distortions'' (employing a potentially non-convex generator) may be exactly re-written as a scaled Bregman divergence computed over transformed data. This property can be viewed from the standpoints of geometry (a scaled isometry with adaptive metrics) or convex optimization (relating generalized perspective transforms). Admissible distortions include {geodesic distances} on curved manifolds and projections or gauge-normalisation. Our theorem allows one to leverage to the wealth and convenience of Bregman divergences when analysing algorithms relying on the aforementioned Bregman distortions. We illustrate this with three novel applications of our theorem: a reduction from multi-class density ratio to class-probability estimation, a new adaptive projection free yet norm-enforcing dual norm mirror descent algorithm, and a reduction from clustering on flat manifolds to clustering on curved manifolds. Experiments on each of these domains validate the analyses and suggest that the scaled Bregman theorem might be a worthy addition to the popular handful of Bregman divergence properties that have been pervasive in machine learning.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning analyses depend on Bregman divergences, a family of measures for comparing points. This paper expands where those analytical tools can be used. Its theorem shows that certain Bregman distortions, including ones generated by potentially nonconvex functions, can be rewritten exactly as scaled Bregman divergences after transforming the data.

The transformation provides two ways to understand the result. Geometrically, it preserves the relevant comparison up to scaling while allowing adaptive metrics. From an optimization perspective, it connects generalized perspective transforms. Admissible distortions include geodesic distances on curved manifolds and distortions involving projections or gauge normalization. The exact rewriting lets existing Bregman theory support analysis in these settings.

summary.tldr: A new theorem rewrites certain geometric distortions as scaled Bregman divergences, extending familiar analytical tools to several learning problems.

title: A scaled Bregman theorem with applications

abstract: We introduce a theoretical and algorithmic framework for multi-way graph partitioning that relies on a multiplicative cut-based objective. We refer to this objective as the Product Cut. We provide a detailed investigation of the mathematical properties of this objective and an effective algorithm for its optimization. The proposed model has strong mathematical underpinnings, and the corresponding algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark data sets.
originalAbstract: We introduce a theoretical and algorithmic framework for multi-way graph partitioning that relies on a multiplicative cut-based objective. We refer to this objective as the Product Cut. We provide a detailed investigation of the mathematical properties of this objective and an effective algorithm for its optimization. The proposed model has strong mathematical underpinnings, and the corresponding algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark data sets.

paragraphs: Graph partitioning divides a graph into groups, and the objective determines which divisions the algorithm prefers. This paper introduces Product Cut, a multiplicative cut-based objective for dividing a graph into multiple groups. The contribution includes both a way to formulate the partitioning task and an algorithm for optimizing that formulation.

The authors investigate the objective’s mathematical properties in detail, providing a theoretical basis for the proposed model. This analysis matters because introducing a new partitioning score creates two connected questions: what mathematical structure the score has, and how an algorithm can use that structure to search for a partition. The paper addresses the objective and its optimization within one framework.

The corresponding algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark datasets used in the study. That reported finding supports the practical effectiveness of Product Cut alongside its mathematical development. The resulting contribution is a theoretically grounded alternative for multi-way graph partitioning whose proposed optimization algorithm also performs strongly in the reported benchmark comparisons.
summary.tldr: Product Cut introduces a multiplicative objective for multi-way graph partitioning with mathematical analysis and strong benchmark performance.

title: The Product Cut

abstract: We present a new algorithm, truncated variance reduction (TruVaR), that treats Bayesian optimization (BO) and level-set estimation (LSE) with Gaussian processes in a unified fashion. The algorithm greedily shrinks a sum of truncated variances within a set of potential maximizers (BO) or unclassified points (LSE), which is updated based on confidence bounds. TruVaR is effective in several important settings that are typically non-trivial to incorporate into myopic algorithms, including pointwise costs and heteroscedastic noise. We provide a general theoretical guarantee for TruVaR covering these aspects, and use it to recover and strengthen existing results on BO and LSE. Moreover, we provide a new result for a setting where one can select from a number of noise levels having associated costs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm on both synthetic and real-world data sets.
originalAbstract: We present a new algorithm, truncated variance reduction (TruVaR), that treats Bayesian optimization (BO) and level-set estimation (LSE) with Gaussian processes in a unified fashion. The algorithm greedily shrinks a sum of truncated variances within a set of potential maximizers (BO) or unclassified points (LSE), which is updated based on confidence bounds. TruVaR is effective in several important settings that are typically non-trivial to incorporate into myopic algorithms, including pointwise costs and heteroscedastic noise. We provide a general theoretical guarantee for TruVaR covering these aspects, and use it to recover and strengthen existing results on BO and LSE. Moreover, we provide a new result for a setting where one can select from a number of noise levels having associated costs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the algorithm on both synthetic and real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization seeks a function’s maximum, while level-set estimation determines which points fall on either side of a threshold. TruVaR handles both tasks within a Gaussian-process framework. The shared idea is to reduce uncertainty over the points that still matter to the task’s unresolved decisions.

At each step, the algorithm greedily reduces a sum of truncated variances. For optimization, the relevant set contains potential maximizers; for level-set estimation, it contains points that remain unclassified. Confidence bounds update these sets as evidence accumulates. This formulation accommodates point-specific evaluation costs and noise that varies across points, features that can be difficult to incorporate into myopic algorithms.

The authors provide a general theoretical guarantee covering these settings and use it to recover and strengthen existing results for both tasks. They also establish a result for choosing among noise levels with associated costs. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate effectiveness. The framework thus connects uncertainty reduction with practical decisions about where, and at what measurement cost, to gather information.
summary.tldr: TruVaR unifies Bayesian optimization and level-set estimation by reducing relevant uncertainty while accommodating varying measurement costs and noise.

title: Truncated Variance Reduction: A Unified Approach to Bayesian Optimization and Level-Set Estimation

abstract: Semi-supervised learning methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) obtained strong empirical results, but it is not clear 1) how the discriminator benefits from joint training with a generator, and 2) why good semi-supervised classification performance and a good generator cannot be obtained at the same time. Theoretically we show that given the discriminator objective, good semi-supervised learning indeed requires a bad generator, and propose the definition of a preferred generator. Empirically, we derive a novel formulation based on our analysis that substantially improves over feature matching GANs, obtaining state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark datasets.
originalAbstract: Semi-supervised learning methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) obtained strong empirical results, but it is not clear 1) how the discriminator benefits from joint training with a generator, and 2) why good semi-supervised classification performance and a good generator cannot be obtained at the same time. Theoretically we show that given the discriminator objective, good semi-supervised learning indeed requires a bad generator, and propose the definition of a preferred generator. Empirically, we derive a novel formulation based on our analysis that substantially improves over feature matching GANs, obtaining state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: GAN-based semi-supervised learning had shown strong classification results, but the generator's role in those results was unclear. This paper asks how jointly training a generator helps the discriminator classify data, and why strong classification and high-quality generation can be difficult to obtain together. It treats these as related questions about the training objective.

The theoretical analysis shows that, given the discriminator objective under consideration, good semi-supervised learning requires a generator that is bad at the generative task. The authors also define a preferred generator for that setting. The condition on the objective matters: the result identifies a tension within the analyzed formulation rather than a universal incompatibility between generation and classification.

Using this analysis, the authors develop a new formulation that substantially improves on feature matching GANs in their experiments. It achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark datasets. The findings show how understanding the generator's role in classification can guide a more effective semi-supervised learning method.
summary.tldr: Under the analyzed discriminator objective, effective semi-supervised classification requires a poor generator, motivating a formulation with stronger benchmark results.

title: Good Semi-supervised Learning That Requires a Bad GAN

abstract: In many biological and medical contexts, we construct a large labeled corpus by aggregating many sources to use in target prediction tasks. Unfortunately, many of the sources may be irrelevant to our target task, so ignoring the structure of the dataset is detrimental. This work proposes a novel approach, the Multiple Domain Matching Network (MDMN), to exploit this structure. MDMN embeds all data into a shared feature space while learning which domains share strong statistical relationships. These relationships are often insightful in their own right, and they allow domains to share strength without interference from irrelevant data. This methodology builds on existing distribution-matching approaches by assuming that source domains are varied and outcomes multi-factorial. Therefore, each domain should only match a relevant subset. Theoretical analysis shows that the proposed approach can have a tighter generalization bound than existing multiple-domain adaptation approaches. Empirically, we show that the proposed methodology handles higher numbers of source domains (up to 21 empirically), and provides state-of-the-art performance on image, text, and multi-channel time series classification, including clinically relevant data of a novel treatment of Autism Spectrum Disorder.

paragraphs: Combining labeled data from many sources can hurt prediction when some sources are irrelevant to the target task. This problem is especially pertinent to biological and medical datasets assembled from varied sources. The paper treats relationships among those sources as something to learn, so that useful sharing depends on which domains are statistically connected.

The Multiple Domain Matching Network maps data into a shared feature space while identifying strong relationships between domains. Its premise is that sources are varied and outcomes can depend on multiple factors, so each domain should match only a relevant subset of the others. This selective matching allows related domains to share information while reducing interference from irrelevant data.

The theoretical analysis shows that the approach can obtain a tighter generalization bound than existing multiple-domain adaptation methods. Experiments handle up to 21 source domains and report state-of-the-art classification performance on images, text, and multichannel time series, including clinically relevant autism treatment data. The learned domain relationships can also be informative themselves, beyond their contribution to prediction.
summary.tldr: The Multiple Domain Matching Network learns which data sources should share information, improving classification through selective domain matching.

title: Extracting Relationships by Multi-Domain Matching

abstract: Scaling model capacity has been vital in the success of deep learning. For a typical network, necessary compute resources and training time grow dramatically with model size. Conditional computation is a promising way to increase the number of parameters with a relatively small increase in resources. We propose a training algorithm that flexibly chooses neural modules based on the data to be processed. Both the decomposition and modules are learned end-to-end. In contrast to existing approaches, training does not rely on regularization to enforce diversity in module use. We apply modular networks both to image recognition and language modeling tasks, where we achieve superior performance compared to several baselines. Introspection reveals that modules specialize in interpretable contexts.

paragraphs: Larger neural networks can provide greater model capacity, but their computational requirements and training time often grow sharply. Conditional computation offers a way to increase the available parameters while activating computation selectively. This paper develops modular networks that choose which neural components to use according to the data being processed.

The training algorithm learns both the modules and the decomposition of computation end to end. Module selection is therefore part of the learned system, rather than a fixed arrangement imposed before training. The method also avoids relying on a regularization term to force diversity in module use, distinguishing how it develops a division of work among components.

Applications to image recognition and language modeling outperform several baselines. Examination of the trained networks reveals modules specializing in interpretable contexts, suggesting that the learned computational organization reflects meaningful differences in the inputs. The findings support learning an input-dependent division of computation as a useful modeling strategy, alongside the broader motivation of expanding capacity with relatively modest additional resource demands.
summary.tldr: Modular networks learn input-dependent module selection and module behavior together, outperforming several baselines and developing interpretable specialization.

title: Modular Networks: Learning to Decompose Neural Computation

abstract: We present the Multi-value Rule Set (MRS) for interpretable classification with feature efficient presentations. Compared to rule sets built from single-value rules, MRS adopts a more generalized form of association rules that allows multiple values in a condition. Rules of this form are more concise than classical single-value rules in capturing and describing patterns in data. Our formulation also pursues a higher efficiency of feature utilization, which reduces possible cost in data collection and storage. We propose a Bayesian framework for formulating an MRS model and develop an efficient inference method for learning a maximum a posteriori, incorporating theoretically grounded bounds to iteratively reduce the search space and improve the search efficiency. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that MRS models have significantly smaller complexity and fewer features than baseline models while being competitive in predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: Rule-based classifiers can explain predictions through explicit conditions, but their descriptions can become cumbersome when similar patterns require many separate rules. Multi-value Rule Sets address this by allowing a condition to contain several values. This more general rule form can express patterns more concisely than rules restricted to a single value per condition.

The formulation also favors efficient use of features, aiming to reduce how many different inputs the model needs. That can potentially lower data collection and storage costs. The authors place these goals within a Bayesian framework and develop an inference method for finding a maximum a posteriori model, balancing the model choices through that framework.

To make the search more efficient, the method uses theoretically grounded bounds to progressively shrink the space of candidate solutions. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data find significantly lower model complexity and fewer features than baseline models, with competitive predictive accuracy. The findings link interpretability to both concise rule presentation and reduced feature requirements, rather than treating explanation solely as a matter of displaying rules.
summary.tldr: Multi-value Rule Sets produce concise classifiers using fewer features while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy.

title: Multi-value Rule Sets for Interpretable Classification with Feature-Efficient Representations

abstract: We introduce a principled approach for unsupervised structure learning of deep neural networks. We propose a new interpretation for depth and inter-layer connectivity where conditional independencies in the input distribution are encoded hierarchically in the network structure. Thus, the depth of the network is determined inherently. The proposed method casts the problem of neural network structure learning as a problem of Bayesian network structure learning. Then, instead of directly learning the discriminative structure, it learns a generative graph, constructs its stochastic inverse, and then constructs a discriminative graph. We prove that conditional-dependency relations among the latent variables in the generative graph are preserved in the class-conditional discriminative graph. We demonstrate on image classification benchmarks that the deepest layers (convolutional and dense) of common networks can be replaced by significantly smaller learned structures, while maintaining classification accuracy---state-of-the-art on tested benchmarks. Our structure learning algorithm requires a small computational cost and runs efficiently on a standard desktop CPU.

paragraphs: This paper treats a neural network's depth and connections as structures that can be learned from dependencies in the input distribution. Its unsupervised approach represents conditional independencies hierarchically, so the resulting structure inherently determines network depth. The aim is to give architectural choices a statistical foundation through relationships present in the data.

The method reformulates neural architecture construction as Bayesian network structure learning. It first learns a generative graph, builds a stochastic inverse of that graph, and then constructs a discriminative graph for prediction. The authors prove that conditional-dependency relationships among latent variables in the generative graph are preserved in the class-conditional discriminative graph.

On image classification benchmarks, the learned structures replace the deepest convolutional and dense layers of common networks with substantially smaller alternatives while maintaining classification accuracy, reported as state of the art on the tested benchmarks. Structure learning also has a small computational cost and runs efficiently on a standard desktop CPU. The results link a principled graph-construction procedure to compact predictive networks without a costly architecture-learning process.
summary.tldr: Learning Bayesian network structure provides a principled way to construct smaller deep-network layers while preserving tested classification accuracy.

title: Constructing Deep Neural Networks by Bayesian Network Structure Learning

abstract: We design differentially private learning algorithms that are agnostic to the learning model assuming access to limited amount of unlabeled public data. First, we give a new differentially private algorithm for answering a sequence of $m$ online classification queries (given by a sequence of $m$ unlabeled public feature vectors) based on a private training set. Our private algorithm follows the paradigm of subsample-and-aggregate, in which any generic non-private learner is trained on disjoint subsets of the private training set, then for each classification query, the votes of the resulting classifiers ensemble are aggregated in a differentially private fashion. Our private aggregation is based on a novel combination of distance-to-instability framework [Smith & Thakurta 2013] and the sparse-vector technique [Dwork et al. 2009, Hardt & Talwar 2010]. We show that our algorithm makes a conservative use of the privacy budget. In particular, if the underlying non-private learner yields classification error at most $\alpha\in (0, 1)$, then our construction answers more queries, by at least a factor of $1/\alpha$ in some cases, than what is implied by a straightforward application of the advanced composition theorem for differential privacy. Next, we apply the knowledge transfer technique to construct a private learner that outputs a classifier, which can be used to answer unlimited number of queries. In the PAC model, we analyze our construction and prove upper bounds on the sample complexity for both the realizable and the non-realizable cases. As in non-private sample complexity, our bounds are completely characterized by the VC dimension of the concept class.
