paragraphs: This paper develops differentially private learning methods that can use a generic non-private learner, assuming access to a limited amount of unlabeled public data. Its first task is to answer an online sequence of classification queries using a private training set. Separate classifiers are trained on disjoint portions of that set, and their votes are combined privately.

The aggregation mechanism combines distance to instability with the sparse-vector technique to conserve the privacy budget. If the underlying learner has error at most α, the construction can, in some cases, answer at least 1/α times as many queries as a straightforward use of advanced composition would imply. This improvement is conditional, rather than a uniform gain for every setting.

The authors then use knowledge transfer to produce a private classifier that can answer unlimited subsequent queries. They establish sample-complexity upper bounds in the PAC framework for both realizable and non-realizable cases. As in non-private learning, these bounds are characterized by the concept class's VC dimension, connecting model-independent privacy mechanisms with established measures of learning complexity.
summary.tldr: Private aggregation and knowledge transfer turn generic learners into privacy-preserving query systems and classifiers, given limited unlabeled public data.

title: Model-Agnostic Private Learning

abstract: In this paper, we provide a theoretical understanding of word embedding and its dimensionality. Motivated by the unitary-invariance of word embedding, we propose the Pairwise Inner Product (PIP) loss, a novel metric on the dissimilarity between word embeddings. Using techniques from matrix perturbation theory, we reveal a fundamental bias-variance trade-off in dimensionality selection for word embeddings. This bias-variance trade-off sheds light on many empirical observations which were previously unexplained, for example the existence of an optimal dimensionality. Moreover, new insights and discoveries, like when and how word embeddings are robust to over-fitting, are revealed. By optimizing over the bias-variance trade-off of the PIP loss, we can explicitly answer the open question of dimensionality selection for word embedding.

paragraphs: Choosing a word embedding's dimension determines how large its vector representation will be, but the best choice needs a principled way to compare embeddings. This paper proposes Pairwise Inner Product, or PIP, loss. Motivated by unitary invariance, it compares relationships encoded by embeddings rather than relying on their particular coordinate orientation.

Using matrix perturbation theory, the authors derive a bias–variance trade-off in the choice of dimension. The analysis explains why increasing representation size need not improve an embedding indefinitely and why an optimal dimension can exist. It also provides insight into when and how embeddings can resist overfitting, linking these behaviors to the same theoretical framework.

The paper then uses optimization of the PIP-loss trade-off to address dimensionality selection explicitly. Its contribution is both a comparison metric and an analysis that turns a representation-size choice into a mathematical optimization problem. The stated insights concern the conditions governing the trade-off, rather than asserting that one dimension is optimal for every embedding or that all large embeddings overfit.
summary.tldr: PIP loss reveals a bias–variance trade-off that explains word-embedding behavior and provides a principled way to choose dimensionality.

title: On the Dimensionality of Word Embedding

abstract: Program translation is an important tool to migrate legacy code in one language into an ecosystem built in a different language. In this work, we are the first to employ deep neural networks toward tackling this problem. We observe that program translation is a modular procedure, in which a sub-tree of the source tree is translated into the corresponding target sub-tree at each step. To capture this intuition, we design a tree-to-tree neural network to translate a source tree into a target one. Meanwhile, we develop an attention mechanism for the tree-to-tree model, so that when the decoder expands one non-terminal in the target tree, the attention mechanism locates the corresponding sub-tree in the source tree to guide the expansion of the decoder. We evaluate the program translation capability of our tree-to-tree model against several state-of-the-art approaches. Compared against other neural translation models, we observe that our approach is consistently better than the baselines with a margin of up to 15 points. Further, our approach can improve the previous state-of-the-art program translation approaches by a margin of 20 points on the translation of real-world projects.

paragraphs: Program translation helps move software from one programming language into another ecosystem. This paper builds on the observation that translation is modular: a subtree in a source program corresponds to a subtree in the target program. The authors design a neural network around that structural relationship, translating a source tree into a target tree.

The model includes an attention mechanism tailored to tree generation. When the decoder expands a nonterminal in the target tree, attention locates the corresponding source subtree and uses it to guide the expansion. This connects each local construction decision to relevant source structure, reflecting the paper's view of translation as a sequence of related subtree transformations.

Evaluation compares the model with other neural translation models and established program-translation approaches. The authors report consistent gains over neural baselines, with margins reaching 15 points, and a 20-point improvement over previous state-of-the-art approaches on real-world projects. These findings support preserving and attending to program structure as a useful design choice for the translation tasks evaluated.
summary.tldr: A tree-to-tree network uses subtree attention to translate program structure and improves results over the evaluated translation approaches.

title: Tree-to-tree Neural Networks for Program Translation

abstract: We study the $k$-median clustering problem for high-dimensional polygonal curves with finite but unbounded number of vertices. We tackle the computational issue that arises from the high number of dimensions by defining a Johnson-Lindenstrauss projection for polygonal curves. We analyze the resulting error in terms of the Fr\'echet distance, which is a tractable and natural dissimilarity measure for curves. Our clustering algorithms achieve sublinear dependency on the number of input curves via subsampling. Also, we show that the Fr\'echet distance can not be approximated within any factor of less than $\sqrt{2}$ by probabilistically reducing the dependency on the number of vertices of the curves. As a consequence we provide a fast, CUDA-parallelized version of the Alt and Godau algorithm for computing the Fr\'echet distance and use it to evaluate our results empirically.

paragraphs: This paper studies k-median clustering for high-dimensional polygonal curves, each with a finite but potentially unbounded number of vertices. Curves introduce several separate computational burdens: the dimension of their coordinates, the number of input curves, and the number of vertices describing each curve. The authors address these sources of complexity through different techniques.

They define a Johnson-Lindenstrauss projection for polygonal curves to reduce the dimensional burden and analyze its error using Fréchet distance. This distance provides the measure of curve dissimilarity used in the study. Their clustering algorithms also use subsampling to achieve sublinear dependence on the number of input curves.

The paper additionally establishes a barrier to reducing dependence on curve vertices probabilistically: the stated approach cannot approximate Fréchet distance within any factor below the square root of two. Alongside the projection and sampling results, the authors provide a fast CUDA-parallelized implementation of the Alt and Godau algorithm for computing Fréchet distance. They use this implementation in their empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: Projection and subsampling accelerate clustering of high-dimensional curves, while a lower bound limits probabilistic shortcuts involving curve vertices.

title: Random Projections and Sampling Algorithms for Clustering of High-Dimensional Polygonal Curves

abstract: In this paper, we propose a general theoretical method for analyzing the risk bound in the presence of adversaries. Specifically, we try to fit the adversarial learning problem into the minimax framework. We first show that the original adversarial learning problem can be transformed into a minimax statistical learning problem by introducing a transport map between distributions. Then, we prove a new risk bound for this minimax problem in terms of covering numbers under a weak version of Lipschitz condition. Our method can be applied to multi-class classification and popular loss functions including the hinge loss and ramp loss. As some illustrative examples, we derive the adversarial risk bounds for SVMs and deep neural networks, and our bounds have two data-dependent terms, which can be optimized for achieving adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework for bounding learning risk in the presence of adversaries. The authors first introduce a transport map between distributions, allowing the adversarial learning problem to be expressed as a minimax statistical learning problem. This reframing provides a common mathematical structure for analyzing how a learner performs against adverse changes.

Within that structure, they prove a risk bound expressed through covering numbers, which measure the complexity of the relevant function class. The proof uses a weak form of a Lipschitz condition. The framework applies to multiclass classification and includes commonly used losses such as hinge loss and ramp loss.

The authors illustrate the method by deriving adversarial risk bounds for support vector machines and deep neural networks. These bounds contain two data-dependent terms that can be optimized to pursue adversarial robustness. The contribution therefore goes beyond a change in mathematical viewpoint: it produces bounds whose components suggest quantities to control during learning, under the stated theoretical conditions.
summary.tldr: A minimax reformulation yields adversarial risk bounds with data-dependent terms that can guide robustness optimization.

title: Theoretical Analysis of Adversarial Learning: A Minimax Approach

abstract: Humans and animals show remarkable flexibility in adjusting their behaviour when their goals, or rewards in the environment change. While such flexibility is a hallmark of intelligent behaviour, these multi-task scenarios remain an important challenge for machine learning algorithms and neurobiological models alike. We investigated two approaches that could enable this flexibility: factorized representations, which abstract away general aspects of a task from those prone to change, and nonparametric, memory-based approaches, which can provide a principled way of using similarity to past experiences to guide current behaviour. In particular, we combine the successor representation (SR), that factors the value of actions into expected outcomes and corresponding rewards, with evaluating task similarity through clustering the space of rewards. The proposed algorithm inverts a generative model over tasks, and dynamically samples from a flexible number of distinct SR maps while accumulating evidence about the current task context through amortized inference. It improves SR's transfer capabilities and outperforms competing algorithms and baselines in settings with both known and unsignalled rewards changes. Further, as a neurobiological model of spatial coding in the hippocampus, it explains important signatures of this representation, such as the "flickering" behaviour of hippocampal maps, and trajectory-dependent place cells (so-called splitter cells) and their dynamics. We thus provide a novel algorithmic approach for multi-task learning, as well as a common normative framework that links together these different characteristics of the brain's spatial representation.

paragraphs: An agent facing a new reward arrangement should be able to reuse relevant experience without treating the entire situation as unfamiliar. This paper combines two ways to support that flexibility: separating expected outcomes from their rewards, and using similarities to remembered tasks to guide current behavior.

The method builds on successor representations, which factor action values into expected outcomes and their associated rewards. It groups tasks through similarities in reward space and infers the current task context using a generative model. As evidence accumulates, the algorithm dynamically samples among a flexible number of successor maps. This lets its choice of representation respond to uncertainty about which task is currently active.

The reported experiments show improved transfer over competing methods when reward changes are either announced or left unsignalled. The framework also offers a model of spatial coding in the hippocampus, accounting for map flickering and place cells whose activity depends on the trajectory taken. Its contribution therefore connects practical adaptation across tasks with a common explanation for several characteristics of biological spatial representations.
summary.tldr: Inferring task context and selecting among successor maps improves transfer after reward changes while explaining several hippocampal spatial-coding patterns.

title: Better Transfer Learning with Inferred Successor Maps

abstract: We determine the sample complexity of pure exploration bandit problems with multiple good answers. We derive a lower bound using a new game equilibrium argument. We show how continuity and convexity properties of single-answer problems ensure that the existing Track-and-Stop algorithm has asymptotically optimal sample complexity. However, that convexity is lost when going to the multiple-answer setting. We present a new algorithm which extends Track-and-Stop to the multiple-answer case and has asymptotic sample complexity matching the lower bound.
originalAbstract: We determine the sample complexity of pure exploration bandit problems with multiple good answers. We derive a lower bound using a new game equilibrium argument. We show how continuity and convexity properties of single-answer problems ensure that the existing Track-and-Stop algorithm has asymptotically optimal sample complexity. However, that convexity is lost when going to the multiple-answer setting. We present a new algorithm which extends Track-and-Stop to the multiple-answer case and has asymptotic sample complexity matching the lower bound.

paragraphs: Pure exploration bandit problems concern gathering enough observations to identify a satisfactory answer. This paper studies cases where several answers can be correct. The central question is sample complexity: how many observations are needed to complete the identification task when the learner has a choice among acceptable outcomes.

The authors derive a lower bound using a new argument based on a game equilibrium. They also explain why the existing Track-and-Stop algorithm achieves asymptotically optimal sample complexity in single-answer problems, connecting that result to continuity and convexity properties. This analysis identifies mathematical structure that supports efficient exploration when there is only one correct answer.

Moving to multiple correct answers removes the relevant convexity property, so the single-answer reasoning does not directly carry over. The paper develops an extension of Track-and-Stop that handles this setting and asymptotically matches the new lower bound. The result establishes both a fundamental sampling limit and an algorithm that reaches it asymptotically despite the changed structure of the answer space.
summary.tldr: An extension of Track-and-Stop achieves asymptotically optimal sampling when a bandit exploration problem has multiple correct answers.

title: Pure Exploration with Multiple Correct Answers

abstract: Multi-task learning is a powerful method for solving multiple correlated tasks simultaneously. However, it is often impossible to find one single solution to optimize all the tasks, since different tasks might conflict with each other. Recently, a novel method is proposed to find one single Pareto optimal solution with good trade-off among different tasks by casting multi-task learning as multiobjective optimization. In this paper, we generalize this idea and propose a novel Pareto multi-task learning algorithm (Pareto MTL) to find a set of well-distributed Pareto solutions which can represent different trade-offs among different tasks. The proposed algorithm first formulates a multi-task learning problem as a multiobjective optimization problem, and then decomposes the multiobjective optimization problem into a set of constrained subproblems with different trade-off preferences. By solving these subproblems in parallel, Pareto MTL can find a set of well-representative Pareto optimal solutions with different trade-off among all tasks. Practitioners can easily select their preferred solution from these Pareto solutions, or use different trade-off solutions for different situations. Experimental results confirm that the proposed algorithm can generate well-representative solutions and outperform some state-of-the-art algorithms on many multi-task learning applications.

The practical contribution is therefore both competitive task performance and a broader set of choices about how performance is shared among tasks.
summary.tldr: Pareto MTL learns a representative set of task trade-offs so practitioners can choose among different performance priorities.

title: Pareto Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Dancing to music is an instinctive move by humans. Learning to model the music-to-dance generation process is, however, a challenging problem. It requires significant efforts to measure the correlation between music and dance as one needs to simultaneously consider multiple aspects, such as style and beat of both music and dance. Additionally, dance is inherently multimodal and various following movements of a pose at any moment are equally likely. In this paper, we propose a synthesis-by-analysis learning framework to generate dance from music. In the top-down analysis phase, we decompose a dance into a series of basic dance units, through which the model learns how to move. In the bottom-up synthesis phase, the model learns how to compose a dance by combining multiple basic dancing movements seamlessly according to input music. Experimental qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that the proposed method can synthesize realistic, diverse, style-consistent, and beat-matching dances from music.

paragraphs: Generating dance from music requires coordinating several kinds of information at once. Movements need to relate to musical style and beat, while also forming a plausible dance sequence. There is no single correct continuation of a pose: several next movements can be equally suitable. The paper treats this diversity as part of the generation problem.

The proposed framework learns through two connected phases. In the analysis phase, it breaks dances into basic movement units, allowing the model to learn how those movements work. In the synthesis phase, it learns to combine multiple units into a complete dance according to the input music, with seamless connections between the component movements.

This division separates learning movement elements from learning how to arrange them musically. Qualitative and quantitative experiments indicate that the method can generate dances that are realistic, varied, consistent in style, and aligned with the beat. The stated findings address both sides of the task: producing credible motion and making that motion correspond to the music.
summary.tldr: A framework that learns basic dance movements and then combines them generates diverse dances aligned with musical style and beat.

title: Dancing to Music

abstract: Recent works have shown that learning from easier instances first can help deep neural networks (DNNs) generalize better. However, knowing which data to present during different stages of training is a challenging problem. In this work, we address this problem by introducing data parameters. More specifically, we equip each sample and class in a dataset with a learnable parameter (data parameters), which governs their importance in the learning process. During training, at each iteration, as we update the model parameters, we also update the data parameters. These updates are done by gradient descent and do not require hand-crafted rules or design. When applied to image classification task on CIFAR10, CIFAR100,WebVision and ImageNet datasets, and object detection task on KITTI dataset, learning a dynamic curriculum via data parameters leads to consistent gains, without any increase in model complexity or training time. When applied to a noisy dataset, the proposed method learns to learn from clean images and improves over the state-of-the-art methods by 14%. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first curriculum learning method to show gains on large scale image classification and detection tasks.

paragraphs: A training curriculum changes which examples matter at different stages of learning. Starting with easier examples can help neural networks generalize, but deciding which examples to emphasize is itself difficult. This paper makes that decision learnable by attaching parameters to individual samples and to classes.

These data parameters govern each sample's and class's importance during training. At every iteration, gradient descent updates them alongside the network's ordinary parameters. The curriculum can therefore evolve as the model learns, without requiring manually designed scheduling rules. The approach treats the allocation of learning emphasis as part of the optimization problem.

The authors report consistent gains on image classification using CIFAR10, CIFAR100, WebVision, and ImageNet, and on object detection using KITTI, without increased model complexity or training time. On a noisy dataset, the method learns to favor clean images and reports a 14% improvement over state-of-the-art methods. These results support learned curricula at the scale of the evaluated classification and detection tasks, including a setting with unreliable training data.
summary.tldr: Learnable sample and class parameters create a changing training curriculum that improves the reported vision results, including learning with noisy data.

title: Data Parameters: A New Family of Parameters for Learning a Differentiable Curriculum

abstract: The Sinkhorn "distance," a variant of the Wasserstein distance with entropic regularization, is an increasingly popular tool in machine learning and statistical inference. However, the time and memory requirements of standard algorithms for computing this distance grow quadratically with the size of the data, rendering them prohibitively expensive on massive data sets. In this work, we show that this challenge is surprisingly easy to circumvent: combining two simple techniques—the Nyström method and Sinkhorn scaling—provably yields an accurate approximation of the Sinkhorn distance with significantly lower time and memory requirements than other approaches. We prove our results via new, explicit analyses of the Nyström method and of the stability properties of Sinkhorn scaling. We validate our claims experimentally by showing that our approach easily computes Sinkhorn distances on data sets hundreds of times larger than can be handled by other techniques.

paragraphs: The Sinkhorn distance is an entropy-regularized variant of Wasserstein distance used in machine learning and statistical inference. Standard computation becomes expensive because both memory and time requirements grow quadratically with dataset size. This paper addresses that scaling barrier with an approximation that combines the Nyström method and Sinkhorn scaling.

The authors prove that the combination produces an accurate approximation while requiring substantially less time and memory than other approaches. Their analysis examines both the Nyström method and the stability of Sinkhorn scaling. The stability component matters because an approximate computation must still lead to a reliable estimate of the final distance.

Experiments show that the method computes Sinkhorn distances on datasets hundreds of times larger than those handled by competing techniques. The contribution therefore links an approximation guarantee with a large practical expansion in manageable data size. It offers a way to retain accurate distance estimation when the resource requirements of standard computation would make the calculation impractical.
summary.tldr: Combining Nyström approximation with Sinkhorn scaling yields provably accurate distances and supports datasets hundreds of times larger in experiments.

title: Massively scalable Sinkhorn distances via the Nyström method

abstract: Consider a team of cooperative players that take actions in a networked-environment. At each turn, each player chooses an action and receives a reward that is an unknown function of all the players' actions. The goal of the team of players is to learn to play together the action profile that maximizes the sum of their rewards. However, players cannot observe the actions or rewards of other players, and can only get this information by communicating with their neighbors. We design a distributed learning algorithm that overcomes the informational bias players have towards maximizing the rewards of nearby players they got more information about. We assume twice continuously differentiable reward functions and constrained convex and compact action sets. Our communication graph is a random time-varying graph that follows an ergodic Markov chain. We prove that even if at every turn players take actions based only on the small random subset of the players' rewards that they know, our algorithm converges with probability 1 to the set of stationary points of (projected) gradient ascent on the sum of rewards function. Hence, if the sum of rewards is concave, then the algorithm converges with probability 1 to an optimal action profile.

paragraphs: The paper considers a team whose members choose actions separately, while each member’s reward depends on everyone’s actions. The team wants to maximize its total reward, but a player cannot directly observe other players’ actions or rewards. Information must travel through neighboring players, creating a bias toward helping nearby participants whose outcomes are better known.

The proposed distributed algorithm corrects this informational imbalance. Its analysis assumes twice continuously differentiable reward functions and convex, compact action sets. Communication follows a randomly changing graph governed by an ergodic Markov chain. Players can act using only the small random subset of rewards currently available to them, rather than requiring complete team information at every turn.

Under these conditions, the algorithm converges with probability one to the stationary points associated with projected gradient ascent on total reward. If total reward is also concave, convergence is to an optimal joint action profile. Concavity is therefore important to the stronger conclusion: the general result establishes stationarity, while the additional condition yields team optimality.
summary.tldr: A distributed bandit algorithm corrects local information bias and converges to stationary team solutions, with optimality when total reward is concave.

title: Cooperative Multi-player Bandit Optimization

abstract: Many recent datasets contain a variety of different data modalities, for instance, image, question, and answer data in visual question answering (VQA). When training deep net classifiers on those multi-modal datasets, the modalities get exploited at different scales, i.e., some modalities can more easily contribute to the classification results than others. This is suboptimal because the classifier is inherently biased towards a subset of the modalities. To alleviate this shortcoming, we propose a novel regularization term based on the functional entropy. Intuitively, this term encourages to balance the contribution of each modality to the classification result. However, regularization with the functional entropy is challenging. To address this, we develop a method based on the log-Sobolev inequality, which bounds the functional entropy with the functional-Fisher-information. Intuitively, this maximizes the amount of information that the modalities contribute. On the two challenging multi-modal datasets VQA-CPv2, and SocialIQ, we obtain state-of-the-art results while more uniformly exploiting the modalities. In addition, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method on Colored MNIST.

paragraphs: A classifier receiving several data modalities may rely much more heavily on some than on others. In visual question answering, for example, the available inputs include images and questions, but their contributions need not be balanced. This paper targets that uneven use of information with a regularizer intended to encourage each modality to contribute to classification.

The proposed term is based on functional entropy. Because using that quantity directly for regularization is challenging, the authors develop an approach using the log-Sobolev inequality, which bounds functional entropy through functional Fisher information. Their interpretation is that this encourages greater information contribution from the modalities and helps distribute the classifier's dependence more uniformly across them.

On VQA-CPv2 and SocialIQ, the method achieves state-of-the-art results while exploiting the modalities more uniformly. The authors also demonstrate effectiveness on Colored MNIST. These findings support the proposed regularization strategy for reducing imbalance in modality use. The bias addressed here is the classifier's tendency to favor a subset of its input sources.
summary.tldr: Functional-entropy-based regularization encourages more balanced use of input modalities and achieves leading reported results on two multimodal datasets.

title: Removing Bias in Multi-modal Classifiers: Regularization by Maximizing Functional Entropies

abstract: A major research direction in contextual bandits is to develop algorithms that are computationally efficient, yet support flexible, general-purpose function approximation. Algorithms based on modeling rewards have shown strong empirical performance, yet typically require a well-specified model, and can fail when this assumption does not hold. Can we design algorithms that are efficient and flexible, yet degrade gracefully in the face of model misspecification? We introduce a new family of oracle-efficient algorithms for $\varepsilon$-misspecified contextual bandits that adapt to unknown model misspecification---both for finite and infinite action settings. Given access to an \emph{online oracle} for square loss regression, our algorithm attains optimal regret and---in particular---optimal dependence on the misspecification level, with \emph{no prior knowledge}. Specializing to linear contextual bandits with infinite actions in $d$ dimensions, we obtain the first algorithm that achieves the optimal $\bigoht(d\sqrt{T} + \varepsilon\sqrt{d}T)$ regret bound for unknown $\varepsilon$. On a conceptual level, our results are enabled by a new optimization-based perspective on the regression oracle reduction framework of Foster and Rakhlin (2020), which we believe will be useful more broadly.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit algorithms choose actions using information about the current situation and learn from the rewards they receive. Reward prediction makes these algorithms flexible, but it can also create a vulnerability: the chosen model may not accurately represent the true rewards. This paper asks how an algorithm can retain computational efficiency while its performance deteriorates gracefully as that modeling mismatch grows.

The authors introduce algorithms that adapt to an unknown amount of misspecification, covering both finite and infinite action spaces. Their approach assumes access to an online square-loss regression oracle: a component that learns reward predictions through squared prediction error. The bandit algorithm uses this component without needing the misspecification level in advance.

The paper establishes optimal regret guarantees, including optimal dependence on the modeling error. For linear models with infinitely many actions, its bound combines a term growing with the square root of the interaction horizon and a misspecification term growing linearly. The result explains how approximation error affects achievable performance while showing that prior knowledge of that error is unnecessary for the stated guarantee.
summary.tldr: New contextual bandit algorithms achieve optimal regret while adapting to an unknown degree of reward-model misspecification.

title: Adapting to Misspecification in Contextual Bandits

abstract: In non-truthful auctions, agents' utility for a strategy depends on the strategies of the opponents and also the prior distribution over their private types; the set of Bayes Nash equilibria generally has an intricate dependence on the prior. Using the First Price Auction as our main demonstrating example, we show that $\tilde O(n / \epsilon^2)$ samples from the prior with $n$ agents suffice for an algorithm to learn the interim utilities for all monotone bidding strategies. As a consequence, this number of samples suffice for learning all approximate equilibria. We give almost matching (up to polylog factors) lower bound on the sample complexity for learning utilities. We also consider a setting where agents must pay a search cost to discover their own types. Drawing on a connection between this setting and the first price auction, discovered recently by Kleinberg et al. (2016), we show that $\tilde O(n / \epsilon^2)$ samples suffice for utilities and equilibria to be estimated in a near welfare-optimal descending auction in this setting. En route, we improve the sample complexity bound, recently obtained by Guo et al. (2019), for the Pandora's Box problem, which is a classical model for sequential consumer search.

paragraphs: In auctions where truthful bidding is not automatically optimal, a bidder's expected benefit depends on opponents' strategies and the distribution of their private information. Equilibria can therefore depend intricately on that distribution. This paper asks how many samples from it are sufficient to learn utilities and approximate equilibrium behavior.

Using first-price auctions as its main example, the paper shows that roughly n divided by epsilon squared samples, up to polylogarithmic factors, suffice to learn interim utilities for all monotone bidding strategies. Here n is the number of agents and epsilon is the accuracy parameter. The same sample count suffices to learn all approximate equilibria. An almost matching lower bound establishes that the utility-learning sample requirement is close to optimal.

The authors also study agents who must pay to discover their own private types. Through a connection to first-price auctions, they obtain the same sample scaling for estimating utilities and equilibria in a near-welfare-optimal descending auction. Along the way, they improve a sample-complexity bound for Pandora's Box, a model of sequential search.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes nearly tight sample requirements for learning utilities in first-price auctions and derives guarantees for approximate equilibria and costly-search settings.

title: Learning Utilities and Equilibria in Non-Truthful Auctions

abstract: Scene classification is a valuable classification subtask and has its own characteristics which still needs more in-depth studies. Basically, scene characteristics are distributed over the whole image, which cause the need of “seeing” comprehensive and informative regions. Previous works mainly focus on region discovery and aggregation, while rarely involves the inherent properties of CNN along with its potential ability to satisfy the requirements of scene classification. In this paper, we propose to understand scene images and the scene classification CNN models in terms of the focus area. From this new perspective, we find that large focus area is preferred in scene classification CNN models as a consequence of learning scene characteristics. Meanwhile, the analysis about existing training schemes helps us to understand the effects of focus area, and also raises the question about optimal training method for scene classification. Pursuing the better usage of scene characteristics, we propose a new learning scheme with a tailored loss in the goal of activating larger focus area on scene images. Since the supervision of the target regions to be enlarged is usually lacked, our alternative learning scheme is to erase already activated area, and allow the CNN models to activate more area during training. The proposed scheme is implemented by keeping the pairwise consistency between the output of the erased image and its original one. In particular, a tailored loss is proposed to keep such pairwise consistency by leveraging category-relevance information. Experiments on Places365 show the significant improvements of our method with various CNNs. Our method shows an inferior result on the object-centric dataset, ImageNet, which experimentally indicates that it captures the unique characteristics of scenes.

This paper examines scene-classification networks through their focus area: the regions they activate when learning scene characteristics. The authors find that a larger focus area is preferred for this task and use that observation to design a training scheme.

Because training usually lacks labels specifying which additional regions should become active, the method erases areas the network already activates. It then encourages consistency between the predictions for the erased image and the original image. A tailored loss uses category-relevance information to maintain this consistency, allowing the network to activate more of the remaining scene during training.

Experiments on Places365 show significant improvements across several convolutional networks. The method performs worse on the object-centered ImageNet dataset, which the authors interpret as evidence that it captures properties specific to scenes. The findings support broadening attention when category information is distributed across the image, while the reported ImageNet result keeps that empirical benefit tied to the scene-classification setting.
summary.tldr: Erasing activated regions and enforcing prediction consistency encourages broader scene focus and improves reported Places365 performance.

title: See More for Scene: Pairwise Consistency Learning for Scene Classification

abstract: In the realm of deep learning, the Fisher information matrix (FIM) gives novel insights and useful tools to characterize the loss landscape, perform second-order optimization, and build geometric learning theories. The exact FIM is either unavailable in closed form or too expensive to compute. In practice, it is almost always estimated based on empirical samples. We investigate two such estimators based on two equivalent representations of the FIM --- both unbiased and consistent. Their estimation quality is naturally gauged by their variance given in closed form. We analyze how the parametric structure of a deep neural network can affect the variance. The meaning of this variance measure and its upper bounds are then discussed in the context of deep learning.

We investigate two such estimators based on two equivalent representations of the FIM --- both unbiased and consistent. The meaning of this variance measure and its upper bounds are then discussed in the context of deep learning.

paragraphs: The Fisher information matrix is used to study neural-network loss landscapes, support second-order optimization, and describe learning geometrically. Computing it exactly is often impractical or impossible in closed form, so applications generally estimate it from samples. This paper examines how much uncertainty those sample-based estimates introduce.

The authors study two estimators derived from mathematically equivalent representations of the Fisher information matrix. Both are unbiased and consistent: they target the correct matrix in expectation and converge appropriately as sampling increases. Those properties do not by themselves describe how much an estimate fluctuates with finite data. The paper derives closed-form variance expressions to characterize that aspect of estimation quality.

The analysis investigates how a deep network's parameter structure affects estimator variance and discusses upper bounds on that variance. This connects the reliability of a Fisher estimate to the model being analyzed. The contribution provides tools for assessing estimation quality when Fisher information is used in deep learning, beyond simply knowing that an estimator has the correct long-run target.
summary.tldr: The paper derives and analyzes the variance of two Fisher information estimators to clarify their reliability for deep neural networks.

title: On the Variance of the Fisher Information for Deep Learning

abstract: We study the approximation power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on latent position random graphs. In the large graph limit, GNNs are known to converge to certain ``continuous'' models known as c-GNNs, which directly enables a study of their approximation power on random graph models. In the absence of input node features however, just as GNNs are limited by the Weisfeiler-Lehman isomorphism test, c-GNNs will be severely limited on simple random graph models. For instance, they will fail to distinguish the communities of a well-separated Stochastic Block Model (SBM) with constant degree function. Thus, we consider recently proposed architectures that augment GNNs with unique node identifiers, referred to as Structural GNNs here (SGNNs). We study the convergence of SGNNs to their continuous counterpart (c-SGNNs) in the large random graph limit, under new conditions on the node identifiers. We then show that c-SGNNs are strictly more powerful than c-GNNs in the continuous limit, and prove their universality on several random graph models of interest, including most SBMs and a large class of random geometric graphs. Our results cover both permutation-invariant and permutation-equivariant architectures.

paragraphs: The paper studies what graph neural networks can approximate on latent-position random graphs as the graphs become very large. In this limit, ordinary GNNs converge to continuous counterparts. Analyzing these limiting models provides a way to investigate expressive power across random graph models rather than examining only individual finite graphs.

Without input node features, the continuous models can have severe limitations. They can fail to distinguish communities even in a well-separated stochastic block model with a constant degree function. The authors therefore study Structural GNNs, which augment networks with unique node identifiers. They establish convergence to continuous structural models under new conditions on those identifiers.

In the continuous limit, the structural models are strictly more expressive than ordinary continuous GNNs. The authors also prove universality for several graph families, including most stochastic block models and a large class of random geometric graphs. The results cover both graph-level outputs unchanged by node relabeling and node-level outputs that follow the relabeling. These guarantees concern the specified random graph families and limiting setting, rather than every possible finite graph.
summary.tldr: Under specified conditions, node identifiers make limiting graph neural networks more expressive and universal on several random graph families.

title: On the Universality of Graph Neural Networks on Large Random Graphs

abstract: Learning object-centric scene representations is essential for attaining structural understanding and abstraction of complex scenes. Yet, as current approaches for unsupervised object-centric representation learning are built upon either a stationary observer assumption or a static scene assumption, they often: i) suffer single-view spatial ambiguities, or ii) infer incorrectly or inaccurately object representations from dynamic scenes. To address this, we propose Dynamics-aware Multi-Object Network (DyMON), a method that broadens the scope of multi-view object-centric representation learning to dynamic scenes. We train DyMON on multi-view-dynamic-scene data and show that DyMON learns---without supervision---to factorize the entangled effects of observer motions and scene object dynamics from a sequence of observations, and constructs scene object spatial representations suitable for rendering at arbitrary times (querying across time) and from arbitrary viewpoints (querying across space). We also show that the factorized scene representations (w.r.t. objects) support querying about a single object by space and time independently.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene as a collection of objects becomes difficult when both the observer and the objects move. A change in an image can arise from either source, and a single viewpoint can leave spatial relationships ambiguous. Earlier unsupervised object-centered approaches often simplify this problem by assuming a stationary observer or an unchanging scene.

Dynamics-aware Multi-Object Network, or DyMON, broadens the setting to dynamic scenes viewed from multiple perspectives. Trained without supervision on such sequences, it learns to separate the effects of observer motion from the dynamics of scene objects. It constructs spatial representations organized around individual objects while accounting for change over time.

The authors show that these representations support rendering at arbitrary queried times and viewpoints. They also support querying an individual object independently across space and time. This means the learned representation exposes more than a sequence of whole-scene appearances: it provides separate access to objects and to the spatial and temporal factors needed to depict them within the demonstrated setting.
summary.tldr: DyMON learns separate representations of objects, observer motion, and scene dynamics to support spatial and temporal queries without supervision.

title: Object-Centric Representation Learning with Generative Spatial-Temporal Factorization

abstract: Implicit planning has emerged as an elegant technique for combining learned models of the world with end-to-end model-free reinforcement learning. We study the class of implicit planners inspired by value iteration, an algorithm that is guaranteed to yield perfect policies in fully-specified tabular environments. We find that prior approaches either assume that the environment is provided in such a tabular form---which is highly restrictive---or infer "local neighbourhoods" of states to run value iteration over---for which we discover an algorithmic bottleneck effect. This effect is caused by explicitly running the planning algorithm based on scalar predictions in every state, which can be harmful to data efficiency if such scalars are improperly predicted. We propose eXecuted Latent Value Iteration Networks (XLVINs), which alleviate the above limitations. Our method performs all planning computations in a high-dimensional latent space, breaking the algorithmic bottleneck. It maintains alignment with value iteration by carefully leveraging neural graph-algorithmic reasoning and contrastive self-supervised learning. Across seven low-data settings---including classical control, navigation and Atari---XLVINs provide significant improvements to data efficiency against value iteration-based implicit planners, as well as relevant model-free baselines. Lastly, we empirically verify that XLVINs can closely align with value iteration.

title: Neural Algorithmic Reasoners are Implicit Planners

abstract: Few-shot NLP research is highly active, yet conducted in disjoint research threads with evaluation suites that lack challenging-yet-realistic testing setups and fail to employ careful experimental design. Consequently, the community does not know which techniques perform best or even if they outperform simple baselines. In response, we formulate the FLEX Principles, a set of requirements and best practices for unified, rigorous, valid, and cost-sensitive few-shot NLP evaluation. These principles include Sample Size Design, a novel approach to benchmark design that optimizes statistical accuracy and precision while keeping evaluation costs manageable. Following the principles, we release the FLEX benchmark, which includes four few-shot transfer settings, zero-shot evaluation, and a public leaderboard that covers diverse NLP tasks. In addition, we present UniFew, a prompt-based model for few-shot learning that unifies pretraining and finetuning prompt formats, eschewing complex machinery of recent prompt-based approaches in adapting downstream task formats to language model pretraining objectives. We demonstrate that despite simplicity, UniFew achieves results competitive with both popular meta-learning and prompt-based approaches.

paragraphs: Few-shot language learning studies adaptation with limited examples, but separate research communities often evaluate methods differently. This paper argues that fragmented evaluations and weak experimental design make it difficult to tell which techniques work best or whether they improve on simple baselines. FLEX addresses the problem at the level of evaluation practice.

The authors introduce principles for rigorous, realistic, unified, and cost-sensitive assessment. One component, Sample Size Design, chooses benchmark designs to improve statistical accuracy and precision while keeping evaluation costs manageable. The resulting FLEX benchmark spans four few-shot transfer settings, includes zero-shot evaluation, and provides a public leaderboard across diverse language tasks.

The paper also introduces UniFew, a prompt-based model that aligns the prompt formats used during pretraining and finetuning. Despite its simplicity, it performs competitively with popular meta-learning and prompt-based methods. Together, the benchmark and model provide a common evaluation framework and a straightforward competitive approach, making comparison across few-shot research directions more meaningful.
summary.tldr: FLEX supplies statistically careful few-shot NLP evaluation, alongside a simple prompt-based model competitive with more elaborate approaches.

title: FLEX: Unifying Evaluation for Few-Shot NLP

abstract: Efficient exploration under sparse rewards remains a key challenge in deep reinforcement learning. Previous exploration methods (e.g., RND) have achieved strong results in multiple hard tasks. However, if there are multiple novel areas to explore, these methods often focus quickly on one without sufficiently trying others (like a depth-wise first search manner). In some scenarios (e.g., four corridor environment in Sec 4.2), we observe they explore in one corridor for long and fail to cover all the states. On the other hand, in theoretical RL, with optimistic initialization and the inverse square root of visitation count as a bonus, it won't suffer from this and explores different novel regions alternatively (like a breadth-first search manner). In this paper, inspired by this, we propose a simple but effective criterion called NovelD by weighting every novel area approximately equally. Our algorithm is very simple but yet shows comparable performance or even outperforms multiple SOTA exploration methods in many hard exploration tasks. Specifically, NovelD solves all the static procedurally-generated tasks in Mini-Grid with just 120M environment steps, without any curriculum learning. In comparison, the previous SOTA only solves 50% of them. NovelD also achieves SOTA on multiple tasks in NetHack, a rogue-like game that contains more challenging procedurally-generated environments. In multiple Atari games (e.g., MonteZuma's Revenge, Venture, Gravitar), NovelD outperforms RND. We analyze NovelD thoroughly in MiniGrid and found that empirically it helps the agent explore the environment more uniformly with a focus on exploring beyond the boundary.

Some novelty-based methods can spend a long time in one unfamiliar region while leaving other unfamiliar regions largely untouched. This paper develops NovelD to address that imbalance by assigning approximately equal weight to different novel areas.

The motivation comes from theoretical exploration methods that combine optimistic initialization with visitation-count bonuses and alternate among novel regions. NovelD turns that inspiration into a simple exploration criterion. In MiniGrid analyses, the authors find that it encourages more uniform exploration while emphasizing movement beyond the boundary of what the agent has explored.

NovelD solves all the evaluated static procedurally generated MiniGrid tasks within 120 million environment steps without curriculum learning; the reported previous state of the art solved half. It also achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple NetHack tasks and beats RND in several Atari games. Across the reported tasks, it matches or exceeds several strong exploration methods, providing empirical support for balancing attention across novel regions.
summary.tldr: NovelD approximately balances attention across novel regions, improving exploration coverage and performance on multiple sparse-reward benchmarks.

title: NovelD: A Simple yet Effective Exploration Criterion

abstract: The adversarial training is a popular tool to remedy the vulnerability of deep learning models against adversarial attacks, and there is rich theoretical literature on the training loss of adversarial training algorithms. In contrast, this paper studies the algorithmic stability of a generic adversarial training algorithm, which can further help to establish an upper bound for generalization error. By figuring out the stability upper bound and lower bound, we argue that the non-differentiability issue of adversarial training causes worse algorithmic stability than their natural counterparts. To tackle this problem, we consider a noise injection method. While the non-differentiability problem seriously affects the stability of adversarial training, injecting noise enables the training trajectory to avoid the occurrence of non-differentiability with dominating probability, hence enhancing the stability performance of adversarial training. Our analysis also studies the relation between the algorithm stability and numerical approximation error of adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to make models less vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper examines its algorithmic stability: how sensitive a training procedure is to changes in its training data. Stability matters because it can help establish an upper bound on generalization error, connecting training behavior to performance beyond the observed samples.

The authors derive both upper and lower stability bounds for a generic adversarial training algorithm. Their analysis attributes worse stability than ordinary training to nondifferentiability in adversarial training. The issue is therefore not just how low the training loss becomes, but how the mathematical behavior of the objective affects sensitivity during learning.

To address this problem, the paper considers injecting noise. The analysis shows that noise allows the training trajectory to avoid nondifferentiability with dominating probability, improving stability. It also examines how stability relates to numerical errors when adversarial attacks are approximated. Together, these results connect generalization analysis to both the objective's irregularities and the computational approximation used during training.
summary.tldr: The paper links weaker stability in adversarial training to nondifferentiability and analyzes noise injection as a remedy.

title: On the Algorithmic Stability of Adversarial Training

abstract: The class imbalance problem, as an important issue in learning node representations, has drawn increasing attention from the community. Although the imbalance considered by existing studies roots from the unequal quantity of labeled examples in different classes (quantity imbalance), we argue that graph data expose a unique source of imbalance from the asymmetric topological properties of the labeled nodes, i.e., labeled nodes are not equal in terms of their structural role in the graph (topology imbalance). In this work, we first probe the previously unknown topology-imbalance issue, including its characteristics, causes, and threats to semisupervised node classification learning. We then provide a unified view to jointly analyzing the quantity- and topology- imbalance issues by considering the node influence shift phenomenon with the Label Propagation algorithm. In light of our analysis, we devise an influence conflict detection–based metric Totoro to measure the degree of graph topology imbalance and propose a model-agnostic method ReNode to address the topology-imbalance issue by re-weighting the influence of labeled nodes adaptively based on their relative positions to class boundaries. Systematic experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our method in relieving topology-imbalance issue and promoting semi-supervised node classification. The further analysis unveils varied sensitivity of different graph neural networks (GNNs) to topology imbalance, which may serve as a new perspective in evaluating GNN architectures.

paragraphs: Class imbalance in graph learning is usually described by counting labeled examples in each class. This paper identifies another source: labeled nodes can occupy structurally unequal positions in a graph. Their influence on learning therefore depends on where they are located, not simply on how many labels each class has.

The authors study this topology imbalance and connect it with quantity imbalance through node-influence shifts under label propagation. They introduce Totoro, a metric based on conflicts in influence, to measure topology imbalance. They also propose ReNode, which adaptively reweights labeled nodes according to their positions relative to class boundaries. The method is designed to work across models.

Systematic experiments show that ReNode reduces the effects of topology imbalance and improves semi-supervised node classification. Further analysis finds that graph neural-network architectures differ in their sensitivity to the issue. The practical implication is that label placement deserves attention alongside label counts: two sets of labeled nodes can provide different learning signals because their structural roles differ, and adaptive weighting can help in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: ReNode addresses unequal structural influence among labeled graph nodes by adaptively reweighting them relative to class boundaries.

title: Topology-Imbalance Learning for Semi-Supervised Node Classification

abstract: Despite the progress in automatic detection of radiologic findings from Chest X-Ray (CXR) images in recent years, a quantitative evaluation of the explainability of these models is hampered by the lack of locally labeled datasets for different findings. With the exception of a few expert-labeled small-scale datasets for specific findings, such as pneumonia and pneumothorax, most of the CXR deep learning models to date are trained on global "weak" labels extracted from text reports, or trained via a joint image and unstructured text learning strategy. Inspired by the Visual Genome effort in the computer vision community, we constructed the first Chest ImaGenome dataset with a scene graph data structure to describe 242,072 images. Local annotations are automatically produced using a joint rule-based natural language processing (NLP) and atlas-based bounding box detection pipeline. Through a radiologist constructed CXR ontology, the annotations for each CXR are connected as an anatomy-centered scene graph, useful for image-level reasoning and multimodal fusion applications. Overall, we provide: i) 1,256 combinations of relation annotations between 29 CXR anatomical locations (objects with bounding box coordinates) and their attributes, structured as a scene graph per image, ii) over 670,000 localized comparison relations (for improved, worsened, or no change) between the anatomical locations across sequential exams, as well as ii) a manually annotated gold standard scene graph dataset from 500 unique patients.

paragraphs: Many chest X-ray models learn from labels describing an entire image or from unstructured reports. Those resources provide limited support for quantitatively evaluating where findings occur and how model explanations relate to anatomy. Chest ImaGenome addresses this gap by organizing annotations for 242,072 images into anatomy-centered scene graphs.

The authors generate local annotations automatically using rule-based processing of reports together with atlas-based detection of anatomical bounding boxes. A radiologist-developed ontology connects anatomical regions and their attributes within each graph. The dataset includes 1,256 combinations of relation annotations involving 29 anatomical locations, giving the image description an explicit structure tied to localized regions.

The resource also contains more than 670,000 localized comparisons across sequential examinations, recording improvement, worsening, or no change. A manually annotated reference set covers 500 unique patients. These components support studying image-level reasoning and combinations of image and text information, while the local structure directly addresses the shortage of anatomy-linked labels described by the authors.
summary.tldr: Chest ImaGenome structures chest X-ray findings and changes over time as localized, anatomy-centered scene graphs.

title: Chest ImaGenome Dataset for Clinical Reasoning

abstract: This paper presents the first large-scale multi-species dataset of acoustic recordings of mosquitoes tracked continuously in free flight. We present 20 hours of audio recordings that we have expertly labelled and tagged precisely in time. Significantly, 18 hours of recordings contain annotations from 36 different species. Mosquitoes are well-known carriers of diseases such as malaria, dengue and yellow fever. Collecting this dataset is motivated by the need to assist applications which utilise mosquito acoustics to conduct surveys to help predict outbreaks and inform intervention policy. The task of detecting mosquitoes from the sound of their wingbeats is challenging due to the difficulty in collecting recordings from realistic scenarios. To address this, as part of the HumBug project, we conducted global experiments to record mosquitoes ranging from those bred in culture cages to mosquitoes captured in the wild. Consequently, the audio recordings vary in signal-to-noise ratio and contain a broad range of indoor and outdoor background environments from Tanzania, Thailand, Kenya, the USA and the UK. In this paper we describe in detail how we collected, labelled and curated the data. The data is provided from a PostgreSQL database, which captures important metadata such as the capture method, age, feeding status and gender of the mosquitoes. Additionally, we provide code to extract features and train Bayesian convolutional neural networks for two key tasks: the identification of mosquitoes from their corresponding background environments, and the classification of detected mosquitoes into species. Our extensive dataset is both challenging to machine learning researchers focusing on acoustic identification, and critical to entomologists, geo-spatial modellers and other domain experts to understand mosquito behaviour, model their distribution, and manage the threat they pose to humans.

paragraphs: HumBugDB provides acoustic recordings for detecting mosquitoes and identifying their species from wingbeat sounds. The motivation is to support mosquito surveys that could inform outbreak prediction and intervention policy. The dataset contains 20 hours of expertly labeled, precisely timed audio, with 18 hours carrying annotations covering 36 species.

Recordings span mosquitoes raised in cages and mosquitoes captured in the wild. They include indoor and outdoor backgrounds from five countries and vary in how clearly mosquito sounds stand out from noise. This variation addresses the challenge of obtaining recordings from realistic conditions. A database also preserves metadata such as capture method, age, feeding status, and sex.

The authors document collection and curation and provide code for feature extraction and Bayesian convolutional neural network training. Two tasks are supported: detecting mosquitoes against their acoustic backgrounds and classifying detected mosquitoes by species. The resource connects machine learning research on difficult audio signals with domain research on mosquito behavior, distribution, and associated threats.
summary.tldr: HumBugDB supplies annotated mosquito audio across species and environments for acoustic detection and species classification.

title: HumBugDB: A Large-scale Acoustic Mosquito Dataset

abstract: We offer an experimental benchmark and empirical study for off-policy policy evaluation (OPE) in reinforcement learning, which is a key problem in many safety critical applications. Given the increasing interest in deploying learning-based methods, there has been a flurry of recent proposals for OPE method, leading to a need for standardized empirical analyses. Our work takes a strong focus on diversity of experimental design to enable stress testing of OPE methods. We provide a comprehensive benchmarking suite to study the interplay of different attributes on method performance. We distill the results into a summarized set of guidelines for OPE in practice. Our software package, the Caltech OPE Benchmarking Suite (COBS), is open-sourced and we invite interested researchers to further contribute to the benchmark.

paragraphs: Off-policy policy evaluation is an important reinforcement learning problem, particularly for applications where evaluating a decision-making method has safety implications. The paper responds to a growing number of proposed evaluation methods by creating an experimental benchmark and an empirical study. Its central motivation is the need for standardized comparisons as interest in deploying learning-based systems increases.

The study emphasizes diversity in experimental design. The benchmarking suite is built to stress-test methods and investigate how different experimental attributes interact to affect performance. This focus matters because a method's empirical behavior can depend on the conditions under which it is assessed. Examining those interactions is therefore part of the benchmark's purpose.

The authors turn their experimental findings into practical guidelines for off-policy evaluation and release the Caltech OPE Benchmarking Suite, or COBS, as open-source software. The contribution joins reusable evaluation infrastructure with guidance derived from experiments. By inviting further contributions, the benchmark also provides a shared starting point for researchers who want to extend the empirical comparison of these methods.
summary.tldr: COBS provides diverse experiments for stress-testing off-policy evaluation methods and distills the resulting evidence into practical guidance.

title: Empirical Study of Off-Policy Policy Evaluation for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Video restoration aims at restoring multiple high-quality frames from multiple low-quality frames. Existing video restoration methods generally fall into two extreme cases, i.e., they either restore all frames in parallel or restore the video frame by frame in a recurrent way, which would result in different merits and drawbacks. Typically, the former has the advantage of temporal information fusion. However, it suffers from large model size and intensive memory consumption; the latter has a relatively small model size as it shares parameters across frames; however, it lacks long-range dependency modeling ability and parallelizability. In this paper, we attempt to integrate the advantages of the two cases by proposing a recurrent video restoration transformer, namely RVRT. RVRT processes local neighboring frames in parallel within a globally recurrent framework which can achieve a good trade-off between model size, effectiveness, and efficiency. Specifically, RVRT divides the video into multiple clips and uses the previously inferred clip feature to estimate the subsequent clip feature. Within each clip, different frame features are jointly updated with implicit feature aggregation. Across different clips, the guided deformable attention is designed for clip-to-clip alignment, which predicts multiple relevant locations from the whole inferred clip and aggregates their features by the attention mechanism. Extensive experiments on video super-resolution, deblurring, and denoising show that the proposed RVRT achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets with balanced model size, testing memory and runtime.

Across different clips, the guided deformable attention is designed for clip-to-clip alignment, which predicts multiple relevant locations from the whole inferred clip and aggregates their features by the attention mechanism. Extensive experiments on video super-resolution, deblurring, and denoising show that the proposed RVRT achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets with balanced model size, testing memory and runtime.

paragraphs: Video restoration can process many frames together or handle them sequentially. Joint processing combines temporal information well but can demand large models and substantial memory. Frame-by-frame recurrence shares parameters efficiently, yet has weaknesses in parallel processing and long-range dependency modeling. RVRT combines these approaches within one restoration architecture.

The model divides a video into clips. Neighboring frames inside each clip are processed in parallel, with their features updated jointly. Across clips, a recurrent structure uses features inferred for the previous clip to help estimate the next. This arrangement combines local parallel processing with information carried through the video.

Guided deformable attention aligns information between clips by predicting multiple relevant locations in the previously inferred clip and aggregating their features through attention. Experiments cover video super-resolution, deblurring, and denoising. The paper reports state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets alongside a balance of model size, testing memory, and runtime. The contribution is a concrete architectural compromise between restoration quality and the resources required to combine information across frames.
summary.tldr: RVRT combines parallel processing within clips and recurrent attention across clips to restore video with strong quality and balanced resource use.

title: Recurrent Video Restoration Transformer with Guided Deformable Attention

abstract: One unique property of time series is that the temporal relations are largely preserved after downsampling into two sub-sequences. By taking advantage of this property, we propose a novel neural network architecture that conducts sample convolution and interaction for temporal modeling and forecasting, named SCINet. Specifically, SCINet is a recursive downsample-convolve-interact architecture. In each layer, we use multiple convolutional filters to extract distinct yet valuable temporal features from the downsampled sub-sequences or features. By combining these rich features aggregated from multiple resolutions, SCINet effectively models time series with complex temporal dynamics. Experimental results show that SCINet achieves significant forecasting accuracy improvements over both existing convolutional models and Transformer-based solutions across various real-world time series forecasting datasets. Our codes and data are available at https://github.com/cure-lab/SCINet.

At each layer, multiple convolutional filters extract different temporal features from the subsequences or their features. Repeating this process produces information at multiple resolutions, which the model combines to represent the dynamics of the series.

The paper reports significant forecasting accuracy improvements over existing convolutional models and Transformer-based approaches across several real-world datasets. These results support the usefulness of combining features from multiple temporal resolutions with interaction between subsequences. The architectural contribution is the coordinated downsample–convolve–interact process: it uses the persistence of temporal relationships after downsampling as a basis for learning richer forecasting representations.
summary.tldr: SCINet combines convolution and interaction across recursively downsampled time series to improve forecasting on the evaluated real-world datasets.

title: SCINet: Time Series Modeling and Forecasting with Sample Convolution and Interaction

abstract: Modern multi-agent reinforcement learning frameworks rely on centralized training and reward shaping to perform well. However, centralized training and dense rewards are not readily available in the real world. Current multi-agent algorithms struggle to learn in the alternative setup of decentralized training or sparse rewards. To address these issues, we propose a self-supervised intrinsic reward \textit{ELIGN - expectation alignment - } inspired by the self-organization principle in Zoology. Similar to how animals collaborate in a decentralized manner with those in their vicinity, agents trained with expectation alignment learn behaviors that match their neighbors' expectations. This allows the agents to learn collaborative behaviors without any external reward or centralized training. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach across 6 tasks in the multi-agent particle and the complex Google Research football environments, comparing ELIGN to sparse and curiosity-based intrinsic rewards. When the number of agents increases, ELIGN scales well in all multi-agent tasks except for one where agents have different capabilities. We show that agent coordination improves through expectation alignment because agents learn to divide tasks amongst themselves, break coordination symmetries, and confuse adversaries. These results identify tasks where expectation alignment is a more useful strategy than curiosity-driven exploration for multi-agent coordination, enabling agents to do zero-shot coordination.

Inspired by decentralized cooperation among animals, the method encourages agents to behave in ways that match what nearby agents expect.

This reward provides a self-supervised basis for collaboration without requiring external rewards or centralized training. The findings identify settings where matching others' expectations is more useful for coordination than curiosity-driven exploration. They also demonstrate zero-shot coordination, supporting expectation alignment as a practical learning signal for the studied multi-agent problems.
summary.tldr: ELIGN encourages decentralized cooperation by rewarding agents for matching their neighbors' expectations.

title: ELIGN: Expectation Alignment as a Multi-Agent Intrinsic Reward

abstract: One of the most overlooked challenges in dance generation is that the auto-regressive frameworks are prone to freezing motions due to noise accumulation. In this paper, we present two modules that can be plugged into the existing models to enable them to generate non-freezing and high fidelity dances. Since the high-dimensional motion data are easily swamped by noise, we propose to learn a low-dimensional manifold representation by an auto-encoder with a bank of latent codes, which can be used to reduce the noise in the predicted motions, thus preventing from freezing. We further extend the bank to provide explicit priors about the future motions to disambiguate motion prediction, which helps the predictors to generate motions with larger magnitude and higher fidelity than possible before. Extensive experiments on AIST++, a public large-scale 3D dance motion benchmark, demonstrate that our method notably outperforms the baselines in terms of quality, diversity and time length.
