We show that through this interpretation it is both efficient and straightforward to improve the approximation by employing normalizing flows while still allowing for local reparametrizations and a tractable lower bound. In experiments we show that with this new approximation we can significantly improve upon classical mean field for Bayesian neural networks on both predictive accuracy as well as predictive uncertainty.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian neural networks learn an approximation to a posterior distribution, making the quality of that approximation important for prediction and uncertainty. This paper offers a way to improve it by reinterpreting multiplicative noise in the network. The noise becomes auxiliary random variables that augment the approximate posterior.

With this interpretation, normalizing flows can make the approximation more expressive. The authors show that the construction remains efficient and straightforward while preserving local reparameterizations and a tractable lower bound. These properties matter together: a richer probability model is useful for learning only if the resulting training objective and computations remain manageable.

Experiments compare the new approximation with classical mean-field inference for Bayesian neural networks. The authors report significant improvements in both predictive accuracy and predictive uncertainty. The contribution thus joins a probabilistic reinterpretation of multiplicative noise with an implementable inference method, and the reported results show benefits for both the predictions themselves and the uncertainty accompanying them.
summary.tldr: Treating multiplicative noise as auxiliary variables enables richer flow-based Bayesian approximations with improved reported accuracy and uncertainty.

title: Multiplicative Normalizing Flows for Variational Bayesian Neural Networks

abstract: Popular approaches to differential privacy, such as the Laplace and exponential mechanisms, calibrate randomised smoothing through global sensitivity of the target non-private function. Bounding such sensitivity is often a prohibitively complex analytic calculation. As an alternative, we propose a straightforward sampler for estimating sensitivity of non-private mechanisms. Since our sensitivity estimates hold with high probability, any mechanism that would be $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differentially private under bounded global sensitivity automatically achieves $(\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)$-random differential privacy (Hall et al. 2012), without any target-specific calculations required. We demonstrate on worked example learners how our usable approach adopts a naturally-relaxed privacy guarantee, while achieving more accurate releases even for non-private functions that are black-box computer programs.

Since our sensitivity estimates hold with high probability, any mechanism that would be $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differentially private under bounded global sensitivity automatically achieves $(\epsilon,\delta,\gamma)$-random differential privacy (Hall et al. 2012), without any target-specific calculations required. paragraphs: Many differential-privacy mechanisms set their randomization using a function's global sensitivity. Deriving a suitable sensitivity bound analytically can be difficult, especially when the function is a complicated program. This paper replaces target-specific sensitivity calculations with a straightforward sampling procedure that estimates sensitivity from the non-private mechanism.

The estimates hold with high probability, so the resulting privacy statement is correspondingly relaxed. A mechanism that would provide epsilon-delta differential privacy with a bounded global sensitivity instead obtains epsilon-delta-gamma random differential privacy through this approach. The distinction is central: sampling makes calibration easier by supporting a probabilistic guarantee rather than supplying a universal global-sensitivity bound.

Worked examples with learning algorithms demonstrate how the procedure can be used, including when the non-private function is available as a black-box computer program. The authors report more accurate releases while adopting the relaxed guarantee. The contribution combines practical accessibility with an explicit change in the privacy assurance, making the cost of avoiding specialized analytical calculations part of the method itself.
summary.tldr: Sampling-based sensitivity estimates simplify privacy calibration while providing a relaxed random differential privacy guarantee and improved accuracy in worked examples.

title: Pain-Free Random Differential Privacy with Sensitivity Sampling

abstract: The cornerstone underpinning deep learning is the guarantee that gradient descent on an objective converges to local minima. Unfortunately, this guarantee fails in settings, such as generative adversarial nets, where there are multiple interacting losses. The behavior of gradient-based methods in games is not well understood – and is becoming increasingly important as adversarial and multi-objective architectures proliferate. In this paper, we develop new techniques to understand and control the dynamics in general games. The key result is to decompose the second-order dynamics into two components. The first is related to potential games, which reduce to gradient descent on an implicit function; the second relates to Hamiltonian games, a new class of games that obey a conservation law, akin to conservation laws in classical mechanical systems. The decomposition motivates Symplectic Gradient Adjustment (SGA), a new algorithm for finding stable fixed points in general games. Basic experiments show SGA is competitive with recently proposed algorithms for finding local Nash equilibria in GANs – whilst at the same time being applicable to – and having guarantees in – much more general games.

paragraphs: Training systems with several interacting losses, such as generative adversarial networks, introduces dynamics that differ from minimizing a single objective. This paper develops tools for understanding and controlling gradient-based learning in general differentiable games. Its starting point is that familiar convergence reasoning for single-objective optimization does not carry over directly to these interactions.

The key result decomposes second-order game dynamics into two components. One relates to potential games, whose behavior can be understood through gradient descent on an implicit function. The other relates to Hamiltonian games, introduced here as a class obeying a conservation law analogous to those in classical mechanics. This separates two distinct mathematical contributions to the learning dynamics.

The authors also establish applicability and guarantees in more general games, connecting the dynamical analysis to an optimization method with scope beyond the experimental GAN setting.
summary.tldr: Decomposing game dynamics into potential and Hamiltonian components motivates Symplectic Gradient Adjustment for finding stable fixed points.

title: The Mechanics of n-Player Differentiable Games

abstract: Many important structured prediction problems, including learning to rank items, correspondence-based natural language processing, and multi-object tracking, can be formulated as weighted bipartite matching optimizations. Existing structured prediction approaches have significant drawbacks when applied under the constraints of perfect bipartite matchings. Exponential family probabilistic models, such as the conditional random field (CRF), provide statistical consistency guarantees, but suffer computationally from the need to compute the normalization term of its distribution over matchings, which is a #P-hard matrix permanent computation. In contrast, the structured support vector machine (SSVM) provides computational efficiency, but lacks Fisher consistency, meaning that there are distributions of data for which it cannot learn the optimal matching even under ideal learning conditions (i.e., given the true distribution and selecting from all measurable potential functions). We propose adversarial bipartite matching to avoid both of these limitations. We develop this approach algorithmically, establish its computational efficiency and Fisher consistency properties, and apply it to matching problems that demonstrate its empirical benefits.

paragraphs: Several structured prediction tasks can be expressed as choosing a weighted matching between two sets. Examples in the abstract include ranking, language-processing correspondences, and tracking multiple objects. Requiring a perfect matching creates difficulties for learning methods that otherwise offer attractive computational or statistical properties.

Conditional random fields provide statistical consistency, but normalizing their distribution over matchings requires a matrix permanent computation, which is #P-hard. Structured support vector machines offer computational efficiency but lack Fisher consistency. Consequently, for some data distributions they cannot recover the optimal matching even with the true distribution and an unrestricted choice of measurable potential functions.

The paper introduces adversarial bipartite matching to address both drawbacks. The authors develop an algorithm, establish computational efficiency and Fisher consistency, and demonstrate empirical benefits on matching problems. Fisher consistency concerns ideal learning conditions; it supports the suitability of the learning formulation rather than guaranteeing perfect predictions from finite data. The contribution combines that statistical property with an efficient computational approach.
summary.tldr: Adversarial bipartite matching combines computational efficiency with Fisher consistency for structured prediction under perfect-matching constraints.

title: Efficient and Consistent Adversarial Bipartite Matching

abstract: Stochastic variance reduction algorithms have recently become popular for minimizing the average of a large, but finite number of loss functions on a Riemannian manifold. The present paper proposes a Riemannian stochastic recursive gradient algorithm (R-SRG), which does not require the inverse of retraction between two distant iterates on the manifold. Convergence analyses of R-SRG are performed on both retraction-convex and non-convex functions under computationally efficient retraction and vector transport operations. The key challenge is analysis of the influence of vector transport along the retraction curve. Numerical evaluations reveal that R-SRG competes well with state-of-the-art Riemannian batch and stochastic gradient algorithms.

The key challenge is analysis of the influence of vector transport along the retraction curve. paragraphs: Some optimization problems constrain their solutions to a curved space called a Riemannian manifold. This paper studies objectives that average a large but finite collection of losses in that setting. It proposes Riemannian stochastic recursive gradient, or R-SRG, within the broader effort to reduce the variability of stochastic optimization updates.

A distinguishing feature is that R-SRG does not require an inverse retraction between distant iterates. Retraction and vector transport are the operations used to move on the manifold and handle update directions as the location changes. Avoiding that inverse operation shapes the algorithm’s computational requirements while retaining efficient retraction and transport operations.

The authors analyze convergence for both retraction-convex and non-convex objectives. A central technical challenge is accounting for the effect of vector transport along the retraction curve. Numerical evaluations show that R-SRG competes well with leading Riemannian batch and stochastic-gradient methods, providing empirical support for the algorithm alongside its convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: R-SRG provides analyzed stochastic optimization on manifolds without requiring inverse retractions between distant iterates.

title: Riemannian Stochastic Recursive Gradient Algorithm

abstract: We investigate regularized algorithms combining with projection for least-squares regression problem over a Hilbert space, covering nonparametric regression over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We prove convergence results with respect to variants of norms, under a capacity assumption on the hypothesis space and a regularity condition on the target function. As a result, we obtain optimal rates for regularized algorithms with randomized sketches, provided that the sketch dimension is proportional to the effective dimension up to a logarithmic factor. As a byproduct, we obtain similar results for Nyström regularized algorithms. Our results provide optimal, distribution-dependent rates for sketched/Nyström regularized algorithms, considering both the attainable and non-attainable cases.

We prove convergence results with respect to variants of norms, under a capacity assumption on the hypothesis space and a regularity condition on the target function. As a result, we obtain optimal rates for regularized algorithms with randomized sketches, provided that the sketch dimension is proportional to the effective dimension up to a logarithmic factor. As a byproduct, we obtain similar results for Nyström regularized algorithms. Our results provide optimal, distribution-dependent rates for sketched/Nyström regularized algorithms, considering both the attainable and non-attainable cases.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes least-squares regression methods that combine regularization with projection into a reduced space. The framework covers Hilbert spaces, including reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces used for nonparametric regression. The central issue is how much the problem can be compressed while preserving strong convergence guarantees.

The authors prove convergence results under a capacity assumption on the hypothesis space and a regularity condition on the target function. For randomized sketches, they obtain optimal rates when the sketch dimension scales with the effective dimension, up to a logarithmic factor. This provides a sufficient relationship between the size of the reduced problem and the statistical structure that must be retained.

Related results also follow for Nyström regularized methods. The rates depend on the data distribution and cover both attainable and non-attainable settings, allowing the target to lie inside or outside the hypothesis space. The contribution is a conditional theoretical justification for reduced-dimensional regression: appropriately sized projections can preserve optimal rates under the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under capacity and regularity assumptions, sufficiently large randomized sketches preserve optimal convergence rates for regularized least-squares regression.

title: Optimal Rates of Sketched-regularized Algorithms for Least-Squares Regression over Hilbert Spaces

abstract: Stochastic differential equations are an important modeling class in many disciplines. Consequently, there exist many methods relying on various discretization and numerical integration schemes. In this paper, we propose a novel, probabilistic model for estimating the drift and diffusion given noisy observations of the underlying stochastic system. Using state-of-the-art adversarial and moment matching inference techniques, we avoid the discretization schemes of classical approaches. This leads to significant improvements in parameter accuracy and robustness given random initial guesses. On four established benchmark systems, we compare the performance of our algorithms to state-of-the-art solutions based on extended Kalman filtering and Gaussian processes.

On four established benchmark systems, we compare the performance of our algorithms to state-of-the-art solutions based on extended Kalman filtering and Gaussian processes.

paragraphs: Stochastic differential equations describe systems with both systematic dynamics and random variation. Learning such a system from noisy observations requires estimating its drift and diffusion. Many existing approaches rely on discretization and numerical integration schemes, making those procedures part of the parameter-estimation process.

The paper proposes a probabilistic model for estimating drift and diffusion using adversarial and moment-matching inference techniques. These provide the basis for the AReS and MaRS approaches named in the title. Their key methodological distinction is that they avoid the discretization schemes used by classical approaches when learning from observations of the stochastic system.

The authors report significant improvements in parameter accuracy and robustness to random initial guesses. They evaluate the algorithms on four established benchmark systems, comparing them with state-of-the-art approaches based on extended Kalman filtering and Gaussian processes. These findings connect the change in inference strategy to two practical concerns: recovering accurate parameters from noisy data and obtaining dependable estimates when the starting parameter guesses vary.
summary.tldr: AReS and MaRS estimate stochastic-system dynamics through adversarial and moment-matching inference, improving reported accuracy and robustness to initialization.

title: AReS and MaRS Adversarial and MMD-Minimizing Regression for SDEs

abstract: We propose a general framework for denoising high-dimensional measurements which requires no prior on the signal, no estimate of the noise, and no clean training data. The only assumption is that the noise exhibits statistical independence across different dimensions of the measurement, while the true signal exhibits some correlation. For a broad class of functions (“$\mathcal{J}$-invariant”), it is then possible to estimate the performance of a denoiser from noisy data alone. This allows us to calibrate $\mathcal{J}$-invariant versions of any parameterised denoising algorithm, from the single hyperparameter of a median filter to the millions of weights of a deep neural network. We demonstrate this on natural image and microscopy data, where we exploit noise independence between pixels, and on single-cell gene expression data, where we exploit independence between detections of individual molecules. This framework generalizes recent work on training neural nets from noisy images and on cross-validation for matrix factorization.

This framework generalizes recent work on training neural nets from noisy images and on cross-validation for matrix factorization.

paragraphs: Noise2Self addresses denoising when clean training examples, a signal prior, and an estimate of the noise are unavailable. Its key assumption separates signal from noise structurally: noise is statistically independent across measurement dimensions, while the underlying signal has some correlation. That distinction makes noisy measurements themselves useful for evaluating a denoiser.

The authors show that performance can be estimated from noisy data alone for a broad class of functions called J-invariant functions. This enables calibration of J-invariant versions of parameterized denoising algorithms. The scope ranges from selecting a median filter’s single hyperparameter to learning the many weights of a deep neural network.

Demonstrations cover natural images and microscopy, using independence of noise between pixels, and single-cell gene expression, using independence between individual molecule detections. The framework also generalizes earlier approaches to learning from noisy images and cross-validating matrix factorization. Its value comes from replacing clean supervision with the stated independence structure, making that assumption central to the method.
summary.tldr: Noise2Self calibrates denoisers using noisy data alone by exploiting independent noise across dimensions and correlated underlying signals.

title: Noise2Self: Blind Denoising by Self-Supervision

abstract: Annotating datasets is one of the main costs in nowadays supervised learning. The goal of weak supervision is to enable models to learn using only forms of labelling which are cheaper to collect, as partial labelling. This is a type of incomplete annotation where, for each datapoint, supervision is cast as a set of labels containing the real one. The problem of supervised learning with partial labelling has been studied for specific instances such as classification, multi-label, ranking or segmentation, but a general framework is still missing. This paper provides a unified framework based on structured prediction and on the concept of \emph{infimum loss} to deal with partial labelling over a wide family of learning problems and loss functions. The framework leads naturally to explicit algorithms that can be easily implemented and for which proved statistical consistency and learning rates. Experiments confirm the superiority of the proposed approach over commonly used baselines.

This is a type of incomplete annotation where, for each datapoint, supervision is cast as a set of labels containing the real one. The problem of supervised learning with partial labelling has been studied for specific instances such as classification, multi-label, ranking or segmentation, but a general framework is still missing. This paper provides a unified framework based on structured prediction and on the concept of \emph{infimum loss} to deal with partial labelling over a wide family of learning problems and loss functions. The framework leads naturally to explicit algorithms that can be easily implemented and for which proved statistical consistency and learning rates. Experiments confirm the superiority of the proposed approach over commonly used baselines.

paragraphs: Collecting precise labels is a major expense in supervised learning. Partial labeling offers a cheaper form of supervision: each example comes with a set of possible labels that contains the correct one. This paper develops a unified approach to learning from that ambiguity across problems such as classification, ranking, multilabel prediction, and segmentation.

The framework combines structured prediction with the infimum loss. This organizes learning around the least loss available among the candidate labels, giving a common way to handle incomplete annotation across a broad family of prediction problems and loss functions. The essential supervision assumption is that the supplied candidate set includes the true label.

The framework leads to explicit algorithms that the authors describe as easy to implement. They prove statistical consistency and learning rates, providing theoretical support for learning from partial labels. Experiments show better performance than commonly used baselines in the evaluated settings. The contribution is a shared formulation that connects practical algorithms and statistical guarantees, reducing the need to treat each partially labeled prediction problem as an unrelated special case.
summary.tldr: An infimum-loss framework unifies learning from candidate label sets across structured prediction tasks, with algorithms and statistical guarantees.

title: Structured Prediction with Partial Labelling through the Infimum Loss

abstract: The current paradigm of deep neural networks has been successful in part due to the use of normalization layers. Normalization layers like Batch Normalization, Layer Normalization and Weight Normalization are ubiquitous in practice as they improve the generalization performance and training speed of neural networks significantly. Nonetheless, the vast majority of current deep learning theory and non-convex optimization literature focuses on the un-normalized setting. We bridge this gap by providing the first global convergence result for 2 layer non-linear neural networks with ReLU activations trained with a normalization layer, namely Weight Normalization. The analysis shows how the introduction of normalization layers changes the optimization landscape and in some settings enables faster convergence as compared with un-normalized neural networks.

Normalization layers like Batch Normalization, Layer Normalization and Weight Normalization are ubiquitous in practice as they improve the generalization performance and training speed of neural networks significantly. Nonetheless, the vast majority of current deep learning theory and non-convex optimization literature focuses on the un-normalized setting. We bridge this gap by providing the first global convergence result for 2 layer non-linear neural networks with ReLU activations trained with a normalization layer, namely Weight Normalization. The analysis shows how the introduction of normalization layers changes the optimization landscape and in some settings enables faster convergence as compared with un-normalized neural networks.

paragraphs: Normalization layers are widely used to improve neural-network training speed and generalization, yet much optimization theory studies networks without them. This paper addresses that mismatch by analyzing a two-layer network with ReLU activations and Weight Normalization. The focus is on how normalization affects the mathematical behavior of training.

The authors provide a global convergence result for this normalized nonlinear network setting. Their analysis examines how adding normalization changes the optimization landscape, connecting a practical architectural choice to the trajectories and convergence of training. Weight Normalization is the specific normalization mechanism covered by the result, rather than every normalization layer mentioned as motivation.

The analysis also shows that normalization can enable faster convergence than an unnormalized network in some settings. That qualification matters: the abstract does not claim that normalization always accelerates training. The contribution supplies theoretical support for a particular normalized architecture and identifies circumstances where the altered landscape helps optimization, narrowing the gap between common training practice and the settings typically treated by theory.
summary.tldr: The paper proves global convergence for two-layer ReLU networks with Weight Normalization and shows faster convergence in some settings.

title: Optimization Theory for ReLU Neural Networks Trained with Normalization Layers

abstract: When training an estimator such as a neural network for tasks like image denoising, it is often preferred to train one estimator and apply it to all noise levels. The de facto training protocol to achieve this goal is to train the estimator with noisy samples whose noise levels are uniformly distributed across the range of interest. However, why should we allocate the samples uniformly? Can we have more training samples that are less noisy, and fewer samples that are more noisy? What is the optimal distribution? How do we obtain such a distribution? The goal of this paper is to address this training sample distribution problem from a minimax risk optimization perspective. We derive a dual ascent algorithm to determine the optimal sampling distribution of which the convergence is guaranteed as long as the set of admissible estimators is closed and convex. For estimators with non-convex admissible sets such as deep neural networks, our dual formulation converges to a solution of the convex relaxation. We discuss how the algorithm can be implemented in practice. We evaluate the algorithm on linear estimators and deep networks.

However, why should we allocate the samples uniformly? Can we have more training samples that are less noisy, and fewer samples that are more noisy? What is the optimal distribution? How do we obtain such a distribution? The goal of this paper is to address this training sample distribution problem from a minimax risk optimization perspective. We derive a dual ascent algorithm to determine the optimal sampling distribution of which the convergence is guaranteed as long as the set of admissible estimators is closed and convex. For estimators with non-convex admissible sets such as deep neural networks, our dual formulation converges to a solution of the convex relaxation. We discuss how the algorithm can be implemented in practice. We evaluate the algorithm on linear estimators and deep networks.

paragraphs: A single denoiser is often trained to handle a range of noise levels by sampling those levels uniformly. This paper questions whether equal allocation is the best use of training examples. The central problem is how to distribute samples across noise levels when the same estimator must serve the whole range.

The authors formulate this choice through minimax risk optimization, making performance under the most demanding conditions central to selecting the sampling distribution. They derive a dual ascent algorithm for finding the optimal distribution. Its convergence guarantee requires the admissible set of estimators to be closed and convex, so the mathematical structure of the estimator family matters.

Deep neural networks generally involve nonconvex admissible sets. In that case, the stated convergence result applies to a solution of the convex relaxation rather than directly establishing the original nonconvex optimum. The paper discusses practical implementation and evaluates the algorithm with linear estimators and deep networks, treating the training distribution itself as a quantity to optimize.
summary.tldr: The paper optimizes how denoising examples are allocated across noise levels, with convergence guarantees that depend on the estimator family.

title: One Size Fits All: Can We Train One Denoiser for All Noise Levels?

abstract: We consider the problem of approximating the stationary distribution of an ergodic Markov chain given a set of sampled transitions. Classical simulation-based approaches assume access to the underlying process so that trajectories of sufficient length can be gathered to approximate stationary sampling. Instead, we consider an alternative setting where a \emph{fixed} set of transitions has been collected beforehand, by a separate, possibly unknown procedure. The goal is still to estimate properties of the stationary distribution, but without additional access to the underlying system. We propose a consistent estimator that is based on recovering a correction ratio function over the given data. In particular, we develop a variational power method (VPM) that provides provably consistent estimates under general conditions. In addition to unifying a number of existing approaches from different subfields, we also find that VPM yields significantly better estimates across a range of problems, including queueing, stochastic differential equations, post-processing MCMC, and off-policy evaluation.

Unlike simulation-based approaches, the learner cannot return to the underlying system and gather longer trajectories. The available transitions may also have been collected by a separate procedure whose details are unknown.

The proposed estimator recovers a correction ratio function over the recorded data. That correction is the basis for estimating properties of the stationary distribution despite the way the batch was collected. The authors develop this idea into a variational power method and prove that its estimates are consistent under general conditions.

Consistency gives the approach a theoretical foundation for recovering the desired quantities as the available information grows under those conditions. The method also unifies approaches from several research areas. Empirically, it produces substantially better estimates across the reported problems, including queueing, stochastic differential equations, processing existing Markov chain Monte Carlo output, and off-policy evaluation. Its practical relevance lies in extracting long-run information when further interaction with the system is unavailable.
summary.tldr: A variational power method estimates stationary-distribution properties from a fixed transition batch without further access to the system.

title: Batch Stationary Distribution Estimation

abstract: We propose a novel method for federated learning that is customized specifically to the objective of a given edge device. In our proposed method, a server trains a global meta-model by collaborating with devices without actually sharing data. The trained global meta-model is then personalized locally by each device to meet its specific objective. Different from the conventional federated learning setting, training customized models for each device is hindered by both the inherent data biases of the various devices, as well as the requirements imposed by the federated architecture. We propose gradient correction methods leveraging prior works, and explicitly de-bias the meta-model in the distributed heterogeneous data setting to learn personalized device models. We present convergence guarantees of our method for strongly convex, convex and nonconvex meta objectives. We empirically evaluate the performance of our method on benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant communication savings.

paragraphs: Federated learning can support devices with different objectives by learning a shared starting point that each device later personalizes. This paper develops that approach through a global meta-model trained collaboratively without sharing device data. Each device then adapts the resulting model locally to its own objective, making personalization central to the training goal.

The challenge comes from both differences in device data and the constraints of federated training. Updates based on heterogeneous local datasets can bias the shared meta-model. The authors propose gradient corrections, building on prior work, that explicitly address this bias in the distributed setting. The corrections are designed to improve the shared model's usefulness for learning personalized device models.

The paper supplies convergence guarantees for strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex meta-objectives. It also evaluates the method on benchmark datasets and reports significant communication savings. These findings support both the optimization behavior of the approach and its communication efficiency in the experiments. The contribution ties together local customization, correction of heterogeneous updates, and a shared training procedure that does not require exchanging the underlying data.
summary.tldr: Gradient corrections debias a federated meta-model for device-specific personalization, with convergence guarantees and significant communication savings on benchmarks.

title: Debiasing Model Updates for Improving Personalized Federated Training

abstract: Recent work has highlighted the role of initialization scale in determining the structure of the solutions that gradient methods converge to. In particular, it was shown that large initialization leads to the neural tangent kernel regime solution, whereas small initialization leads to so called “rich regimes”. However, the initialization structure is richer than the overall scale alone and involves relative magnitudes of different weights and layers in the network. Here we show that these relative scales, which we refer to as initialization shape, play an important role in determining the learned model. We develop a novel technique for deriving the inductive bias of gradient-flow and use it to obtain closed-form implicit regularizers for multiple cases of interest.

paragraphs: A neural network's starting weights can influence the kind of model training produces. Earlier work emphasized their overall scale, connecting large initialization to a neural tangent kernel regime and small initialization to richer regimes. This paper investigates information about the starting configuration that a single overall magnitude does not capture.

The authors call this additional structure initialization shape: the relative magnitudes of different weights and layers. They show that these relationships play an important role in determining the learned model. The implication is that understanding initialization requires examining how magnitude is distributed through the network, alongside how large the initialization is overall.

To analyze that effect, the paper develops a technique for deriving the inductive bias of gradient flow, a continuous-time description of gradient-based training. The technique produces closed-form implicit regularizers in multiple cases of interest. These expressions make the preferences induced by training mathematically explicit, providing a way to study how relative initialization scales influence the solutions favored by the learning dynamics.
summary.tldr: Relative weight and layer scales at initialization influence learned models, and a new gradient-flow analysis makes this implicit bias explicit in several cases.

title: On the Implicit Bias of Initialization Shape: Beyond Infinitesimal Mirror Descent

abstract: Marginalized importance sampling (MIS), which measures the density ratio between the state-action occupancy of a target policy and that of a sampling distribution, is a promising approach for off-policy evaluation. However, current state-of-the-art MIS methods rely on complex optimization tricks and succeed mostly on simple toy problems. We bridge the gap between MIS and deep reinforcement learning by observing that the density ratio can be computed from the successor representation of the target policy. The successor representation can be trained through deep reinforcement learning methodology and decouples the reward optimization from the dynamics of the environment, making the resulting algorithm stable and applicable to high-dimensional domains. We evaluate the empirical performance of our approach on a variety of challenging Atari and MuJoCo environments.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation asks how a policy would perform using data collected under a different sampling process. Marginalized importance sampling addresses this by comparing how frequently the target policy and the data source visit different state-action pairs. Estimating that ratio is central to the method, but the paper describes existing approaches as difficult to optimize and mostly successful on simple problems.

The paper connects this estimation problem to the target policy’s successor representation, which describes its future visitation behavior. Its key observation is that the required density ratio can be computed from this representation. That makes it possible to train the relevant representation using deep reinforcement learning methods while separating reward optimization from environmental dynamics.

The authors present this separation as a route to a stable algorithm that can operate in high-dimensional settings. They evaluate the approach on challenging Atari and MuJoCo environments. The contribution is a different computational route to importance weights, connecting off-policy evaluation to representation-learning machinery suitable for more complex environments.
summary.tldr: The paper computes marginalized importance-sampling ratios through successor representations, connecting off-policy evaluation to deep reinforcement learning.

title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach to Marginalized Importance Sampling with the Successor Representation

abstract: Individuality is essential in human society. It induces the division of labor and thus improves the efficiency and productivity. Similarly, it should also be a key to multi-agent cooperation. Inspired by that individuality is of being an individual separate from others, we propose a simple yet efficient method for the emergence of individuality (EOI) in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). EOI learns a probabilistic classifier that predicts a probability distribution over agents given their observation and gives each agent an intrinsic reward of being correctly predicted by the classifier. The intrinsic reward encourages the agents to visit their own familiar observations, and learning the classifier by such observations makes the intrinsic reward signals stronger and in turn makes the agents more identifiable. To further enhance the intrinsic reward and promote the emergence of individuality, two regularizers are proposed to increase the discriminability of the classifier. We implement EOI on top of popular MARL algorithms. Empirically, we show that EOI outperforms existing methods in a variety of multi-agent cooperative scenarios.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents may benefit from developing distinct patterns of behavior, creating opportunities for a division of labor. This paper proposes emergence of individuality, or EOI, as a way to encourage such differentiation in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Its mechanism rewards agents for becoming recognizable from their observations.

EOI trains a probabilistic classifier to predict which agent produced a given observation. An agent receives an intrinsic reward when the classifier correctly identifies it. This encourages agents to revisit observations associated with themselves. Training the classifier on those observations strengthens the identification signal, producing a reinforcing interaction between behavior and classification.

The authors add two regularizers that improve the classifier's ability to distinguish agents and thereby strengthen the intrinsic reward. They implement EOI on top of popular multi-agent learning algorithms and report better performance than existing methods across varied cooperative scenarios. The experiments support individuality as a useful training incentive in those settings, without requiring the method to assign a predefined role to each agent.
summary.tldr: EOI encourages distinctive agent behavior through identification-based intrinsic rewards and improves performance in tested cooperative multi-agent settings.

title: The Emergence of Individuality

abstract: This paper presents {\em Gem}, a model-agnostic approach for providing interpretable explanations for any GNNs on various graph learning tasks. Specifically, we formulate the problem of providing explanations for the decisions of GNNs as a causal learning task. Then we train a causal explanation model equipped with a loss function based on Granger causality. Different from existing explainers for GNNs, {\em Gem} explains GNNs on graph-structured data from a causal perspective. It has better generalization ability as it has no requirements on the internal structure of the GNNs or prior knowledge on the graph learning tasks. In addition, {\em Gem}, once trained, can be used to explain the target GNN very quickly. Our theoretical analysis shows that several recent explainers fall into a unified framework of {\em additive feature attribution methods}. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets show that {\em Gem} achieves a relative increase of the explanation accuracy by up to $30%$ and speeds up the explanation process by up to $110\times$ as compared to its state-of-the-art alternatives.

Once the explanation model has been trained, it can explain the target GNN quickly, separating the initial learning effort from the cost of producing subsequent explanations.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report relative explanation-accuracy improvements of up to 30% and explanation speedups of up to 110 times over the compared alternatives. These are reported upper-end gains, supporting both explanation quality and efficiency in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Gem learns model-agnostic GNN explanations using a Granger-causality-based objective, with reported gains in explanation accuracy and speed.

title: Generative Causal Explanations for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is among the most effective and widely-used blackbox optimization methods. BO proposes solutions according to an explore-exploit trade-off criterion encoded in an acquisition function, many of which are computed from the posterior predictive of a probabilistic surrogate model. Prevalent among these is the expected improvement (EI). The need to ensure analytical tractability of the predictive often poses limitations that can hinder the efficiency and applicability of BO. In this paper, we cast the computation of EI as a binary classification problem, building on the link between class-probability estimation and density-ratio estimation, and the lesser-known link between density-ratios and EI. By circumventing the tractability constraints, this reformulation provides numerous advantages, not least in terms of expressiveness, versatility, and scalability.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to a black-box function by balancing exploration with exploitation. An acquisition function expresses that balance and determines which inputs are promising to evaluate next. Expected improvement is a common choice, but computing it often depends on a probabilistic prediction model whose mathematics must remain manageable.

BORE changes how expected improvement is computed by turning the problem into binary classification. The reformulation connects three quantities: class probabilities, ratios between probability densities, and expected improvement. Estimating class probabilities therefore provides a route to the density ratios needed to express the acquisition criterion. This makes classification machinery useful for guiding the optimization search.

The approach matters because requiring an analytically convenient predictive distribution can restrict the models available to Bayesian optimization. BORE bypasses those tractability constraints through its classification formulation. The paper identifies greater expressiveness, versatility, and scalability as advantages of this change, presenting a different computational route to expected improvement rather than a separate optimization objective.
summary.tldr: BORE reformulates expected improvement as binary classification, using density-ratio estimation to relax modeling constraints in Bayesian optimization.

title: BORE: Bayesian Optimization by Density-Ratio Estimation

abstract: Spectral Graph Neural Network is a kind of Graph Neural Network (GNN) based on graph signal filters. Some models able to learn arbitrary spectral filters have emerged recently. However, few works analyze the expressive power of spectral GNNs. This paper studies spectral GNNs’ expressive power theoretically. We first prove that even spectral GNNs without nonlinearity can produce arbitrary graph signals and give two conditions for reaching universality. They are: 1) no multiple eigenvalues of graph Laplacian, and 2) no missing frequency components in node features. We also establish a connection between the expressive power of spectral GNNs and Graph Isomorphism (GI) testing, the latter of which is often used to characterize spatial GNNs’ expressive power. Moreover, we study the difference in empirical performance among different spectral GNNs with the same expressive power from an optimization perspective, and motivate the use of an orthogonal basis whose weight function corresponds to the graph signal density in the spectrum. Inspired by the analysis, we propose JacobiConv, which uses Jacobi basis due to its orthogonality and flexibility to adapt to a wide range of weight functions. JacobiConv deserts nonlinearity while outperforming all baselines on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Spectral graph neural networks process information through filters defined over a graph's frequencies. This paper asks how expressive these networks can be, including when they contain no nonlinear transformations. It proves that such networks can generate arbitrary graph signals under two stated conditions: the graph Laplacian has no repeated eigenvalues, and the node features contain every frequency component.

These conditions make the universality result specific rather than unconditional. The authors also connect spectral expressiveness to graph-isomorphism testing, a common way to study the capabilities of spatial graph networks. They then examine why models with equal theoretical expressive power can still perform differently, shifting attention from what a model can represent to how effectively it can be optimized.

That analysis motivates an orthogonal filter basis whose weighting matches the graph signal's distribution across frequencies. The resulting JacobiConv model uses the flexible Jacobi basis and omits nonlinearities. It outperforms all evaluated baselines on the reported synthetic and real-world datasets. The findings show that optimization choices can matter even when models share the same representational capabilities.
summary.tldr: Spectral GNNs can be universal under two conditions, and the analysis motivates the empirically strong, nonlinear-free JacobiConv.

title: How Powerful are Spectral Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) extends the paradigm of classical RL algorithms to purely learning from static datasets, without interacting with the underlying environment during the learning process. A key challenge of offline RL is the instability of policy training, caused by the mismatch between the distribution of the offline data and the undiscounted stationary state-action distribution of the learned policy. To avoid the detrimental impact of distribution mismatch, we regularize the undiscounted stationary distribution of the current policy towards the offline data during the policy optimization process. Further, we train a dynamics model to both implement this regularization and better estimate the stationary distribution of the current policy, reducing the error induced by distribution mismatch. On a wide range of continuous-control offline RL datasets, our method indicates competitive performance, which validates our algorithm. The code is publicly available.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains a policy entirely from a fixed dataset, without gathering new experience during learning. This paper addresses instability caused by a mismatch between that dataset and the states and actions associated with the learned policy’s undiscounted stationary distribution. The policy can therefore be optimized using data distributed differently from its own behavior.

The authors regularize the current policy’s stationary state-action distribution toward the offline data during optimization. This directly targets the distribution mismatch identified as the source of instability. The object being constrained is the policy’s distribution over states and actions, connecting the training adjustment to the behavior the policy would sustain.

A learned dynamics model supports both implementation of the regularization and improved estimation of the policy’s stationary distribution. The authors use it to reduce error induced by the mismatch. Evaluation on a wide range of continuous-control offline datasets indicates competitive performance. The result supports this distribution-focused approach as a way to stabilize offline learning, with the empirical finding stated as competitiveness rather than universal superiority.
summary.tldr: A learned dynamics model helps regularize a policy’s stationary distribution toward offline data, addressing mismatch that can destabilize training.

title: Regularizing a Model-based Policy Stationary Distribution to Stabilize Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deep neural networks often fail catastrophically by relying on spurious correlations. Most prior work assumes a clear dichotomy into spurious and reliable features; however, this is often unrealistic. For example, most of the time we do not want an autonomous car to simply copy the speed of surrounding cars—we don’t want our car to run a red light if a neighboring car does so. However, we cannot simply enforce invariance to next-lane speed, since it could provide valuable information about an unobservable pedestrian at a crosswalk. Thus, universally ignoring features that are sometimes (but not always) reliable can lead to non-robust performance. We formalize a new setting called contextual reliability which accounts for the fact that the "right" features to use may vary depending on the context. We propose and analyze a two-stage framework called Explicit Non-spurious feature Prediction (ENP) which first identifies the relevant features to use for a given context, then trains a model to rely exclusively on these features. Our work theoretically and empirically demonstrates the advantages of ENP over existing methods and provides new benchmarks for contextual reliability.

paragraphs: A feature can be useful in one situation and misleading in another. The paper illustrates this with surrounding traffic: copying another car's speed could encourage running a red light, yet that same speed could reveal an otherwise unseen pedestrian. Treating the feature as permanently trustworthy or permanently irrelevant loses this distinction.

The authors formalize this problem as contextual reliability, where the appropriate features depend on the context. They propose Explicit Non-spurious feature Prediction, or ENP, as a two-stage approach. It first identifies which features are relevant in a particular context, then trains a prediction model to depend exclusively on those selected features.

This changes the target of robustness from ignoring a fixed set of suspicious signals to deciding when each signal is appropriate. The paper analyzes ENP theoretically, reports empirical advantages over existing methods, and introduces benchmarks for the setting. The findings support context-dependent feature selection as a useful response to spurious correlations when a single global division between reliable and unreliable features is inadequate.
summary.tldr: ENP improves contextual reliability by identifying which features matter in each context and restricting predictions to those features.

title: Contextual Reliability: When Different Features Matter in Different Contexts

abstract: In this paper, we tackle a novel federated learning (FL) problem for optimizing a family of X-risks, to which no existing FL algorithms are applicable. In particular, the objective has the form of $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim \mathcal{S}_1} f(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}’\sim\mathcal{S}_2} \ell(\mathbf{w}; \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}’))$, where two sets of data $\mathcal S_1, \mathcal S_2$ are distributed over multiple machines, $\ell(\cdot; \cdot,\cdot)$ is a pairwise loss that only depends on the prediction outputs of the input data pairs $(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}’)$. This problem has important applications in machine learning, e.g., AUROC maximization with a pairwise loss, and partial AUROC maximization with a compositional loss. The challenges for designing an FL algorithm for X-risks lie in the non-decomposability of the objective over multiple machines and the interdependency between different machines. To this end, we propose an active-passive decomposition framework that decouples the gradient’s components with two types, namely active parts and passive parts, where the active parts depend on local data that are computed with the local model and the passive parts depend on other machines that are communicated/computed based on historical models and samples. Under this framework, we design two FL algorithms (FeDXL) for handling linear and nonlinear $f$, respectively, based on federated averaging and merging and develop a novel theoretical analysis to combat the latency of the passive parts and the interdependency between the local model parameters and the involved data for computing local gradient estimators. We establish both iteration and communication complexities and show that using the historical samples and models for computing the passive parts do not degrade the complexities. We conduct empirical studies of FeDXL for deep AUROC and partial AUROC maximization, and demonstrate their performance compared with several baselines.

paragraphs: FeDXL addresses federated objectives that compare pairs of examples drawn from data spread across machines. These X-risk objectives include AUROC and partial AUROC maximization. Because the pairwise loss depends on predictions for both examples, the objective does not separate neatly into independent local problems, creating dependencies between machines.

The authors split gradient calculations into active and passive components. Active components use local data and the current local model. Passive components depend on other machines and are communicated or computed using historical models and samples. This decomposition provides a way to organize local training despite the cross-machine dependencies.

The framework yields two algorithms, covering linear and nonlinear outer functions in the objective. The analysis handles delayed passive information and dependencies between local parameters and the data used in gradient estimates. It establishes iteration and communication complexity bounds, showing that historical information does not degrade those complexities in the analyzed setting. Experiments on deep AUROC and partial AUROC optimization demonstrate performance relative to several baselines.
summary.tldr: FeDXL enables federated optimization of pairwise and compositional risks by separating local gradient work from cross-machine dependencies.

title: FeDXL: Provable Federated Learning for Deep X-Risk Optimization

abstract: We consider non-clairvoyant scheduling with online precedence constraints, where an algorithm is oblivious to any job dependencies and learns about a job only if all of its predecessors have been completed. Given strong impossibility results in classical competitive analysis, we investigate the problem in a learning-augmented setting, where an algorithm has access to predictions without any quality guarantee. We discuss different prediction models: novel problem-specific models as well as general ones, which have been proposed in previous works. We present lower bounds and algorithmic upper bounds for different precedence topologies, and thereby give a structured overview on which and how additional (possibly erroneous) information helps for designing better algorithms. Along the way, we also improve bounds on traditional competitive ratios for existing algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies scheduling when dependencies between jobs are hidden. The algorithm learns that a job exists only after all its predecessors have finished, leaving it unable to inspect the full dependency structure in advance. Strong impossibility results for classical competitive analysis motivate asking whether predictions can provide enough additional information to improve scheduling.

The authors investigate a learning-augmented setting in which predictions are available but carry no guarantee of correctness. They compare several ways of supplying predictions, including new models tailored to this scheduling problem and more general models from earlier work. This makes the form of information part of the research question, alongside the algorithm that uses it.

For different dependency topologies, the paper supplies algorithmic upper bounds and lower bounds on achievable performance. Together, these results organize which kinds of potentially erroneous information help and how they can support better scheduling algorithms. The analysis also improves traditional competitive-ratio bounds for existing algorithms. The contribution is thus a structured account of the value of predictions under hidden precedence constraints, including boundaries on what algorithms can achieve.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how different, potentially erroneous predictions can improve scheduling when jobs and their dependencies are revealed online.

title: Minimalistic Predictions to Schedule Jobs with Online Precedence Constraints

abstract: We theoretically study the impact of differential privacy on fairness in classification. We prove that, given a class of models, popular group fairness measures are pointwise Lipschitz-continuous with respect to the parameters of the model. This result is a consequence of a more general statement on accuracy conditioned on an arbitrary event (such as membership to a sensitive group), which may be of independent interest. We use this Lipschitz property to prove a non-asymptotic bound showing that, as the number of samples increases, the fairness level of private models gets closer to the one of their non-private counterparts. This bound also highlights the importance of the confidence margin of a model on the disparate impact of differential privacy.

This bound also highlights the importance of the confidence margin of a model on the disparate impact of differential privacy.

paragraphs: Differential privacy protects information about individual training records, but changing a learning procedure for privacy can also affect fairness between groups. This paper studies that relationship mathematically. Its goal is to bound how far a private classifier’s fairness can move from that of its non-private counterpart.

The authors prove that popular group fairness measures have a pointwise Lipschitz property with respect to model parameters. In plain terms, parameter changes can be related to controlled changes in those fairness measures. This follows from a broader result about accuracy conditional on an arbitrary event, including membership in a sensitive group.

Using that property, the paper derives a finite-sample bound under which the fairness of private models approaches that of corresponding non-private models as sample size grows. The bound also identifies confidence margins as important to privacy’s disparate impact. This is a statement about the difference privacy introduces: approaching a non-private model’s fairness does not itself establish that either model satisfies a desired fairness standard.
summary.tldr: A finite-sample analysis bounds privacy-induced changes in group fairness and shows that those differences shrink with more data.

title: Differential Privacy has Bounded Impact on Fairness in Classification

abstract: Control variates are variance reduction tools for Monte Carlo estimators. They can provide significant variance reduction, but usually require a large number of samples, which can be prohibitive when sampling or evaluating the integrand is computationally expensive. Furthermore, there are many scenarios where we need to compute multiple related integrals simultaneously or sequentially, which can further exacerbate computational costs. In this paper, we propose vector-valued control variates, an extension of control variates which can be used to reduce the variance of multiple Monte Carlo estimators jointly. This allows for the transfer of information across integration tasks, and hence reduces the need for a large number of samples. We focus on control variates based on kernel interpolants and our novel construction is obtained through a generalised Stein identity and the development of novel matrix-valued Stein reproducing kernels. We demonstrate our methodology on a range of problems including multifidelity modelling, Bayesian inference for dynamical systems, and model evidence computation through thermodynamic integration.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo estimators approximate integrals using samples, and control variates can reduce the variability of those estimates. Building effective control variates can itself require many samples, which becomes costly when sampling or function evaluation is expensive. The burden grows when several related integrals must be computed, either together or in sequence.

This paper introduces vector-valued control variates that reduce the variance of multiple estimators jointly. The key benefit is information transfer between integration tasks, reducing the need to gather a large sample collection separately for each one. The construction focuses on kernel interpolants and develops a generalized Stein identity together with matrix-valued Stein reproducing kernels.

The authors demonstrate the method on multifidelity modeling, Bayesian inference for dynamical systems, and model evidence calculation through thermodynamic integration. These applications illustrate the intended setting: multiple integrals whose relationship can be used during estimation. The contribution turns variance reduction into a shared problem across related tasks, providing a mathematical construction for using that relationship rather than treating each estimate in isolation.
summary.tldr: Vector-valued control variates share information across related integrals to jointly reduce Monte Carlo variance and sampling needs.

title: Vector-Valued Control Variates

abstract: Natural intelligences (NIs) thrive in a dynamic world - they learn quickly, sometimes with only a few samples. In contrast, artificial intelligences (AIs) typically learn with a prohibitive number of training samples and computational power. What design principle difference between NI and AI could contribute to such a discrepancy? Here, we investigate the role of weight polarity: development processes initialize NIs with advantageous polarity configurations; as NIs grow and learn, synapse magnitudes update, yet polarities are largely kept unchanged. We demonstrate with simulation and image classification tasks that if weight polarities are adequately set a priori , then networks learn with less time and data. We also explicitly illustrate situations in which a priori setting the weight polarities is disadvantageous for networks. Our work illustrates the value of weight polarities from the perspective of statistical and computational efficiency during learning.

paragraphs: A neural-network weight has both a magnitude and a polarity: its sign determines whether its contribution is positive or negative. This paper investigates whether setting those signs advantageously before learning can reduce training demands. Its motivation comes from biological development, where synaptic magnitudes change during learning while polarities remain largely stable.

The authors study this idea through simulations and image-classification tasks. They show that networks can learn with less time and data when weight polarities are adequately chosen in advance. This makes the initial sign configuration a meaningful part of the learning setup, with consequences for both the amount of evidence needed and the computation required.

The benefit is explicitly conditional on how the signs are set. The paper also demonstrates situations where choosing polarities beforehand disadvantages the network. Its conclusion is therefore about the value of suitable polarity configurations, not a universal advantage from fixing signs. The findings highlight a design choice that can influence statistical and computational efficiency during learning.
summary.tldr: Adequately chosen weight polarities can reduce learning time and data needs, although preset polarities can also be disadvantageous.

title: Polarity Is All You Need to Learn and Transfer Faster

abstract: This paper explores the expressive power of deep neural networks through the framework of function compositions. We demonstrate that the repeated compositions of a single fixed-size ReLU network exhibit surprising expressive power, despite the limited expressive capabilities of the individual network itself. Specifically, we prove by construction that $\mathcal{L}_2\circ \boldsymbol{g}^{\circ r}\circ \boldsymbol{\mathcal{L}}_1$ can approximate $1$-Lipschitz continuous functions on $[0,1]^d$ with an error $\mathcal{O}(r^{-1/d})$, where $\boldsymbol{g}$ is realized by a fixed-size ReLU network, $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{L}}_1$ and $\mathcal{L}_2$ are two affine linear maps matching the dimensions, and $\boldsymbol{g}^{\circ r}$ denotes the $r$-times composition of $\boldsymbol{g}$. Furthermore, we extend such a result to generic continuous functions on $[0,1]^d$ with the approximation error characterized by the modulus of continuity. Our results reveal that a continuous-depth network generated via a dynamical system has immense approximation power even if its dynamics function is time-independent and realized by a fixed-size ReLU network.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much expressive power can come from repeatedly applying the same small neural network. Although a single fixed-size ReLU network has limited capabilities on its own, composing that network with itself creates a deeper computation. The authors analyze the approximation power available through this repeated use.

They construct a model consisting of an affine input map, r applications of the same ReLU network, and an affine output map. For 1-Lipschitz continuous functions on the d-dimensional unit cube, the construction achieves approximation error of order r raised to the power −1/d. Thus, increasing the number of compositions improves the guaranteed error, with a rate that depends on input dimension.

The result also extends to general continuous functions, with error described by their modulus of continuity, which captures how their values vary with input distance. The authors connect these findings to continuous-depth networks generated by dynamical systems. Even time-independent dynamics implemented by a fixed-size ReLU network can have substantial approximation power. This is a constructive expressiveness result about what repeated computation can represent.
summary.tldr: Repeatedly composing a single fixed-size ReLU network yields provable approximation power that increases with the number of repetitions.

title: On Enhancing Expressive Power via Compositions of Single Fixed-Size ReLU Network

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the online allocation problem of maximizing the overall revenue subject to both lower and upper bound constraints. Compared to the extensively studied online problems with only resource upper bounds, the two-sided constraints affect the prospects of resource consumption more severely. As a result, only limited violations of constraints or pessimistic competitive bounds could be guaranteed. To tackle the challenge, we define a measure of feasibility $\xi^*$ to evaluate the hardness of this problem, and estimate this measurement by an optimization routine with theoretical guarantees. We propose an online algorithm adopting a constructive framework, where we initialize a threshold price vector using the estimation, then dynamically update the price vector and use it for decision-making at each step. It can be shown that the proposed algorithm is $\big(1-O(\frac{\varepsilon}{\xi^*-\varepsilon})\big)$ or $\big(1-O(\frac{\varepsilon}{\xi^*-\sqrt{\varepsilon}})\big)$ competitive with high probability for $\xi^*$ known or unknown respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result establishing a nearly optimal competitive algorithm for solving two-sided constrained online allocation problems with a high probability of feasibility.

paragraphs: Online allocation requires making decisions as requests arrive while trying to maximize total revenue. This paper considers resources with both minimum and maximum consumption requirements. The lower bounds complicate decisions because conserving resources is not enough: the final allocation must also consume enough of each constrained resource.

The authors introduce a feasibility measure, xi*, that captures how difficult the constrained problem is, together with an optimization procedure for estimating it with theoretical guarantees. Their online algorithm uses that information to initialize threshold prices. It then updates those prices dynamically and uses them to decide how to handle each incoming request.

The analysis gives high-probability competitive guarantees whose error terms scale as epsilon divided by xi* minus epsilon when feasibility is known, and epsilon divided by xi* minus the square root of epsilon when it is unknown. Thus, the guarantees depend on the feasibility measure and these denominators. The result establishes nearly optimal performance together with a high probability of satisfying both sides of the resource constraints.
summary.tldr: An adaptive pricing algorithm achieves nearly optimal online allocation guarantees that depend on feasibility under lower and upper resource bounds.

title: Nearly Optimal Competitive Ratio for Online Allocation Problems with Two-sided Resource Constraints and Finite Requests

abstract: Current approaches for training robust models are typically tailored to scenarios where data variations are accessible in the training set. While shown effective in achieving robustness to these foreseen variations, these approaches are ineffective in learning unforeseen robustness, i.e., robustness to data variations without known characterization or training examples reflecting them. In this work, we learn unforeseen robustness by harnessing the variations in the abundant out-of-distribution data. To overcome the main challenge of using such data, the domain gap, we use a domain translator to bridge it and bound the unforeseen robustness on the target distribution. As implied by our analysis, we propose a two-step algorithm that first trains an equivariant domain translator to map out-of-distribution data to the target distribution while preserving the considered variation, and then regularizes a model’s output consistency on the domain-translated data to improve its robustness. We empirically show the effectiveness of our approach in improving unforeseen and foreseen robustness compared to existing approaches. Additionally, we show that training the equivariant domain translator serves as an effective criterion for source data selection.

paragraphs: Robust training usually addresses variations already represented or characterized in the training setting. This paper instead seeks robustness to unforeseen variations by drawing on out-of-distribution data. The central difficulty is that useful variation in an outside dataset comes bundled with a domain gap separating it from the target task.

The proposed algorithm has two stages. First, it trains an equivariant domain translator to map outside data toward the target distribution while preserving the variation being considered. Second, it regularizes the predictive model to produce consistent outputs on the translated data. Preserving variation during translation is central: the outside data must retain the property from which robustness is supposed to be learned.

The authors provide an analysis that bounds unforeseen robustness on the target distribution and motivates this procedure. Empirical results report improvements in both unforeseen and foreseen robustness over existing approaches. They also find that training the translator provides an effective criterion for selecting source data, linking the transfer mechanism to the choice of outside datasets.
summary.tldr: An equivariant domain translator transfers useful variations from outside data to improve robustness through output-consistency training.

title: Learning Unforeseen Robustness from Out-of-distribution Data Using Equivariant Domain Translator

abstract: Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are widely used to describe dynamical systems in science, but identifying parameters that explain experimental measurements is challenging. In particular, although ODEs are differentiable and would allow for gradient-based parameter optimization, the nonlinear dynamics of ODEs often lead to many local minima and extreme sensitivity to initial conditions. We therefore propose diffusion tempering, a novel regularization technique for probabilistic numerical methods which improves convergence of gradient-based parameter optimization in ODEs. By iteratively reducing a noise parameter of the probabilistic integrator, the proposed method converges more reliably to the true parameters. We demonstrate that our method is effective for dynamical systems of different complexity and show that it obtains reliable parameter estimates for a Hodgkin–Huxley model with a practically relevant number of parameters.

We therefore propose diffusion tempering, a novel regularization technique for probabilistic numerical methods which improves convergence of gradient-based parameter optimization in ODEs. paragraphs: Ordinary differential equations describe how a system changes over time, but their parameters must often be inferred from measurements. Even when gradients are available, this fitting problem can be difficult. Nonlinear dynamics can create many local minima, and strong sensitivity to initial conditions can make parameter optimization unreliable.

The paper introduces diffusion tempering, a regularization technique for probabilistic numerical integrators. Its central operation is to reduce an integrator’s noise parameter iteratively during gradient-based parameter fitting. This makes the noise setting part of the optimization procedure, rather than leaving it fixed throughout the search. The authors report that the resulting procedure converges more reliably to the true parameters.

The method is demonstrated on dynamical systems with different levels of complexity. The evaluation includes a Hodgkin–Huxley model with a practically relevant number of parameters, for which reliable parameter estimates are reported. These results support using the numerical integrator itself to improve parameter fitting: the contribution concerns how the differential equations are handled during optimization, addressing difficulties that differentiability alone does not resolve.
summary.tldr: Diffusion tempering gradually reduces probabilistic-integrator noise to make gradient-based ODE parameter estimation more reliable.

title: Diffusion Tempering Improves Parameter Estimation with Probabilistic Integrators for Ordinary Differential Equations

abstract: Diffusion models have revolutionized various application domains, including computer vision and audio generation. Despite the state-of-the-art performance, diffusion models are known for their slow sample generation due to the extensive number of steps involved. In response, consistency models have been developed to merge multiple steps in the sampling process, thereby significantly boosting the speed of sample generation without compromising quality. This paper contributes towards the first statistical theory for consistency models, formulating their training as a distribution discrepancy minimization problem. Our analysis yields statistical estimation rates based on the Wasserstein distance for consistency models, matching those of vanilla diffusion models. Additionally, our results encompass the training of consistency models through both distillation and isolation methods, demystifying their underlying advantage.
