paragraphs: Many scientific measurements reveal only indirect evidence of the hidden structures that produced them. The goal may be to recover a real set or graph, rather than learn an arbitrary internal representation. Such problems become difficult when the number of possible hidden structures grows combinatorially, limiting classical inference methods.

GReinSS approaches this task through policy learning. It learns distributions over latent states that maximize the likelihood of the observed data, using rewards that are dynamically rescaled during learning. This connects the search over discrete structures to how well those structures explain the measurements, while targeting mechanistic latent states.

In simulations, the method accurately reconstructs hidden sets and graphs and outperforms the alternative policy-learning and generative-modeling approaches evaluated. On real short-read RNA sequencing data, its reconstructed isoforms agree better with isoforms detected through independent long-read sequencing than those produced by RSEM. The results support its usefulness for recovering interpretable combinatorial structures, with evidence spanning controlled latent-state reconstruction and a biological inference application.
summary.tldr: GReinSS uses dynamically rescaled policy-learning rewards to infer discrete hidden structures that explain indirect observations.

title: Generative Modeling of Discrete Latent Structures via Dynamic Policy Gradients

abstract: By introducing routers to selectively activate experts in Transformer layers, the mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture significantly reduces computational costs in large language models (LLMs) while maintaining competitive performance, especially for models with massive parameters. However, prior work has largely focused on utility and efficiency, leaving the safety risks associated with this sparse architecture underexplored. In this work, we show that the safety of MoE LLMs is as sparse as their architecture by discovering $\text{\emph{unsafe routes}}$: routing configurations that, once activated, convert safe outputs into harmful ones. Specifically, we first introduce the $\underline{\text{Ro}}$uter $\underline{\text{Sa}}$fety $\underline{\text{i}}$mportance $\underline{\text{s}}$core ($\textbf{RoSais}$) to quantify the safety criticality of each layer’s router. Manipulation of only the high-RoSais router(s) can flip the default route into an unsafe one. We further propose a $\underline{\text{F}}$ine-grained token-layer-wise $\underline{\text{S}}$tochastic $\underline{\text{O}}$ptimization framework to discover more concrete $\underline{\text{U}}$nsafe $\underline{\text{R}}$outes ($\textbf{F-SOUR}$), which explicitly considers the sequentiality and dynamics of input tokens. Across four representative MoE LLM families, F-SOUR achieves an average ASR of 0.90 and 0.98 on JailbreakBench and AdvBench, respectively. Finally, we outline defensive perspectives, including safety-aware route disabling and router training, as promising directions to safeguard MoE LLMs. We hope our work can inform future red-teaming and safeguarding of MoE LLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/TrustAIRLab/UnsafeMoE.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models save computation by using routers to activate selected experts at each layer. This paper investigates how those routing decisions affect safety. It identifies unsafe routes: configurations that can change an otherwise safe response into a harmful one. The finding makes the internal selection of experts an explicit subject for safety evaluation.

The authors introduce RoSais, a score measuring how important each layer's router is to safe behavior. They find that manipulating only routers with high scores can produce an unsafe route. They also develop F-SOUR, a fine-grained optimization framework that accounts for how routing varies across tokens and layers and for the sequential nature of input.

Across four representative MoE model families, F-SOUR reaches average attack success rates of 0.90 on JailbreakBench and 0.98 on AdvBench. These results demonstrate substantial vulnerability in the evaluated routing configurations. Safety-aware route disabling and router training are proposed as promising defensive directions, rather than established solutions, highlighting the potential value of incorporating routing behavior into future safeguards.
summary.tldr: The study finds routing configurations that undermine MoE model safety and identifies router-focused evaluation and defenses as important directions.

title: Sparse Models, Sparse Safety: Unsafe Routes in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs

abstract: In many modern machine learning pipelines, abundant pretrained representations serve as noisy proxy covariates, while task-specific labels remain scarce. We study semi-supervised regression in this setting, and propose a simple two stage estimator that learns kernel eigenfeatures from all proxy covariates and fits a ridge predictor on labeled data. We derive finite sample bounds showing that fast labeled sample rates are recovered when proxy perturbation is controlled and unlabeled proxy covariates are sufficiently abundant. We also show that distribution regression is a direct special case, with analogous guarantees when the finite bag size is large enough. Experiments show consistent gains over supervised and semi-supervised baselines, especially in low label regimes.

paragraphs: Many learning pipelines have abundant pretrained representations but few labels for the actual prediction task. Those representations can be noisy proxies for the covariates the task needs. This paper studies semi-supervised regression in that setting, asking how unlabeled proxy observations can help learn a predictor when reliable labels are scarce.

The proposed estimator has two stages. It first learns kernel eigenfeatures from all available proxy covariates, including unlabeled observations. It then fits a ridge predictor using the labeled examples. Finite-sample bounds show that fast rates in the number of labeled samples can be recovered when proxy perturbations are controlled and sufficiently many unlabeled proxy observations are available.

The authors also establish distribution regression as a direct special case, with analogous guarantees when each finite bag contains enough observations. Experiments report consistent gains over supervised and semi-supervised baselines, particularly with few labels. The findings connect practical use of abundant imperfect representations to explicit conditions under which unlabeled data can support efficient learning from a small labeled set.
summary.tldr: A two-stage regression estimator uses abundant noisy proxy features to improve learning with few labels, with guarantees under controlled noise and sufficient unlabeled data.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning with Noisy Proxy Covariates: Generalization Bounds and Distribution Regression

abstract: This paper presents a theoretical framework that explains why fine-tuning small, randomly selected subnetworks (slices) within pre-trained models is sufficient for downstream adaptation. We establish that pretrained networks exhibit a universal winning slice property, arising from two phenomena: (1) spectral balance— the eigenspectra of different weight matrix slices are remarkably similar—and (2) high task energy—their backbone representations (pretrained weights) retain rich, task-relevant features. This leads to the Universal Winning Slice Hypothesis, which provides a theoretical foundation for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) in large-scale models. Inspired by this, we propose SliceFine, a PEFT method that uses this inherent redundancy by updating only selected slices of the origi- nal weights—introducing zero new parameters, unlike adapter-based approaches. Empirically, SliceFine matches the performance of SOTA PEFT methods across various language and vision tasks, while significantly improving training speed, memory efficiency, and model compactness. Our work bridges theory and prac- tice, offering a theoretically grounded alternative to existing PEFT techniques.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a small part of a pretrained model can be sufficient for adaptation, even when that part is randomly selected. This paper develops a theoretical explanation for this behavior through the Universal Winning Slice Hypothesis. It connects the usefulness of small subnetworks to properties already present in pretrained weights and representations.

The explanation has two components. Spectral balance means that different slices of weight matrices have remarkably similar eigenspectra. High task energy means that the pretrained backbone retains rich features relevant to downstream tasks. Across the reported language and vision tasks, it matches state-of-the-art parameter-efficient fine-tuning performance while improving training speed, memory efficiency, and model compactness. The work links an account of pretrained-model redundancy to a practical adaptation method that uses existing parameter capacity directly.
summary.tldr: SliceFine adapts pretrained models by updating small slices of existing weights, supported by a theory of spectral balance and retained task information.

title: SliceFine: The Universal Winning-Slice Hypothesis for Pretrained Networks

abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation relies on integrating multimodal inputs to perform complex real-world tasks. To address the challenges of effectively combining these modalities, we propose DECO, a decoupled multimodal diffusion transformer that disentangles vision, proprioception, and tactile signals through specialized conditioning pathways, enabling structured and controllable integration of multimodal inputs, with a lightweight adapter for parameter-efficient injection of additional signals. Alongside DECO, we release DECO-50 dataset for bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing, consisting of 50 hours of data and over 5M frames, collected via teleoperation on real dual-arm robots. We train DECO on DECO-50 and conduct extensive real-world evaluation with over 2,000 robot rollouts. Experimental results show that DECO achieves the best performance across all tasks, with a 72.25% average success rate and a 21% improvement over the baseline. Moreover, the tactile adapter brings an additional 10.25% average success rate across all tasks and a 20% gain on complex contact-rich tasks while tuning less than 10% of the model parameters.

paragraphs: DECO addresses how a two-arm robot should combine visual input, information about its own configuration, and touch. These signals describe different aspects of manipulation. The model gives them specialized conditioning pathways within a diffusion transformer, allowing their contributions to be integrated in a structured and controllable way.

A lightweight adapter provides a parameter-efficient route for adding signals, including tactile information. The authors also release DECO-50, containing 50 hours and more than five million frames of tactile-enabled manipulation data collected by teleoperating real dual-arm robots. They train DECO on this dataset and evaluate it through more than 2,000 real-world robot rollouts.

DECO reports the best performance across the evaluated tasks, with 72.25% average success and a reported 21% improvement over the baseline. The tactile adapter contributes an additional reported 10.25% average success rate across tasks and a 20% gain on complex tasks involving substantial contact, while tuning fewer than 10% of model parameters. These findings support both separating sensory pathways and adding touch through a small adaptable component.
summary.tldr: DECO separates sensory conditioning for two-arm manipulation and uses a lightweight tactile adapter to improve real-world task success.

title: DECO: Decoupled Multimodal Diffusion Transformer for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation with a Plugin Tactile Adapter

abstract: Scaling inference-time computation has enabled Large Language Models (LLMs) to achieve strong reasoning performance, but their inherently sequential decoding incurs substantial latency, motivating parallelization of the generation process. However, existing parallel reasoning approaches suffer from performance degradation compared to their sequential counterparts, and often rely on specialized inference engines. We introduce ThreadWeaver, a framework for adaptive parallel reasoning that matches the accuracy of comparably sized sequential reasoning models while significantly reducing inference latency via three key innovations: 1) a two-stage parallel trajectory generator that produces high-quality parallel chain-of-thought data for supervised fine-tuning; 2) a trie-based rollout design that enables parallel reasoning on any off-the-shelf autoregressive inference engine; and 3) a parallelization-aware reinforcement learning framework that trains the model to balance reasoning accuracy with effective parallelization. Across six challenging math reasoning benchmarks, ThreadWeaver trained on top of Qwen3-8B achieves performance on par with cutting-edge sequential reasoning models (79.9% on AIME24 and 71.9% on average) while delivering up to 1.53x speedup in token latency, establishing a new Pareto frontier between accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Giving language models more inference-time computation can improve reasoning, but sequential generation creates delays. Parallel reasoning aims to reduce those delays, yet existing approaches can lose accuracy or require specialized inference systems. ThreadWeaver develops a training and execution framework intended to make parallel reasoning both accurate and broadly usable.

The framework has three components. A two-stage generator creates parallel reasoning trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. A trie-based rollout structure allows those trajectories to run on standard autoregressive inference engines. Reinforcement learning then explicitly balances reasoning accuracy with effective parallelization, making the ability to use parallel computation part of the model's training objective.

Built on Qwen3-8B, ThreadWeaver is evaluated on six difficult mathematics benchmarks. It reports 79.9% on AIME24 and a 71.9% average, matching the performance of comparably sized leading sequential reasoning models while achieving up to 1.53 times speedup in token latency. These findings establish an improved reported accuracy-efficiency tradeoff. The speedup is an upper reported result, and the empirical evidence concerns the evaluated mathematical reasoning tasks.
summary.tldr: ThreadWeaver trains adaptive parallel reasoning that matches comparable sequential models' math accuracy with up to 1.53 times faster token latency.

title: ThreadWeaver: Adaptive Threading for Efficient Parallel Reasoning in Language Models

abstract: Quantization is a key method for reducing the GPU memory requirement of training large language models (LLMs). Yet, current approaches are ineffective for 4-bit activations and 8-bit gradients, which would easily cause slow convergence or accuracy loss. To address this, we introduce AGoQ, incorporating two new techniques: 1) a layer-aware activation quantization algorithm that allocates appropriate bit-widths for activations of various layers based on their types and pipeline stages to achieve near 4-bit activation storage, and 2) a gradient quantization algorithm that reduces memory usage and shortens communication time by employing 8-bit gradient storage and precision-preserving 8-bit All-Reduce communication. We conduct extensive experiments using different sizes of LLMs on two GPU clusters (up to 64 GPUs), and the experimental results show that our AGoQ reduces the memory by up to 52% and achieves up to 1.34$\times$ improvement of training speed compared to state-of-the-art training systems Megatron-LM (w/ or w/o ZeRO), COAT and DeepSpeed with 8B to 32B LLaMA models, while achieving convergence loss on pretraining and comparable accuracy on downstream tasks with LLaMA architectures.

paragraphs: AGoQ targets the memory and communication costs of distributed language-model training. Reducing numerical precision can save GPU memory, but aggressive compression of activations and gradients can slow convergence or reduce accuracy. The paper addresses both kinds of training data with separate quantization techniques designed to retain useful precision.

For activations, AGoQ assigns bit widths according to layer type and position in the training pipeline. This brings activation storage close to four bits without requiring every layer to use the same precision. For gradients, it combines eight-bit storage with an eight-bit All-Reduce operation that preserves precision during communication between GPUs. The two components address stored training state and the exchange of updates across devices.

Experiments use LLaMA models with 8–32 billion parameters on two clusters containing up to 64 GPUs. Against the named training systems, the authors report memory reductions of up to 52% and training speed improvements of up to 1.34 times. They also report pretraining convergence and comparable downstream accuracy, supporting the practical combination of these compression mechanisms.
summary.tldr: AGoQ combines layer-aware activation compression with eight-bit gradient storage and communication to reduce distributed LLM training costs.

title: AGoQ: Activation and Gradient Quantization for Memory-Efficient Distributed Training of LLMs

abstract: Linear attention mitigates the quadratic complexity of softmax attention but suffers from a critical loss of expressiveness. We identify two primary causes: (1) The normalization operation cancels the query norm, which breaks the correlation between a query’s norm and the spikiness (entropy) of the attention distribution as in softmax attention. (2) Standard techniques for enforcing non-negativity cause destructive information loss by nullifying valid inner-product interactions. To address these challenges, we introduce NaLaFormer, a novel linear attention mechanism built upon a norm$\times$direction (ND) decomposition of the query and key vectors. We leverage each component to solve a distinct problem: The query norm is injected into our kernel to create a query-norm-aware map that restores the attention distribution’s spikiness. The direction vectors are processed by a geometric, cosine-based similarity metric that guarantees non-negativity while preserving the rich, fine-grained information of the inner product. We validate NaLaFormer through a comprehensive multi-modal evaluation, where it sets new state-of-the-art benchmarks for linear attention. Our model achieves up to a 7.5% accuracy gain on ImageNet-1K and a 4.7% mIoU improvement on ADE20K over comparable baselines. It demonstrates profound efficiency, reducing peak memory by a transformative 92.3% in token-intensive super-resolution tasks (70K+ tokens). NaLaFormer’s versatility is further confirmed as it surpasses strong baselines like Mamba on common-sense reasoning and sets a new state-of-the-art on the Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark. Source code can be found in the supplementary materials.

This paper identifies two mechanisms: normalization removes the query’s magnitude, weakening its connection to how concentrated attention becomes, and common non-negativity transformations discard valid inner-product interactions.

Direction is handled through a geometric cosine-based similarity that guarantees non-negative values while preserving fine-grained inner-product information. Each component of the decomposition therefore addresses a different source of lost expressiveness.

In super-resolution tasks with more than 70,000 tokens, peak memory falls by 92.3%. Together, these findings support the decomposition across the tested visual and sequence-processing tasks.
summary.tldr: NaLaFormer restores query magnitude and preserves directional interactions to improve linear attention’s accuracy and efficiency across evaluated tasks.

title: Norm$\times$Direction: Restoring the Missing Query Norm in Vision Linear Attention

abstract: Upcycling pre-trained dense models into sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoEs) efficiently increases model capacity but often suffers from poor expert specialization due to naive weight replication. We introduce Dirichlet-Prior Shaping Loss (DPSL), a novel router regularization technique that directly shapes routing probability distributions by matching expert assignments to a target Dirichlet prior resulting in enhanced expert specialization. DPSL enables encoding of inductive biases such as encouraging experts to focus on specific modalities or tasks, without requiring manual intervention. DPSL is a general tool applicable to any module that outputs categorical probability distributions, extending its utility beyond MoE training. Experiments on upcycled MoE vision-language models show that DPSL consistently outperforms upcycling strategies and regularization techniques across standard vision-language benchmarks, addressing the critical issue of poor specialization and fostering higher-performing models.

paragraphs: Upcycling expands a pretrained dense model into a sparse mixture of experts, increasing capacity while reusing existing weights. A problem arises when experts begin as simple copies: they may fail to develop distinct specialties. The router, which assigns inputs to experts, is therefore an important place to influence how specialization develops.

Dirichlet-Prior Shaping Loss regularizes the router's probability distributions by matching expert assignments to a target Dirichlet prior. That target can express preferences for how experts should divide work, including specialization by modality or task. The intended division is encoded in the training objective, allowing specialization to emerge without manually intervening in individual assignments.

Experiments on upcycled vision-language models report consistent improvements over the compared upcycling strategies and regularization methods across standard benchmarks. The paper also presents the loss as applicable beyond expert routing, to modules that output categorical probabilities. Its central contribution is a way to guide the shape of assignment distributions directly and thereby encourage more useful differentiation among initially similar experts.
summary.tldr: DPSL shapes routing probabilities with a Dirichlet prior to encourage specialization and improve upcycled vision-language mixture-of-experts models.

title: Dirichlet-Prior Shaping: Guiding Expert Specialization in Upcycled MoEs

abstract: Recent advances in generative models have shown promise in generating behavior plans for long-horizon, sparse reward tasks. While these approaches have achieved promising results, they often lack a principled framework for hierarchical decomposition and struggle with the computational demands of real-time execution, due to their iterative denoising process. In this work, we introduce $\textbf{Hierarchical Diffusion-Flow}$ ($\texttt{\textbf{HDFlow}}$), a novel hierarchical planning framework that optimally leverages the strengths of $\textit{diffusion}$ and $\textit{rectified flow}$ models to overcome the limitations of single-paradigm generative planners. $\texttt{\textbf{HDFlow}}$ employs a high-level diffusion planner to generate sequences of strategic subgoals in a learned latent space, capitalizing on diffusion’s powerful exploratory capabilities. These subgoals then guide a low-level rectified flow planner that generates smooth and dense trajectories, exploiting the speed and efficiency of ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based trajectory generation. We evaluate $\texttt{\textbf{HDFlow}}$ on four challenging furniture assembly tasks in both simulation and real-world, where it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we also showcase our method’s generalizability on two long-horizon benchmarks comprising diverse locomotion and manipulation tasks. Project website: https://hdflow-page.github.io/

paragraphs: Long-horizon tasks require plans that connect many actions, often with sparse reward signals. Generative planners can produce such behavior, but repeated denoising creates computational demands for real-time execution. They can also lack a clear way to divide strategic planning from detailed movement. HDFlow introduces a hierarchy that assigns these responsibilities to different generative models.

A high-level diffusion model produces a sequence of strategic subgoals in a learned latent space. These subgoals guide a low-level rectified-flow planner, which generates smooth, dense trajectories using an ordinary-differential-equation-based process. The design combines diffusion's exploration capabilities with the speed and efficiency of rectified flow for detailed trajectory generation.

The authors evaluate HDFlow on four furniture-assembly tasks in simulation and the real world, reporting significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. They also demonstrate generalization on two long-horizon benchmarks covering locomotion and manipulation. These findings support dividing a generative planning problem across complementary models, so that exploring useful intermediate goals and producing executable trajectories have distinct roles within one framework.
summary.tldr: HDFlow combines diffusion-generated subgoals with rectified-flow trajectories to improve hierarchical planning for long-horizon tasks.

title: HDFlow: Hierarchical Diffusion-Flow Planning for Long-horizon Tasks

abstract: Controlling generative models—whether via inference-time steering or fine-tuning—is expensive. Control relies on estimating the value function—typically necessitating costly trajectory simulations. To eliminate this bottleneck, we introduce Meta Flow Maps (MFMs), stochastic extensions of consistency models and flow maps. MFMs are trained to perform one-step posterior sampling, generating arbitrarily many i.i.d. draws of clean data $x_1$ from any noisy state $x_t$. Crucially, these samples are differentiable in the conditioning state $x_t$, unlocking efficient estimation of the value function gradient. We leverage this capability to enable both inference-time steering without inner rollouts, and unbiased, off-policy fine-tuning to general rewards. Among our fine-tuning and steering experiments on ImageNet, we highlight that our single-particle steered-MFM sampler outperforms a Best-of-1000 baseline across multiple rewards at a fraction of the compute.

paragraphs: Steering a generative model toward a reward often requires estimating how valuable its current noisy state is. Doing so through repeated trajectory simulations is expensive. This paper introduces Meta Flow Maps to make that estimation more efficient, supporting both steering during generation and changes to the model through fine-tuning.

Meta Flow Maps are stochastic extensions of consistency models and flow maps. They are trained to produce clean-data posterior samples from a noisy state in one step, allowing arbitrarily many independent draws. Crucially, the samples are differentiable with respect to the conditioning state, which enables efficient estimation of the value-function gradient needed for control.

The authors use this capability for inference-time steering without inner rollouts and for unbiased, off-policy fine-tuning to general rewards. In ImageNet experiments, a single-particle steered sampler outperforms a Best-of-1000 baseline across multiple rewards at a fraction of the computation. The result demonstrates the potential of direct posterior sampling to replace costly trajectory-based calculations in reward alignment.
summary.tldr: Meta Flow Maps use differentiable one-step posterior sampling to make generative-model steering and reward fine-tuning more efficient.

title: Meta Flow Maps enable scalable reward alignment

abstract: Spherical signals provide a natural representation for omnidirectional perception and often benefit from equivariance to 3D rotations. Recent spherical vision transformers implement local self-attention on spherical grids, but most retain only partial $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ equivariance and rely on $\textit{location-dependent}$ local positional embeddings (LPEs). Such LPEs can degrade robustness to camera tilt or object reorientation and introduce additional memory and computational overhead. We propose $\textit{Spherical $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-Equivariant Local Attention}$ (SoLA), an LPE-free local attention mechanism for spherical signals. SoLA achieves full $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ equivariance through a distance-preserving positional modulation that couples query/key features with each token’s unit direction. Specifically, the modulation lifts queries and keys using an outer-product with the 4D direction dependent vector. The induced similarity of the modulated queries and keys depends on content affinity and great-circle distance while remaining invariant to global $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ rotations. The same formulation admits a softmax-free linear variant that computes local attention via key-value aggregation without per-query neighbor materialization. We integrate SoLA into a U-shaped spherical transformer for $360^\circ$ depth estimation and semantic segmentation, demonstrating substantially improved robustness to arbitrary 3D rotations compared to prior spherical transformers with similar computational costs.

paragraphs: Spherical signals represent observations in all directions, making behavior under three-dimensional rotations especially relevant. Existing spherical transformers often provide only partial rotation equivariance and use position embeddings tied to location. SoLA introduces local attention designed to retain full SO(3) equivariance without those local positional embeddings.

The mechanism combines query and key features with a four-dimensional vector derived from each token’s direction, using an outer product. The resulting similarity depends on content and great-circle distance, both arranged so that a global rotation leaves the similarity unchanged. This supplies positional information through spherical geometry while avoiding the location-dependent embeddings identified as a source of overhead and reduced robustness.

The formulation also supports a linear variant without softmax, aggregating keys and values without materializing neighbors separately for every query. Integrated into a U-shaped spherical transformer, SoLA is evaluated on 360-degree depth estimation and semantic segmentation. The authors report substantially greater robustness to arbitrary three-dimensional rotations than prior spherical transformers at similar computational costs.
summary.tldr: SoLA builds fully rotation-equivariant spherical attention from content and geometric distance, improving reported robustness at similar computational cost.

title: Spherical SO(3) Equivariant Local Attention

abstract: LLM agents are rapidly becoming a practical interface for task automation, yet selecting suitable deployable configurations remains underexplored. Existing LLM leaderboards and tool/agent benchmarks evaluate components in isolation and are fragmented across tasks, metrics, and candidate pools, leaving a critical research gap: there is little query-conditioned supervision for learning to recommend end-to-end compositional agent configurations. We introduce AgentSelect, a benchmark that reframes agent selection as narrative query-to-agent recommendation over capability profiles. AgentSelect systematically converts heterogeneous evaluation artifacts into unified positive-only interaction data, comprising 111,179 queries, 107,721 deployable agents, and 251,103 interaction records from 40+ sources across LLM-only, toolkit-only, and compositional agents. Our analyses reveal a shift from dense head reuse to long-tail, near one-off supervision, where ID-based interaction methods become fragile and reliable recommendation increasingly requires content-aware intent-to-capability matching. We validate the synthesized supervision through counterfactual, ablation, and show practical transferability on the MuleRun agent marketplace and a small-scale end to end Agno deployment study. Overall, AgentSelect provides the first unified data and evaluation infrastructure for agent recommendation, which establishes a reproducible foundation to study and accelerate the emerging agent ecosystem. The resources are available at [https://github.com/Ancientshi/AgentSelect].

paragraphs: Choosing an agent for a task requires matching a user’s request to a deployable combination of capabilities. Existing evaluations often score models, tools, or agents separately, using incompatible tasks and metrics. AgentSelect turns this fragmented evidence into a recommendation problem: given a narrative description of a task, identify suitable agents through their capability profiles.

The benchmark converts evaluation artifacts from more than 40 sources into a common collection of positive interactions. It contains 111,179 queries, 107,721 deployable agents, and 251,103 interaction records, covering model-only, toolkit-only, and compositional agents. Its positive-only construction represents observed suitable matches rather than providing explicit negative examples for every alternative.

The analysis finds increasingly sparse supervision, with many agents appearing almost once rather than repeatedly. Under these conditions, methods centered on agent identifiers become fragile, increasing the importance of matching request content to capabilities. Counterfactual and ablation analyses examine the synthesized supervision, while marketplace transfer and a small Agno deployment study provide evidence of practical applicability.
summary.tldr: AgentSelect unifies evaluation evidence into a benchmark for matching natural-language task requests with suitable deployable agents.

title: AgentSelect: Benchmark for Narrative Query-to-Agent Recommendation

abstract: We present Creat3r, an iterative next-best-view (NBV) selection framework for efficient, high-quality 3D reconstruction. Starting from a small seed set of image-pose pairs, Creat3r repeatedly selects the most informative next camera pose. After each pose is chosen, the corresponding image is acquired and added to the multi-view set to update a 3DGS reconstruction. To guide selection, Creat3r constructs an intermediate point cloud and estimates reconstruction reliability via a novel 3D confidence field, which is projected to candidate poses through Gaussian projection to produce 2D confidence and exploration maps. These maps balance exploitation of reliable regions and exploration of uncertain or unseen areas under computational constraints. Experiments with standard 3DGS show that Creat3r consistently outperforms baselines in novel view synthesis and surface reconstruction, achieving higher SSIM and F1 scores with fewer views.

paragraphs: Building a three-dimensional scene from images involves deciding where to look next as well as reconstructing what has already been observed. Creat3r addresses this camera-selection problem. It begins with a small collection of images and their camera poses, then repeatedly chooses an informative next pose, acquires that image, and updates a reconstruction based on 3D Gaussian splatting.

The selection mechanism uses an intermediate point cloud and a three-dimensional confidence field that estimates reconstruction reliability. Gaussian projection converts this information into confidence and exploration maps for candidate camera poses. These maps help weigh reliable regions against uncertain or unseen areas, so camera selection can account for both existing reconstruction quality and opportunities to collect new information under computational constraints.

In experiments using standard 3D Gaussian splatting, Creat3r consistently improves on the compared baselines while requiring fewer views. The reported gains cover both novel-view image quality, measured with SSIM, and reconstructed surface quality, measured with F1. Together, these results indicate that confidence-guided acquisition can make the collected images more useful for both appearance and geometry.
summary.tldr: Creat3r uses projected reconstruction confidence to choose camera views that improve 3D reconstruction with fewer images.

title: Creat3r: Confidence Reaggregation for Exploration-aware Active 3D Reconstruction

abstract: Uniform Discrete Diffusion Model (UDM) has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for discrete generative modeling; however, its integration with reinforcement learning remains largely unexplored. We observe that naively applying GRPO to UDM leads to training instability and marginal performance gains. To address this, we propose UDM-GRPO, the first framework to integrate UDM with RL. Our method is guided by two key insights: (i) treating the final clean sample as the action provides more accurate and stable optimization signals; and (ii) reconstructing trajectories via the diffusion forward process better aligns probability paths with the pretraining distribution. Additionally, we introduce two strategies, Reduced-Step and CFG-Free, to further improve training efficiency. UDM-GRPO significantly improves base model performance across multiple T2I tasks. Notably, GenEval accuracy improves from $69%$ to $96%$ and PickScore increases from $20.46$ to $23.81$, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both continuous and discrete settings. On the OCR benchmark, accuracy rises from $8%$ to $57%$, further validating the generalization ability of our method. Code is available at https://github.com/Yovecent/UDM-GRPO.

paragraphs: Uniform discrete diffusion models offer a way to generate discrete outputs, but directly applying Group Relative Policy Optimization produces unstable training and only modest gains. UDM-GRPO adapts reinforcement learning to this model family by reconsidering which output is treated as the action and how training trajectories are reconstructed.

The framework treats the final clean sample as the action, providing a more accurate and stable optimization signal. It reconstructs trajectories through the forward diffusion process so that probability paths align better with the pretraining distribution. Two additional strategies, Reduced-Step and CFG-Free, further improve training efficiency.

Across multiple text-to-image tasks, the authors report substantial improvements over the base model. GenEval accuracy rises from 69% to 96%, while PickScore increases from 20.46 to 23.81, with reported state-of-the-art performance across continuous and discrete settings. OCR benchmark accuracy also increases from 8% to 57%. These results support adapting the reinforcement-learning formulation to the diffusion model’s structure instead of applying GRPO unchanged.
summary.tldr: UDM-GRPO stabilizes reinforcement learning for uniform discrete diffusion models and delivers large reported gains on text-to-image and OCR benchmarks.

title: UDM-GRPO: Stable and Efficient Group Relative Policy Optimization for Uniform Discrete Diffusion Models

abstract: Block-sparse attention is promising for accelerating long-context LLM pre-filling, yet identifying relevant blocks efficiently remains a bottleneck. Existing methods typically employ coarse-grained attention as a proxy for block importance estimation, but often resort to expensive token-level searching or scoring, resulting in significant selection overhead. In this work, we trace the inaccuracy of standard coarse-grained attention via mean pooling to a theoretical root cause: the interaction between mean pooling and Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE). We prove that mean pooling acts as a low-pass filter that induces destructive interference in high-frequency dimensions, effectively creating a "blind spot" for local positional information (e.g., slash patterns). To address this, we introduce Prism, a training-free spectral-aware approach that decomposes block selection into high-frequency and low-frequency branches. By applying energy-based temperature calibration, Prism restores the attenuated positional signals directly from pooled representations, enabling block importance estimation using purely block-level operations, thereby improving efficiency. Extensive evaluations confirm that Prism maintains accuracy parity with full attention while delivering up to $\mathbf{5.1\times}$ speedup. Code available at https://github.com/xinghaow99/prism.

To address this, we introduce Prism, a training-free spectral-aware approach that decomposes block selection into high-frequency and low-frequency branches. By applying energy-based temperature calibration, Prism restores the attenuated positional signals directly from pooled representations, enabling block importance estimation using purely block-level operations, thereby improving efficiency. Extensive evaluations confirm that Prism maintains accuracy parity with full attention while delivering up to $\mathbf{5.1\times}$ speedup. Code available at https://github.com/xinghaow99/prism.

paragraphs: Block-sparse attention can accelerate the processing of long prompts by computing attention only for selected blocks. Choosing those blocks can itself be expensive. Prism addresses why inexpensive block summaries sometimes miss important attention patterns, forcing existing methods to return to costly token-level scoring.

The authors trace the problem to the interaction between mean pooling and rotary positional embeddings. Their analysis shows that averaging behaves like a low-pass filter: high-frequency dimensions can interfere destructively, weakening signals that carry local positional information. Prism separates block selection into high- and low-frequency branches, then uses energy-based temperature calibration to restore attenuated positional signals from the pooled representations.

Because the selection process operates entirely at block level, it avoids the token-level searching that can undermine sparse attention’s efficiency. The method requires no training. Evaluations report accuracy parity with full attention and speedups of up to 5.1 times. These findings show that accounting for positional frequency structure can improve block selection while preserving accuracy in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Prism corrects frequency-related distortions in pooled attention summaries to select sparse blocks efficiently without training.

title: Prism: Spectral-Aware Block-Sparse Attention

abstract: While long-horizon agentic tasks require language agents to perform dozens of sequential decisions, training such agents with reinforcement learning remains challenging. We identify two root causes: credit misattribution, where correct early actions are penalized due to terminal failures, and sample inefficiency, where scarce successful trajectories result in near-total loss of learning signal. We introduce a milestone-guided policy learning framework, BEACON, that leverages the compositional structure of long-horizon tasks to ensure precise credit assignment. BEACON partitions trajectories at milestone boundaries, applies temporal reward shaping within segments to credit partial progress, and estimates advantages at dual scales to prevent distant failures from corrupting the evaluation of local actions. On ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, BEACON consistently outperforms GRPO and GiGPO. Notably, on long-horizon ALFWorld tasks, BEACON achieves 92.9% success rate, nearly doubling GRPO’s 53.5%, while improving effective sample utilization from 23.7% to 82.0%. These results establish milestone-anchored credit assignment as an effective paradigm for training long-horizon language agents. Code is in supplementary materials and will be publicly released.

paragraphs: An agent may make several correct decisions before a later mistake causes the entire task to fail. Training from that final outcome can penalize useful early behavior and discard learning opportunities from partially successful attempts. This paper identifies those credit-assignment and sample-efficiency problems as obstacles for language agents facing long sequences of decisions.

BEACON uses the compositional structure of tasks to divide trajectories at milestones. Within each segment, temporal reward shaping gives credit for partial progress. Advantage estimates at two scales help evaluate local actions without letting distant failures dominate their assessment. Milestones therefore provide intermediate boundaries for deciding which parts of a trajectory deserve reinforcement.

BEACON consistently outperforms GRPO and GiGPO on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld. On long-horizon ALFWorld tasks, it reaches a 92.9% success rate versus GRPO's 53.5%, while effective sample utilization increases from 23.7% to 82.0%. These results indicate that milestone-based feedback can extract substantially more useful training signal from the trajectories agents already generate.
summary.tldr: BEACON credits progress between task milestones, improving long-horizon agent success and effective use of training trajectories.

title: Milestone-Guided Policy Learning for Long-Horizon Language Agents

abstract: Reference-guided video editing takes a source video, a text instruction, and a reference image as inputs, requiring the model to faithfully apply the instructed edits while preserving original motion and unedited content. Existing methods fall into two paradigms, each with inherent limitations: decoupled encoders suffer from modality gaps when processing instructions and visual content independently, while unified vision-language encoders lose fine-grained spatial details by relying solely on final-layer representations. We observe that VLM layers encode complementary information hierarchically—early layers capture localized spatial details essential for precise editing, while deeper layers encode global semantics for instruction comprehension. Building on this insight, we present MiVE (Multiscale Vision-language features for reference-guided video Editing), a framework that repurposes VLMs as multiscale feature extractors. MiVE extracts hierarchical features from Qwen3-VL and integrates them into a unified self-attention Diffusion Transformer, eliminating the modality mismatch inherent in cross-attention designs. Experiments demonstrate that MiVE achieves state-of-the-art performance by ranking highest in human preference, outperforming both academic methods and commercial systems.

paragraphs: Reference-guided video editing combines a source video, a written instruction, and a reference image. The model must apply the requested change while retaining motion and untouched content. Processing language and imagery separately can create a mismatch between their representations, but using only a unified model’s final layer can discard spatial details needed for precise edits.

MiVE draws on the observation that different vision-language model layers provide complementary information. Earlier layers capture localized details, while deeper layers represent broader meaning useful for interpreting instructions. The framework extracts features across layers of Qwen3-VL and integrates them into a diffusion transformer using unified self-attention.

This architecture gives the editor access to both spatial detail and instruction-level meaning, addressing the modality mismatch associated with the cross-attention designs discussed in the paper. In the reported experiments, MiVE achieves the highest human preference ranking and outperforms academic methods and commercial systems. The findings support using a hierarchy of vision-language features for editing tasks that need both precise visual placement and semantic understanding.
summary.tldr: MiVE combines features from multiple vision-language model layers to improve reference-guided video editing and achieves the highest reported human preference ranking.

title: MiVE: Multiscale Vision-language features for reference-guided video Editing

abstract: We identify and analyze a surprising phenomenon of $\textit{Latent}$ Diffusion Models (LDMs) where the final steps of the diffusion can $\textit{degrade}$ sample quality. In contrast to conventional arguments that justify early stopping for numerical stability, this phenomenon is intrinsic to the dimensionality reduction in LDMs. We provide a principled explanation by analyzing the interaction between latent dimension and stopping time. Under a Gaussian framework with linear autoencoders, we characterize the conditions under which early stopping is needed to minimize the distance between generated and target distributions. More precisely, we show that lower-dimensional representations benefit from earlier termination, whereas higher-dimensional latent spaces require later stopping time. We further establish that the latent dimension interplays with other hyperparameters of the problem such as constraints in the parameters of score matching. Crucially, this framework suggests that the reconstruction quality of the autoencoder alone can serve as a proxy to estimate the potential performance of the full LDM. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate these properties, underlining that early stopping can improve generative quality. Together, our results offer a theoretical foundation for understanding how the latent dimension influences the sample quality, and highlight stopping time as a key hyperparameter in LDMs.

paragraphs: Completing every denoising step can sometimes make a latent diffusion model’s samples worse. This paper attributes that phenomenon to the dimensionality reduction used by latent models. It analyzes how the size of the latent representation interacts with the point at which generation stops, providing a reason for early stopping beyond numerical stability.

The theoretical analysis assumes Gaussian distributions and linear autoencoders. Within this framework, the authors characterize conditions where stopping early minimizes the distance between generated and target distributions. Lower-dimensional representations benefit from earlier termination, whereas higher-dimensional latent spaces call for later stopping. The analysis also connects latent dimension with other settings, including constraints on score-matching parameters.

The framework suggests that autoencoder reconstruction quality alone can serve as a proxy for the potential performance of the complete latent diffusion model. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate the analyzed properties and show that early stopping can improve generation quality. The main implication is to treat stopping time and latent dimension as interacting design choices.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian linear-autoencoder analysis explains how latent dimensionality can make early stopping beneficial for diffusion sample quality.

title: Optimal Stopping in Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit high reasoning capacity in medical question-answering, but their tendency to produce hallucinations and outdated knowledge poses critical risks in healthcare fields. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates these issues, existing methods rely on noisy token-level signals and lack the multi-round refinement required for complex reasoning. In this paper, we propose MA-RAG (Multi-Round Agentic RAG), a framework that facilitates test-time scaling for complex medical reasoning by iteratively evolving both external evidence and internal reasoning history within an agentic refinement loop. At each round, the agent transforms semantic conflict among candidate responses into actionable queries to retrieve external evidence, while optimizing history reasoning traces to mitigate long-context degradation. MA-RAG extends the self-consistency principle by leveraging the lack of consistency as a proactive signal for multi-round agentic reasoning and retrieval, and mirrors a boosting mechanism that iteratively minimizes the residual error toward a stable, high-fidelity medical consensus. Extensive evaluations across 7 medical Q&A benchmarks show that MA-RAG consistently surpasses competitive inference-time scaling and RAG baselines, delivering substantial +6.8 points on average accuracy over the backbone model. Our code is available at https://github.com/NJU-RL/MA-RAG.

paragraphs: Medical question answering can be undermined by hallucinated or outdated information, even when a language model has strong reasoning abilities. MA-RAG tackles this through repeated retrieval and reasoning. Its central idea is to use disagreement among candidate responses as a signal identifying what evidence the system should seek next.

At each round, the agent turns semantic conflicts into retrieval queries and gathers external evidence to address them. It also refines the stored reasoning history to reduce degradation from long contexts. Both the evidence and the reasoning record therefore evolve during inference. This extends self-consistency from a way of identifying agreement into a process that actively investigates inconsistency.

The authors compare the iterative refinement to boosting, with successive rounds working on residual errors toward a more stable consensus. Across seven medical question-answering benchmarks, MA-RAG consistently exceeds the tested retrieval and inference-time scaling baselines and improves average accuracy by 6.8 points over its backbone model. The reported gain supports using unresolved disagreements to direct additional reasoning and retrieval effort on these tasks.
summary.tldr: MA-RAG turns disagreement between medical answers into targeted retrieval, improving reasoning through repeated evidence and history refinement.

title: From Conflict to Consensus: Boosting Medical Reasoning via Multi-Round Agentic RAG

abstract: Video understanding requires identifying and reasoning over semantically discriminative visual objects across frames, yet existing object-agnostic solutions struggle to effectively handle substantial object variations over time. To address this, we introduce Chain-of-Glimpse, a search-guided progressive object-grounded reasoning framework that explicitly anchors each reasoning step to specific visual evidence regions, enabling compositional and multi-step decision-making. Formally, Chain-of-Glimpse formulates video reasoning as a step-by-step process that incrementally builds spatially grounded traces around task-relevant visual objects, thereby mitigating over-reliance on saliency-driven cues. Specifically, Chain-of-Glimpse features a search-guided controller, optimized via reinforcement learning with a evidence reward that significantly incentivizes grounding capability, to iteratively ground visual evidence regions and form reliable reasoning trajectories, yielding accurate and interpretable multi-step decisions. Extensive evaluations across two categories of video reasoning benchmarks, including general video reasoning benchmarks such as NExTQA, Video-Holmes, CG-Bench-Reasoning, and VRBench, and grounded video reasoning benchmarks such as NExT-GQA, demonstrate that Chain-of-Glimpse consistently improves performance while exhibiting strong robustness and generalization across diverse video reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Understanding a video often requires following relevant objects as their appearance and situation change across frames. Chain-of-Glimpse addresses this by connecting each reasoning step to a particular visual region. The goal is to build decisions from identifiable evidence, reducing reliance on whatever happens to be visually prominent.

The framework develops its reasoning progressively. A search-guided controller selects evidence regions around objects relevant to the task, building a sequence of spatially grounded steps. Reinforcement learning trains this controller with an evidence reward that encourages grounding. This ties the process of deciding where to look to the process of constructing a multi-step answer.

Evaluations cover both general video reasoning and tasks that explicitly assess grounded reasoning, including NExTQA and NExT-GQA. The authors report consistent performance improvements, robustness, and generalization across the evaluated tasks. Because intermediate steps point to visual evidence, the resulting decisions are also more interpretable. The contribution is therefore a reasoning procedure that makes object selection an explicit, trained part of video understanding.
summary.tldr: Chain-of-Glimpse improves video reasoning by training a controller to build multi-step decisions around explicit visual evidence regions.

title: Chain-of-Glimpse: Search-Guided Progressive Object-Grounded Reasoning for Video Understanding

abstract: Irregular multivariate time series impose a trade-off for long-horizon forecasting: discrete methods can distort temporal structure via re-gridding, while continuous-time models often require sequential solvers prone to drift. To bridge this gap, we present Latent Laplace Diffusion (LLapDiff), a generative framework that models the target as a low-dimensional latent trajectory, enabling horizon-wide generation without step-by-step integration over physical time. We guide the reverse process utilizing a stable modal parameterization motivated by stochastic port-Hamiltonian dynamics, and parameterize its mean evolution in the Laplace domain via learnable complex-conjugate poles, enabling direct evaluation over irregular timestamps. We also link continuous dynamics to irregular observations through renewal-averaging analysis, which maps sampling gaps to effective event-domain poles and motivates a gap-aware history summarizer. Extensive experiments show that LLapDiff improves over baselines in long-horizon forecasting, and its continuous-time generative nature supports missing-value imputation by querying the same model at historical timestamps. Code is available at https://github.com/pixelhero98/LLapDiffusion.

paragraphs: Forecasting several signals observed at irregular times creates a difficult trade-off. Converting observations onto a regular grid can distort their timing, while continuous-time approaches often rely on sequential solvers that can drift. LLapDiff addresses this by representing the forecast as a low-dimensional latent trajectory generated across the entire prediction horizon.

Its reverse generative process uses a stable modal parameterization motivated by stochastic port-Hamiltonian dynamics. Mean evolution is represented in the Laplace domain with learnable complex-conjugate poles, allowing evaluation directly at irregular timestamps. This avoids step-by-step integration over physical time. The paper also analyzes how observation gaps affect the dynamics seen at sampling events, motivating a history summarizer that accounts for those gaps.

Experiments report improved long-horizon forecasts over baselines. Because the model represents a continuous-time trajectory, it can also fill missing values by being queried at historical timestamps. The contribution links horizon-wide generation with explicit treatment of irregular sampling, allowing forecasting and historical imputation to use the same underlying model.
summary.tldr: LLapDiff generates continuous latent trajectories for irregular time series, improving long-horizon forecasts and supporting imputation without sequential physical-time integration.

title: Latent Laplace Diffusion for Irregular Multivariate Time Series

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) learns representations from massive unlabeled data, yet the resulting models typically operate as black boxes, necessitating domain-specific explanations. We introduce KREPES, a unified framework to analytically interpret the learned representations of SSL objectives, including SimCLR, BYOL, and VICReg. By bridging empirical neural tangent kernel approximations of neural networks with the Representer Theorem for kernels, we express the learned latent space directly via "Representer Landmarks", which are the representations of influential unlabeled training examples. We introduce novel metrics, "Sample-Specific Influence Score", "Concept-Conditioned Influence Score" and "Feature Alignment Gap", to quantify the transparency of the learned representations. KREPES enables direct audit of the latent space without supervision, for example, revealing an algorithmic bias in the Adult-1M dataset where SSL uses demographic proxies for income. Finally, to ensure scalability to benchmarks with 1M+ samples (ImageNet-1K, Adult-1M), KREPES introduces a novel Nyström approximation-based analytical inference framework for SSL objectives.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning creates useful representations from unlabeled data, but understanding what shapes those representations remains difficult. KREPES offers an analytical framework for interpreting objectives including SimCLR, BYOL, and VICReg. It relates the learned latent space to influential training examples, making those examples a basis for examining model behavior.

The framework connects empirical neural tangent kernel approximations with the kernel Representer Theorem. This produces Representer Landmarks: representations of influential unlabeled examples through which the learned space can be expressed. The authors also introduce measures of sample-specific influence, concept-conditioned influence, and feature alignment gaps to quantify aspects of representation transparency.

KREPES supports direct latent-space auditing without supervision. In Adult-1M, the analysis reveals reliance on demographic proxies for income, showing how an explanation can expose a substantive algorithmic bias. A Nyström approximation-based inference framework extends the approach to benchmarks with over a million samples, including ImageNet-1K and Adult-1M. The contribution brings example-based interpretation, quantitative auditing, and large-dataset scalability into a single framework for self-supervised representations.
summary.tldr: KREPES explains self-supervised representations through influential unlabeled examples and scales analytical auditing to million-sample datasets.

title: Interpretable Self-Supervised Learning via Representer Landmarks and Nyström Approximation

abstract: We study the problem of monitoring model performance in dynamic environments where labeled data are limited. To this end, we propose prediction-powered risk monitoring (PPRM), a semi-supervised risk-monitoring approach based on prediction-powered inference (PPI). PPRM constructs anytime-valid lower bounds on the running risk by combining synthetic labels with a small set of true labels. Harmful shifts are detected via a threshold-based comparison with an upper bound on the nominal risk, satisfying assumption-free finite-sample guarantees on the type-I error. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PPRM through extensive experiments on image classification, large language model (LLM), and telecommunications monitoring tasks.

To this end, we propose prediction-powered risk monitoring (PPRM), a semi-supervised risk-monitoring approach based on prediction-powered inference (PPI). PPRM constructs anytime-valid lower bounds on the running risk by combining synthetic labels with a small set of true labels. Harmful shifts are detected via a threshold-based comparison with an upper bound on the nominal risk, satisfying assumption-free finite-sample guarantees on the type-I error. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PPRM through extensive experiments on image classification, large language model (LLM), and telecommunications monitoring tasks.

paragraphs: A deployed model’s performance can deteriorate as its operating environment changes, but obtaining true labels for ongoing monitoring may be difficult. Prediction-powered risk monitoring addresses this setting by combining synthetic labels with a small amount of genuinely labeled data. Its purpose is to detect changes that harm performance, using limited supervision to support statistical monitoring.

The method builds on prediction-powered inference to construct lower bounds on running risk. These bounds are anytime-valid, so their validity supports monitoring as observations accumulate. A harmful-shift alarm comes from a threshold-based comparison between the running-risk lower bound and an upper bound on nominal risk, the reference level of model performance.

The paper establishes assumption-free, finite-sample guarantees on type-I error, controlling false alarms in this monitoring procedure. Experiments on image classification, language-model tasks, and telecommunications monitoring demonstrate its effectiveness. The combination matters because synthetic labels extend the available monitoring information, while true labels and statistical bounds support a controlled decision about whether observed performance has become harmful.
summary.tldr: PPRM combines synthetic and scarce true labels to detect harmful performance shifts with anytime-valid risk bounds and finite-sample false-alarm guarantees.

title: Prediction-Powered Risk Monitoring of Deployed Models for Detecting Harmful Distribution Shifts

abstract: Human spatial understanding arises from jointly perceiving geometry and semantics, enabling consistent object identification and localization across viewpoints and time. Current video segmentation models depend on explicit object appearance memory banks for instance tracking, yet they remain vulnerable to large viewpoint changes and long-term occlusions. Leveraging the spatial consistency afforded by modern feed-forward 3D reconstruction models, we propose the Geometry Grounded Tracking Anything Model (G$^2$TAM), a unified framework for promptable instance tracking in 3D using only unordered RGB images or videos. G$^2$TAM employs spatially aligned geometric representations as implicit memory, ensuring stable instance identity and localization across frames and views. At its core is a cross-modal spatial encoder that integrates visual and textual prompts into a shared geometric space, enabling end-to-end spatial reconstruction and instance-consistent mask prediction. To support training and evaluation, we construct InsTrack, a large-scale dataset with a dedicated validation split for benchmarking. Extensive experiments show that G$^2$TAM delivers strong cross-view consistency, promptable instance spatial tracking, video object segmentation, and spatial reconstruction, establishing a foundation for interactive, geometry-grounded spatial reasoning.

paragraphs: Tracking an object across images becomes difficult when viewpoints change substantially or the object disappears behind an obstruction. Existing video segmentation models often rely on stored appearance information. G²TAM instead uses the spatial consistency available from feed-forward 3D reconstruction, treating aligned geometry as an implicit memory for object identity and location.

The framework accepts unordered RGB images or video and supports prompts that specify the instance to track. Its cross-modal spatial encoder brings visual and textual prompts into a shared geometric space. This links spatial reconstruction with instance-consistent mask prediction in an end-to-end system, allowing the same geometric representation to support both locating an object and identifying its image regions.

The authors also introduce InsTrack, a large-scale dataset with a dedicated validation split for training and benchmarking. Experiments report strong cross-view consistency, promptable spatial tracking, video object segmentation, and reconstruction. The contribution is a unified approach that connects object semantics to geometry across views and time, providing a foundation for interactive spatial reasoning grounded in reconstructed scene structure.
summary.tldr: G²TAM uses shared 3D geometry as implicit memory to track prompted objects consistently across images, viewpoints, and video.

title: G$^2$TAM: Geometry Grounded Track Anything Model
Learning to Program by Examining and Modifying Cases
Characterizing Model Erros and Differences

abstract: In the information regularization framework by Corduneanu and Jaakkola (2005), the distributions of labels are propagated on a hypergraph for semi-supervised learning. The learning is efficiently done by a BlahutArimoto-like two step algorithm, but, unfortunately, one of the steps cannot be solved in a closed form. In this paper, we propose a dual version of information regularization, which is considered as more natural in terms of information geometry. Our learning algorithm has two steps, each of which can be solved in a closed form. Also it can be naturally applied to exponential family distributions such as Gaussians. In experiments, our algorithm is applied to protein classification based on a metabolic network and known functional categories.

The learning is efficiently done by a BlahutArimoto-like two step algorithm, but, unfortunately, one of the steps cannot be solved in a closed form. In this paper, we propose a dual version of information regularization, which is considered as more natural in terms of information geometry. Our learning algorithm has two steps, each of which can be solved in a closed form. Also it can be naturally applied to exponential family distributions such as Gaussians. paragraphs: Information regularization can support semi-supervised learning by propagating label distributions across a hypergraph. In the existing framework discussed here, learning alternates between two steps in an efficient procedure resembling the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm. One of those steps, however, lacks a closed-form solution. This paper proposes a dual formulation that changes that computational property.

The new learning algorithm also has two steps, but both admit closed-form solutions. This gives each update an explicit solution within the alternating procedure. The authors additionally argue that the dual formulation is more natural from an information-geometric perspective, connecting the computational change with the geometry used to describe distributions.

The approach extends naturally to exponential-family distributions, including Gaussians, broadening the kinds of distributions it can propagate. Experiments apply it to protein classification using a metabolic network and known functional categories. The abstract presents that application as a demonstration of the method, while the central methodological result is the dual formulation with two closed-form learning steps.
summary.tldr: Dual information regularization propagates distributions on hypergraphs using two closed-form updates and extends naturally to exponential families.

title: Propagating distributions on a hypergraph by dual information regularization
Dynamic topic models

abstract: Uncertainty arises in reinforcement learning from various sources, and therefore it is necessary to consider statistics based on several roll-outs for evaluating behavioral policies. We add an adaptive uncertainty handling based on Hoeffding and empirical Bernstein races to the CMA-ES, a variable metric evolution strategy proposed for direct policy search. The uncertainty handling adjusts individually the number of episodes considered for the evaluation of a policy. The performance estimation is kept just accurate enough for a sufficiently good ranking of candidate policies, which is in turn sufficient for the CMA-ES to find better solutions. This increases the learning speed as well as the robustness of the algorithm.

We add an adaptive uncertainty handling based on Hoeffding and empirical Bernstein races to the CMA-ES, a variable metric evolution strategy proposed for direct policy search. The uncertainty handling adjusts individually the number of episodes considered for the evaluation of a policy. paragraphs: Evaluating a behavioral policy in reinforcement learning involves uncertainty, so a single rollout is not enough to characterize its performance reliably. Repeating every candidate policy for the same number of episodes, however, does not account for differences in how much evidence each candidate needs. This paper introduces adaptive uncertainty handling for evolutionary direct policy search.

The method adds Hoeffding and empirical Bernstein races to CMA-ES, an evolution strategy used to search for policies. These procedures adjust the number of evaluation episodes separately for each policy. Their objective is to make performance estimates accurate enough to establish a sufficiently good ranking of candidates, which is what the search procedure needs to find better solutions.

The abstract reports improvements in both learning speed and robustness. The key idea is to align evaluation effort with the decision being made: selecting among candidate policies. Accurate ranking can be sufficient for productive search, so the method focuses repeated evaluation on obtaining the uncertainty reduction needed for that ranking.
summary.tldr: Adaptive statistical races allocate policy-evaluation episodes to obtain useful candidate rankings, improving CMA-ES learning speed and robustness.

title: Hoeffding and Bernstein races for selecting policies in evolutionary direct policy search

abstract: We address the problem of minimizing a convex function over the space of large matrices with low rank. While this optimization problem is hard in general, we propose an efficient greedy algorithm and derive its formal approximation guarantees. Each iteration of the algorithm involves (approximately) finding the left and right singular vectors corresponding to the largest singular value of a certain matrix, which can be calculated in linear time. This leads to an algorithm which can scale to large matrices arising in several applications such as matrix completion for collaborative filtering and robust low rank matrix approximation.
originalAbstract: We address the problem of minimizing a convex function over the space of large matrices with low rank. While this optimization problem is hard in general, we propose an efficient greedy algorithm and derive its formal approximation guarantees. Each iteration of the algorithm involves (approximately) finding the left and right singular vectors corresponding to the largest singular value of a certain matrix, which can be calculated in linear time. This leads to an algorithm which can scale to large matrices arising in several applications such as matrix completion for collaborative filtering and robust low rank matrix approximation.

paragraphs: This paper studies minimizing a convex objective over large matrices while requiring the solution to have low rank. Low rank restricts the complexity of the matrix representation, but it also makes the optimization problem difficult in general. A convex objective alone does not remove the difficulty introduced by that constraint.

The authors propose an efficient greedy algorithm and establish formal approximation guarantees. Each iteration approximately finds the left and right singular vectors associated with the largest singular value of a particular matrix. The abstract states that this calculation can be performed in linear time, providing the computational basis for handling large matrices.

The approach is relevant to applications including matrix completion for collaborative filtering and robust low-rank matrix approximation. Its significance lies in pairing a scalable iterative calculation with guarantees on approximation quality. The result offers a principled way to work with large low-rank matrix problems while retaining the paper's distinction between efficient approximation and the general difficulty of the constrained optimization task.
summary.tldr: A greedy algorithm uses approximate leading singular vectors to scale low-rank matrix optimization while providing approximation guarantees.

title: Large-Scale Convex Minimization with a Low-Rank Constraint

abstract: We consider the problem of parameter estimation using weakly supervised datasets, where a training sample consists of the input and a partially specified annotation (called the output). In addition, the missing information in the annotation is modeled using latent variables. Traditional methods, such as expectation-maximization, overburden a single distribution with two separate tasks: (i) modeling the uncertainty in the latent variables during training; and (ii) making accurate predictions for the output and the latent variables during testing. We propose a novel framework that separates the demands of the two tasks using two distributions: (i) a conditional distribution to model the uncertainty of the latent variables for a given input-output pair; and (ii) a delta distribution to predict the output and the latent variables for a given input. During learning, we encourage agreement between the two distributions by minimizing a loss-based dissimilarity coefficient. Our approach generalizes latent SVM in two important ways: (i) it models the uncertainty over latent variables instead of relying on a pointwise estimate; and (ii) it allows the use of loss functions that depend on latent variables, which greatly increases its applicability. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on two challenging problems—object detection and action detection—using publicly available datasets.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised learning uses annotations that leave some information unspecified. The paper represents that missing information with latent variables and examines how to learn while accounting for their uncertainty. Its starting point is that expressing uncertainty during training and making a definite prediction at test time place different demands on a model.

The proposed framework assigns these roles to two distributions. A conditional distribution represents uncertainty over latent variables for a known input and partial annotation. A delta distribution represents a single prediction of both the output and latent variables from an input. Training encourages these distributions to agree by minimizing a dissimilarity measure based on the chosen loss.

The framework extends latent support vector machines by retaining uncertainty over hidden variables and allowing losses that depend on those variables. These changes broaden how incomplete annotations and prediction errors can be modeled together. Evaluations on object detection and action detection using public datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to connect uncertain training information with definite predictions through an explicit loss-based agreement objective.
summary.tldr: Two coordinated distributions separate latent-variable uncertainty during training from definite predictions, extending latent SVM learning.

title: Modeling Latent Variable Uncertainty for Loss-based Learning
